chem-1-1: chem-1-1-1
Which of the following fuels is renewable?
Biogas produced by anaerobic digestion of food waste
Natural gas from Bass Strait
Brown coal from the Latrobe Valley
Petrodiesel
Biogas comes from biomass that can be replaced within a human lifetime; the others are fossil fuels formed over millions of years.
chem-1-1-2
Which equation correctly represents the fermentation of glucose by yeast?
C₆H₁₂O₆(aq) + 6O₂(g) → 6CO₂(g) + 6H₂O(l)
C₆H₁₂O₆(aq) → 2C₂H₅OH(aq) + 2CO₂(g)
C₆H₁₂O₆(aq) → 3C₂H₅OH(aq)
C₆H₁₂O₆(aq) → 2C₂H₅OH(aq) + 2O₂(g)
Anaerobic fermentation converts glucose into ethanol and carbon dioxide; the second equation is cellular respiration and the others are unbalanced.
chem-1-1-3
Biodiesel is produced industrially by
fermenting glucose with yeast under anaerobic conditions
fractional distillation of crude oil
reacting a triglyceride with methanol in the presence of a strong base catalyst
anaerobic digestion of animal manure
Transesterification of plant oils or animal fats with methanol, catalysed by KOH or NaOH, produces fatty acid methyl esters (biodiesel).
chem-1-1-4
Explain why bioethanol produced from sugar cane is not completely carbon neutral in practice.

Fossil fuels are burnt to power farm machinery, make fertilisers, transport the crop and heat the distillation process, so the total CO₂ released exceeds the CO₂ absorbed by the crop during photosynthesis.
Award marks for identifying at least one fossil-fuel energy input in the production chain and linking it to net CO₂ emissions.
chem-1-1-5
Which by-product is formed alongside biodiesel during transesterification of a triglyceride?
Ethanol
Carbon dioxide
Methane
Glycerol
Each triglyceride releases its glycerol backbone (propane-1,2,3-triol) as the fatty acid chains are converted into methyl esters.
chem-1-1-6
The main combustible component of biogas is
methane
hydrogen
ethanol
carbon monoxide
Biogas is typically 50–70% methane, with most of the remainder being carbon dioxide.
chem-1-1-7
Biodiesel is more viscous than petrodiesel mainly because biodiesel molecules
form hydrogen bonds with each other through O–H groups
are generally larger and contain polar ester groups, giving stronger intermolecular forces
contain ionic bonds
have a lower molar mass
Long-chain fatty acid methyl esters have strong dispersion forces plus dipole–dipole attractions from the ester group; esters have no O–H so cannot hydrogen bond to each other.
chem-1-1-8
Name the two products formed when a triglyceride reacts with methanol in the presence of KOH, and state which one is used as the fuel.
Fatty acid methyl esters (biodiesel) and glycerol; the methyl esters are the biodiesel fuel.
Glycerol is a by-product; both products must be named.
chem-1-1-9
Biodiesel absorbs water from the atmosphere more readily than petrodiesel because
it contains O–H groups that hydrogen bond with each other
its molecules are non-polar alkanes
the oxygen atoms in its ester groups can form hydrogen bonds with water molecules
it has a lower boiling point
The lone pairs on ester oxygen atoms accept hydrogen bonds from water, making biodiesel hygroscopic; petrodiesel alkanes cannot do this.
Bioethanol is sometimes described as 'carbon neutral' because
burning ethanol produces no carbon dioxide
ethanol contains no carbon atoms
fermentation absorbs carbon dioxide from the air
the CO₂ released when it burns is approximately equal to the CO₂ absorbed by the crop during photosynthesis
In the idealised model, CO₂ taken up by photosynthesis balances the CO₂ released in fermentation and combustion.
Which statement about coal is correct?
It formed from plant material compressed and heated over millions of years
It is a renewable fuel because plants are still growing
It is mainly composed of methane
It forms from the fermentation of sugars
Coal is a fossil fuel formed from ancient plant matter under heat and pressure over geological time, so it is non-renewable.
Explain why biodiesel is more hygroscopic than petrodiesel.

Biodiesel contains ester functional groups whose oxygen atoms can accept hydrogen bonds from water molecules, so it attracts and absorbs water. Petrodiesel consists of non-polar hydrocarbons that cannot hydrogen bond with water.
Link the ester oxygen atoms to hydrogen bonding with water; mention that alkanes cannot.
Which of the following is a fossil fuel?
Bioethanol
Liquefied petroleum gas (LPG)
Biodiesel
Biogas
LPG (mainly propane and butane) is obtained from natural gas processing and crude oil refining, both fossil sources.
A Victorian company wants to produce bioethanol without competing with food production. Which feedstock is most suitable?
Wheat grain
Sugar cane juice
Wheat straw left after harvest
Corn grain
Crop residues like straw are lignocellulosic waste not used as human food, so using them avoids the food-versus-fuel conflict.
Compared with petrodiesel, biodiesel typically has
a higher energy content per gram
no oxygen atoms in its molecules
a lower viscosity
a lower energy content per gram
Biodiesel molecules are already partly oxidised (they contain oxygen), so they release less energy per gram (about 37–38 kJ g⁻¹ compared with about 45 kJ g⁻¹).
Give one advantage and one disadvantage of using E10 (10% ethanol) instead of regular unleaded petrol.

Advantage: ethanol is renewable and can lower net greenhouse emissions (it also burns more cleanly). Disadvantage: ethanol releases less energy per gram than petrol, so fuel consumption increases (or it absorbs water, or crops compete with food).
Any valid advantage and any valid disadvantage, each clearly explained.
The best reason crude-oil-derived fuels are classified as non-renewable is that
they form over millions of years, far more slowly than they are consumed
they release carbon dioxide when burnt
they are liquids at room temperature
they contain sulfur impurities
Renewability depends on the rate of replenishment; crude oil cannot be replaced within a human timescale.
Which set of conditions is used to produce ethanol by fermentation?
Yeast, plentiful oxygen, 100 °C
Yeast, anaerobic conditions, about 30–40 °C
Nickel catalyst, high pressure, 200 °C
Concentrated sulfuric acid, 300 °C
Yeast enzymes ferment sugars in the absence of oxygen; temperatures that are too high denature the enzymes.
Ethanol is separated from the fermentation mixture by
filtration
transesterification
fractional distillation
electrolysis
Ethanol (b.p. 78 °C) and water (b.p. 100 °C) are miscible liquids with different boiling points, so they are separated by fractional distillation.
Distinguish between a renewable and a non-renewable fuel, using one Australian example of each.

A renewable fuel can be replaced by natural processes within a relatively short (human) timescale, e.g. biogas from a Gippsland dairy farm. A non-renewable fuel is used faster than it can be replaced, taking millions of years to form, e.g. Latrobe Valley brown coal.
The key idea is the rate of replenishment compared with the rate of use.
Which statement about biogas is correct?
It is produced by aerobic decomposition of waste
It consists mainly of hydrogen gas
It is classified as a fossil fuel
It contains a significant proportion of carbon dioxide, which lowers its energy content per kilogram compared with pure methane
Non-combustible CO₂ makes up much of biogas, diluting the methane and reducing the energy released per kilogram of gas.
In complete transesterification, one triglyceride molecule reacts with how many methanol molecules?
Each of the three ester linkages reacts with one methanol molecule, forming three methyl ester molecules and one glycerol molecule.
Petrodiesel is composed mainly of
fatty acid methyl esters
hydrocarbons such as long-chain alkanes
alcohols
carbohydrates
Petrodiesel is a crude oil fraction made up largely of alkanes of about C₁₄–C₂₀; fatty acid methyl esters are biodiesel.
A dairy farm in northern Victoria captures gas from its manure ponds to run a generator. Explain why this gas is classified as a renewable fuel.

The gas is biogas, mainly methane, produced by anaerobic bacteria digesting manure. The manure is continuously replaced by the cows' feed, which is regrown each season, so the fuel source is replenished within a short timescale.
Must identify biomass origin and rapid replenishment.
Explain, in terms of intermolecular forces, why ethanol mixes completely with water but octane does not.

Ethanol has a polar O–H group that forms hydrogen bonds with water molecules, so it is miscible. Octane is non-polar and has only dispersion forces, which cannot compete with the hydrogen bonding between water molecules, so it does not dissolve.
Refer to hydrogen bonding for ethanol and dispersion forces only for octane.
chem34a1-ffb-1
Which statement best explains why bioethanol is classified as a renewable fuel while petrol is not?
Bioethanol releases no carbon dioxide when it burns.
Bioethanol has a higher energy content per gram than petrol.
The plant material used to make bioethanol can be regrown on a human timescale, whereas petrol comes from crude oil formed over millions of years.
Bioethanol is produced by fractional distillation, which uses less energy than refining.

A renewable resource is replenished at a rate comparable to its use; crops regrow within a season or a few years. Bioethanol still releases CO₂ when it burns, and its energy content per gram (about 29.6 kJ g⁻¹) is lower than that of petrol.
chem34a1-ffb-2
Biodiesel is produced from vegetable oils by a reaction with methanol in the presence of a catalyst such as KOH. This reaction is called
fermentation.
transesterification.
anaerobic digestion.
cracking.

Triglycerides react with methanol to form fatty acid methyl esters (biodiesel) and glycerol; swapping the alcohol part of an ester is transesterification. Fermentation produces ethanol and anaerobic digestion produces biogas.
chem34a1-ffb-3
A dairy farm in Gippsland collects cow manure in a sealed tank where bacteria break it down without oxygen. The main combustible product is
methane.
ethanol.
hydrogen.
carbon monoxide.
Anaerobic digestion of organic waste produces biogas, which is mostly methane (with CO₂). Ethanol comes from yeast fermentation of sugars, not from digestion of manure.
chem34a1-ffb-4
Compared with petrodiesel of similar chain length, biodiesel tends to be more viscous and to gel at higher temperatures. The best explanation is that biodiesel molecules
are non-polar and form only weak dispersion forces.
contain ester groups that add dipole–dipole attractions between molecules.
form hydrogen bonds with each other through O–H groups.
are much smaller than petrodiesel molecules.

The ester functional group is polar, so biodiesel molecules experience dipole–dipole attractions in addition to dispersion forces, which raises viscosity and cloud point. Esters have no O–H group, so they cannot hydrogen bond with each other.
chem34a1-ffb-5
Which of the following is a disadvantage of bioethanol compared with petrol as a transport fuel?
Bioethanol produces more soot when it burns.
Bioethanol cannot be blended with petrol.
Bioethanol is non-renewable.
Bioethanol absorbs water from the air, which can cause corrosion and phase separation in fuel tanks.

Ethanol is hygroscopic because its hydroxyl group hydrogen bonds with water, which can lead to corrosion and separation in blends. Ethanol actually burns more cleanly than petrol and is commonly blended with it as E10.
chem34a1-ffb-6
Write a balanced equation, including states, for the production of ethanol by the fermentation of glucose, and name the organism that catalyses it. (2 marks)
C₆H₁₂O₆(aq) → 2C₂H₅OH(aq) + 2CO₂(g); the reaction is catalysed by enzymes in yeast (anaerobic conditions).
chem34a1-ffb-7
Some people describe biofuels as 'carbon neutral'. Explain the reasoning behind this claim and give one reason why it is not entirely accurate. (3 marks)

The CO₂ released when a biofuel burns was absorbed from the atmosphere by the plants during photosynthesis, so in theory there is no net increase in atmospheric CO₂; however, fossil fuels are used in farming, fertiliser production, harvesting, transport and processing (e.g. distillation), so there is a net release of CO₂; land clearing for crops can also release CO₂.
chem34a1-ffb-8
Coal, crude oil and natural gas are fossil fuels. Describe how they formed and explain why this makes them non-renewable. (2 marks)

They formed from the remains of ancient plants and marine organisms buried and subjected to heat and pressure over millions of years; they are used far faster than they are formed, so supplies cannot be replenished on a human timescale.
chem-1-1-c1
Biodiesel is often described as carbon neutral. The best reason this is not strictly true is that:
Burning biodiesel releases more CO₂ than the crop absorbed from the air while it was growing
Biodiesel releases carbon that was absorbed millions of years ago, just as fossil fuels do
Biodiesel contains no carbon, so its emissions cannot be balanced by growing new plants
Fossil fuels are used to grow, harvest and transport the crop and to make the methanol used to process it
The CO₂ released on combustion was absorbed by the crop, but energy from fossil fuels is used along the production chain, so there is a net release.
chem-1-2: Which equation represents the complete combustion of methane?
Complete combustion in excess oxygen produces only carbon dioxide and water; the other equations show incomplete combustion or impossible products.
In the balanced equation for the complete combustion of octane, 2C₈H₁₈ + xO₂ → 16CO₂ + 18H₂O, the value of x is
Oxygen atoms on the right: 16 × 2 + 18 × 1 = 50, so 25 O₂ molecules are needed.
Incomplete combustion of a hydrocarbon fuel in a poorly ventilated room is most likely to produce
With limited oxygen, carbon is only partly oxidised, forming CO and/or elemental carbon (soot) along with water.
Write a balanced thermochemical equation, including states at SLC, for the complete combustion of ethanol. The molar heat of combustion of ethanol is 1364 kJ mol⁻¹.
Check balancing (O: 1 + 6 = 4 + 3), states, the negative sign and units.
Carbon monoxide from a faulty gas heater is dangerous mainly because it
is a strong acid that burns the lungs
is a potent greenhouse gas that warms the room
reacts with water in the body to form methane
binds strongly to haemoglobin, reducing oxygen transport in the blood
CO binds to haemoglobin far more strongly than O₂, starving tissues of oxygen; it is also colourless and odourless.
Given CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l), ΔH = −890 kJ mol⁻¹, what is ΔH for 2CH₄(g) + 4O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g) + 4H₂O(l)?
Doubling all coefficients doubles the enthalpy change: 2 × (−890) = −1780 kJ mol⁻¹.
Given CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l), ΔH = −890 kJ mol⁻¹, what is ΔH for CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l) → CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g)?
Reversing a reaction reverses the sign of ΔH but keeps the magnitude.
The molar heat of combustion of hydrogen is 286 kJ mol⁻¹. Write the thermochemical equation for the combustion of 2 mol of hydrogen gas at SLC.
ΔH must be doubled to match the 2 mol of H₂ in the equation.
For an exothermic reaction, which statement is correct?
The products have higher enthalpy than the reactants and ΔH is positive
The products have lower enthalpy than the reactants and ΔH is positive
The products have lower enthalpy than the reactants and ΔH is negative
The reactants and products have equal enthalpy
Energy is released to the surroundings, so H(products) < H(reactants) and ΔH = H(products) − H(reactants) < 0.
Which of the following processes is endothermic?
Photosynthesis absorbs light energy to build glucose from CO₂ and water; the others release energy.
The molar heat of combustion of butane is 2876 kJ mol⁻¹. Which thermochemical equation is correct?
The equation shows 2 mol of butane, so ΔH = 2 × (−2876) = −5752 kJ mol⁻¹; combustion is exothermic.
Explain why ΔH for an exothermic reaction is given a negative sign.
ΔH = H(products) − H(reactants). In an exothermic reaction energy is released to the surroundings, so the products have less enthalpy than the reactants and ΔH is negative.
Refer to the definition of ΔH and energy released to the surroundings.
For an exothermic reaction, the activation energy of the reverse reaction is
less than the activation energy of the forward reaction
greater than the activation energy of the forward reaction
equal to the activation energy of the forward reaction
equal to ΔH of the forward reaction
Ea(reverse) = Ea(forward) + |ΔH|, so for an exothermic reaction the reverse barrier is larger.
A reaction has a forward activation energy of 120 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔH = −80 kJ mol⁻¹. The activation energy of the reverse reaction is
A reaction has a forward activation energy of 50 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔH = +30 kJ mol⁻¹. The activation energy of the reverse reaction is
Given C₃H₈(g) + 5O₂(g) → 3CO₂(g) + 4H₂O(l), ΔH = −2220 kJ mol⁻¹, determine ΔH for 6CO₂(g) + 8H₂O(l) → 2C₃H₈(g) + 10O₂(g).
The reaction is reversed (sign changes) and doubled: −(2 × −2220) = +4440 kJ mol⁻¹.
The enthalpy change for the combustion of methane is more negative when the water product is liquid rather than gaseous because
condensing water vapour to liquid releases additional energy
liquid water has more enthalpy than water vapour
more oxygen is consumed when liquid water forms
gaseous water cannot be formed by combustion
H₂O(g) → H₂O(l) is exothermic, so forming liquid water releases extra energy, making ΔH more negative.
Which statement best describes the energy changes during the combustion of a fuel?
The energy absorbed breaking bonds is greater than the energy released forming bonds
The energy absorbed breaking bonds in the reactants is less than the energy released forming bonds in the products
Bond breaking releases energy and bond forming absorbs energy
No bonds are broken; energy comes only from forming new bonds
Bond breaking is endothermic and bond forming is exothermic; combustion is exothermic overall because more energy is released than absorbed.
Propane burns according to C₃H₈(g) + 5O₂(g) → 3CO₂(g) + 4H₂O(l). How many moles of oxygen are needed to completely burn 2.0 mol of propane?
The mole ratio O₂ : C₃H₈ is 5 : 1, so 2.0 × 5 = 10 mol of O₂.
A gas heater in a Ballarat house is operating with a blocked air vent. Explain what type of combustion is likely to occur and name the possible products.
With limited oxygen, incomplete combustion occurs. Products include carbon monoxide, carbon (soot) and water, along with less carbon dioxide; less energy is released per mole of fuel.
Must name incomplete combustion and CO and/or soot as products.
What mass of carbon dioxide is produced by the complete combustion of 1.00 mol of propane, C₃H₈?
1 mol C₃H₈ produces 3 mol CO₂; 3 × 44.0 = 132 g.
What volume of CO₂, measured at SLC (25 °C, 100 kPa, molar volume 24.8 L mol⁻¹), is produced by the complete combustion of 0.500 mol of butane, C₄H₁₀?
0.500 mol C₄H₁₀ produces 4 × 0.500 = 2.00 mol CO₂; 2.00 × 24.8 = 49.6 L.
Which balanced equation represents the incomplete combustion of methane to form carbon monoxide?
Checking atoms: 2 C, 8 H and 6 O on each side; each of the other equations has unequal numbers of oxygen atoms.
Given CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l), ΔH = −890 kJ mol⁻¹ and H₂O(l) → H₂O(g), ΔH = +44 kJ mol⁻¹, calculate ΔH for the combustion of methane when water is produced as a gas.
Two moles of water must be vaporised, absorbing 88 kJ, so less energy is released overall.
Balance the equation for the complete combustion of pentane, C₅H₁₂, and state the mole ratio of CO₂ produced to pentane consumed.
C₅H₁₂(l) + 8O₂(g) → 5CO₂(g) + 6H₂O(l); the mole ratio CO₂ : C₅H₁₂ is 5 : 1.
Check: O atoms on the right = 10 + 6 = 16 = 8 O₂.
Which equation correctly represents the complete combustion of propane at SLC?
Complete combustion forms CO₂ and, at SLC, liquid water; combustion is exothermic so ΔH is negative. Doubling the coefficients would require ΔH to double to −4440 kJ mol⁻¹.
For the reaction 2C₈H₁₈(l) + 25O₂(g) → 16CO₂(g) + 18H₂O(l) ΔH = −10 928 kJ mol⁻¹, the enthalpy change when 1.00 mol of octane burns completely is
The ΔH value applies to the mole amounts in the equation as written (2 mol octane), so 1 mol releases half: −10 928 ÷ 2 = −5464 kJ.
A gas heater in a poorly ventilated room burns methane with a limited supply of oxygen. Compared with complete combustion, incomplete combustion
releases more energy per mole of methane and produces only CO₂.
releases less energy per mole of methane and can produce carbon monoxide and soot.
releases the same energy but produces hydrogen gas.
is endothermic because oxygen must be absorbed.
In incomplete combustion carbon is only partially oxidised to CO or C, so less energy is released per mole of fuel, and toxic CO and soot are produced.
Given H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → H₂O(l) ΔH = −286 kJ mol⁻¹, what is ΔH for 2H₂O(l) → 2H₂(g) + O₂(g)?
Reversing the equation changes the sign (+286) and doubling the coefficients doubles the value: +572 kJ mol⁻¹.
Which balanced equation correctly shows the incomplete combustion of ethanol producing carbon monoxide?
Products contain 2 + 3 = 5 O atoms; ethanol supplies 1, so 4 O atoms (2 O₂) are needed. Option D is not balanced for oxygen (7 O atoms on the right).
Write a balanced thermochemical equation, including states, for the complete combustion of butane at SLC. ΔcH(butane) = −2874 kJ mol⁻¹. (2 marks)

2C₄H₁₀(g) + 13O₂(g) → 8CO₂(g) + 10H₂O(l) ΔH = −5748 kJ mol⁻¹ (or C₄H₁₀(g) + 13/2 O₂(g) → 4CO₂(g) + 5H₂O(l) ΔH = −2874 kJ mol⁻¹); correct formulas, balancing and states; ΔH sign and value consistent with the coefficients.
Methanol (CH₃OH) burns with ΔcH = −726 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate the energy released when 80.0 g of methanol burns completely. (2 marks)
n(CH₃OH) = 80.0 ÷ 32.0 = 2.50 mol; energy = 2.50 × 726 = 1815 kJ ≈ 1.82 × 10³ kJ released.

Explain why the heat of combustion values in the VCAA data book are quoted with water in the liquid state, and predict how the magnitude of ΔH would change if the water product were gaseous. (2 marks)

At SLC (25 °C, 100 kPa) water is a liquid, so the standard value refers to liquid water; if water were formed as a gas, less energy would be released because energy is absorbed when water vaporises, so |ΔH| would be smaller (less negative).
Octane burns in a limited supply of oxygen to form carbon monoxide and water only. In the balanced equation with the smallest whole-number coefficients, the coefficient of O₂ is:
2C₈H₁₈(l) + 17O₂(g) → 16CO(g) + 18H₂O(l). Oxygen atoms: 16 + 18 = 34, so 17 O₂. (Complete combustion needs 25.)
chem-1-3: Methane has ΔcH = −890 kJ mol⁻¹ (M = 16.0 g mol⁻¹). How much energy is released by the complete combustion of 32.0 g of methane?
Ethanol has a molar heat of combustion of 1364 kJ mol⁻¹ and M = 46.0 g mol⁻¹. Its heat of combustion per gram is
Octane has ΔcH = −5464 kJ mol⁻¹ (M = 114.0 g mol⁻¹). How much energy is released by burning 1.00 kg of octane?
Calculate the heat of combustion of propane in kJ g⁻¹, given ΔcH = −2220 kJ mol⁻¹ and M(C₃H₈) = 44.0 g mol⁻¹.
Divide molar enthalpy by molar mass; give 3 significant figures.
What mass of methane (ΔcH = −890 kJ mol⁻¹, M = 16.0 g mol⁻¹) must be burnt to release 2225 kJ of energy?
What volume of methane at SLC (24.8 L mol⁻¹) must be burnt to release 445 kJ of energy? ΔcH(CH₄) = −890 kJ mol⁻¹.
Propane has ΔcH = −2220 kJ mol⁻¹. How much energy is released when 10.0 L of propane, measured at SLC (24.8 L mol⁻¹), is burnt completely?
n = 10.0 / 24.8 = 0.403 mol; energy = 0.403 × 2220 = 895 kJ (991 kJ would result from wrongly using 22.4 L mol⁻¹).
Calculate the mass of CO₂ released per megajoule of energy produced by burning ethanol (ΔcH = −1364 kJ mol⁻¹).
Remember the 2 : 1 mole ratio of CO₂ to ethanol.
Given molar heats of combustion: H₂ 286, CH₄ 890, C₂H₅OH 1364 and C₈H₁₈ 5464 kJ mol⁻¹, which fuel releases the most energy per gram?
Given molar heats of combustion: CH₄ 890, C₃H₈ 2220, C₂H₅OH 1364 and C₈H₁₈ 5464 kJ mol⁻¹, which fuel releases the most energy per mole of CO₂ produced?
Energy per mol CO₂: CH₄ 890/1 = 890; C₃H₈ 2220/3 = 740; C₂H₅OH 1364/2 = 682; C₈H₁₈ 5464/8 = 683 kJ.
How much energy is released by the complete combustion of 5.00 g of ethanol (ΔcH = −1364 kJ mol⁻¹, M = 46.0 g mol⁻¹)?
Calculate the volume of methane, measured at SLC (24.8 L mol⁻¹), that must be burnt to provide 10.0 MJ of energy. ΔcH(CH₄) = −890 kJ mol⁻¹.
Convert MJ to kJ first: 10.0 MJ = 10 000 kJ.
Butane (M = 58.0 g mol⁻¹) releases 49.6 kJ of energy per gram on complete combustion. Its molar enthalpy of combustion is
49.6 kJ g⁻¹ × 58.0 g mol⁻¹ = 2877 kJ mol⁻¹, released, so ΔH = −2.88 × 10³ kJ mol⁻¹.
A car's 45.0 L petrol tank is filled with fuel modelled as octane (density 0.700 g mL⁻¹, M = 114.0 g mol⁻¹, ΔcH = −5464 kJ mol⁻¹). The energy available from a full tank is closest to
C(s) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g), ΔH = −394 kJ mol⁻¹. How much energy is released by burning 6.0 g of carbon?
A 9.0 kg barbecue gas cylinder contains propane (M = 44.0 g mol⁻¹, ΔcH = −2220 kJ mol⁻¹). Calculate the energy, in MJ, released by complete combustion of all the propane.
Convert kg to g and kJ to MJ; 2 significant figures matches the 9.0 kg data.
Brown coal is modelled as pure carbon (ΔcH = −394 kJ mol⁻¹). How much energy is released by burning 1.00 tonne of this coal?
What mass of CO₂ is released per megajoule of energy obtained from burning methane (ΔcH = −890 kJ mol⁻¹)?
How much energy is released when 0.250 mol of octane (ΔcH = −5464 kJ mol⁻¹) burns completely?
What mass of ethanol (ΔcH = −1364 kJ mol⁻¹, M = 46.0) releases the same energy as 1.00 g of octane (ΔcH = −5464 kJ mol⁻¹, M = 114.0)?
Energy from 1.00 g octane = (1.00 / 114.0) × 5464 = 47.9 kJ; ethanol releases 1364 / 46.0 = 29.7 kJ g⁻¹, so mass = 47.9 / 29.7 = 1.62 g
Shows why E10 vehicles use slightly more fuel per kilometre.
For 2C₈H₁₈(l) + 25O₂(g) → 16CO₂(g) + 18H₂O(l), ΔH = −10 928 kJ mol⁻¹. The molar enthalpy of combustion of octane is
ΔH in the equation is for 2 mol of octane, so per mole it is −10 928 / 2 = −5464 kJ mol⁻¹.
A sample of biogas is 60.0% methane by volume, the rest being CO₂. How much energy is released when 100 L of this biogas at SLC (24.8 L mol⁻¹) burns completely? ΔcH(CH₄) = −890 kJ mol⁻¹.
V(CH₄) = 60.0 L; n = 60.0 / 24.8 = 2.42 mol; energy = 2.42 × 890 = 2.15 × 10³ kJ (CO₂ does not burn).
A hydrogen fuel cell bus in Melbourne needs 2.86 × 10⁵ kJ of energy. Assuming ΔcH(H₂) = −286 kJ mol⁻¹ and 100% efficiency, what mass of hydrogen is required?
Calculate the mass of hydrogen gas that must be burnt to release 1.00 MJ of energy. ΔcH(H₂) = −286 kJ mol⁻¹.
Explain why the energy released per gram (or per kilogram) is often more useful than the energy per mole when comparing fuels for vehicles.

Vehicles carry fuel by mass (and volume), so the energy per gram tells how much energy is available for a given mass of fuel carried. Molar values ignore that molecules of different fuels have very different masses.
Link to the practical limitation of fuel mass and storage in vehicles.
In an energy profile diagram for an exothermic reaction,
the products are at a higher enthalpy than the reactants.
the products are at a lower enthalpy than the reactants and ΔH is negative.
An exothermic reaction releases energy to the surroundings, so the products have lower enthalpy and ΔH < 0. All reactions, including exothermic ones, have an activation energy.
An energy profile shows reactants at 50 kJ mol⁻¹, the transition state at 230 kJ mol⁻¹ and products at 140 kJ mol⁻¹. The activation energy for the forward reaction and ΔH are respectively
Ea = 230 − 50 = 180 kJ mol⁻¹; ΔH = H(products) − H(reactants) = 140 − 50 = +90 kJ mol⁻¹, so the reaction is endothermic.
For the reaction in which reactants are at 50 kJ mol⁻¹, the transition state at 230 kJ mol⁻¹ and products at 140 kJ mol⁻¹, the activation energy of the reverse reaction is
The reverse reaction starts from the products: Ea(reverse) = 230 − 140 = 90 kJ mol⁻¹.
A cold pack contains ammonium nitrate that dissolves in water and the pack becomes cold. Which statement is correct?
The process is exothermic because heat leaves the pack.
The process is exothermic because the products have lower enthalpy.
The process has a negative ΔH because the temperature falls.
The process is endothermic; the system absorbs energy from the surroundings, so ΔH is positive.
The temperature of the surroundings (the water and your hand) falls because the dissolving process absorbs energy, so it is endothermic with ΔH > 0.
Breaking chemical bonds in reactants and forming bonds in products are, respectively,

Energy must be absorbed to break bonds (endothermic) and is released when new bonds form (exothermic). An overall reaction is exothermic when more energy is released forming bonds than absorbed breaking them.

Sketch (describe in words) a labelled energy profile for the complete combustion of methane, ΔH = −890 kJ mol⁻¹, assuming an activation energy of 250 kJ mol⁻¹. State the activation energy of the reverse reaction. (3 marks)

Axes: enthalpy (vertical) against reaction progress (horizontal); reactants CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) on a higher level, products CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l) 890 kJ mol⁻¹ lower, with a hump between labelled transition state; Ea arrow from reactants to top of hump (250 kJ mol⁻¹) and ΔH arrow from reactants down to products; Ea(reverse) = 250 + 890 = 1140 kJ mol⁻¹.
Methane burns very exothermically, yet a mixture of methane and air can sit unreacted at room temperature indefinitely. Explain this using the concept of activation energy. (2 marks)

The reaction has a high activation energy, so at room temperature very few collisions between CH₄ and O₂ have enough energy to break the reactant bonds; a spark or flame provides enough energy to overcome Ea, after which the energy released sustains the reaction.
Hydrogen and oxygen react: 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(g). Bond energies: H–H 436 kJ mol⁻¹, O=O 498 kJ mol⁻¹, O–H 463 kJ mol⁻¹. Estimate ΔH for this reaction. (3 marks)
Energy absorbed breaking bonds = 2(436) + 498 = 1370 kJ; energy released forming bonds = 4 × 463 = 1852 kJ; ΔH = 1370 − 1852 = −482 kJ mol⁻¹ (exothermic).
What volume of carbon dioxide at SLC is produced when 10.0 g of propane (M = 44.0 g mol⁻¹) burns completely?
How much energy is released when 50.0 L of methane at SLC burns completely? (ΔcH = −890 kJ mol⁻¹)
A 2.00 L gas cylinder holds hydrogen at 150 kPa and 35 °C. The amount of hydrogen in the cylinder is
n = PV ÷ RT = (150 × 2.00) ÷ (8.31 × 308) = 0.117 mol. Temperature must be in kelvin (35 + 273 = 308 K); using 35 gives 1.03 mol.
At SLC, what volume of oxygen is needed to completely burn 6.20 L of ethane? 2C₂H₆(g) + 7O₂(g) → 4CO₂(g) + 6H₂O(l)
For gases at the same temperature and pressure, volume ratios equal mole ratios: V(O₂) = 6.20 × 7/2 = 21.7 L.
Ethanol releases 29.6 kJ g⁻¹ and octane releases 47.9 kJ g⁻¹. What mass of ethanol releases the same energy as 1.00 kg of octane?
Energy from octane = 1000 × 47.9 = 47 900 kJ; mass of ethanol = 47 900 ÷ 29.6 = 1618 g ≈ 1.62 kg.
A household barbecue uses 450 g of propane per hour (ΔcH = −2220 kJ mol⁻¹). Calculate (a) the energy released per hour and (b) the volume of CO₂ produced per hour at SLC. (3 marks)

A gas sample of methane occupies 5.00 L at 25 °C and 100 kPa. It is burnt in a water heater that is 65.0% efficient at transferring energy to water. Calculate the energy transferred to the water. (ΔcH(CH₄) = −890 kJ mol⁻¹) (3 marks)
n(CH₄) = 5.00 ÷ 24.8 = 0.202 mol; energy released = 0.202 × 890 = 179 kJ; energy transferred = 0.650 × 179 = 117 kJ.

Hydrogen (ΔcH = −286 kJ mol⁻¹) and methane (ΔcH = −890 kJ mol⁻¹) are compared as fuels. Calculate the energy released per litre of each gas at SLC and comment on one implication for storing hydrogen. (3 marks)

H₂: (1 ÷ 24.8) × 286 = 11.5 kJ L⁻¹; CH₄: (1 ÷ 24.8) × 890 = 35.9 kJ L⁻¹; hydrogen releases about one-third the energy per litre, so it must be compressed to high pressure or liquefied at very low temperature to store useful amounts, which costs energy and needs strong tanks.
Methane has ΔH = −890 kJ/mol. Calculate the energy released when 10.0 L of methane, measured at SLC, burns completely.
chem-1-4: How much energy is needed to heat 250 g of water from 20.0 °C to 80.0 °C? (c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹)
The specific heat capacity of a substance is the energy required to
raise the temperature of 1 mol of the substance by 1 °C
raise the temperature of 1 g of the substance by 1 °C
raise the temperature of the whole calorimeter by 1 °C
Specific heat capacity is measured per gram per degree, in J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹; the energy per degree for the whole calorimeter is the calibration factor.
Water has an unusually high specific heat capacity mainly because
extensive hydrogen bonding between molecules absorbs energy before the molecules move faster
Much of the added energy goes into disrupting hydrogen bonds rather than increasing the kinetic energy of the molecules, so temperature rises slowly.
A calorimeter is calibrated with a heater operating at 5.00 V and 3.00 A for 120 s. The temperature rises by 0.750 °C. Calculate the calibration factor.
Include units; time must be in seconds.
A calorimeter is calibrated by passing a current of 2.50 A at 6.00 V for 180 s, and the temperature rises by 1.35 °C. The calibration factor is
A calorimeter has a calibration factor of 3.50 kJ °C⁻¹. A reaction raises its temperature by 4.20 °C. The energy released by the reaction is
In a spirit-burner experiment, burning 0.460 g of ethanol (M = 46.0 g mol⁻¹) heats 200 g of water by 12.0 °C. Ignoring heat losses, the experimental molar enthalpy of combustion of ethanol is

Burning 1.15 g of ethanol (M = 46.0 g mol⁻¹) in a calorimeter with a calibration factor of 4.25 kJ °C⁻¹ raises the temperature by 6.80 °C. Calculate the experimental molar enthalpy of combustion of ethanol.
Negative sign required as combustion is exothermic.
A student's experimental value for the heat of combustion of ethanol using a spirit burner and a metal can of water is much lower than the data book value. The most likely reason is
the water had too high a specific heat capacity
significant heat is lost to the surroundings rather than absorbed by the water
the thermometer read the temperature too high
In open spirit-burner setups much of the heat escapes to the air and the can, and combustion may be incomplete, so less energy is measured.
Which change would most improve the accuracy of a spirit-burner experiment to determine the heat of combustion of a fuel?
Using a larger flame placed further from the can
Using a smaller volume of water
Measuring the mass of the burner only before burning
Using a draught shield and insulating lid around the can
A draught shield and lid reduce heat loss to the surroundings, so more of the energy released is transferred to the water.
When 4.00 g of ammonium nitrate (M = 80.0 g mol⁻¹) dissolves in 100 g of water, the temperature falls by 3.10 °C. Assuming c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹ for the solution, ΔH for dissolving ammonium nitrate is
q = 100 × 4.18 × 3.10 = 1296 J; n = 4.00 / 80.0 = 0.0500 mol; ΔH = +1.296 / 0.0500 = +25.9 kJ mol⁻¹ (positive because temperature fell).
Explain why using an electrically determined calibration factor gives a more accurate result than using q = mcΔT with only the mass of water.

q = mcΔT accounts only for energy absorbed by the water, whereas the calibration factor includes the energy absorbed by the container, stirrer, thermometer and any other parts of the calorimeter, as well as typical heat losses under the same conditions.
Key idea: the calibration factor measures the whole system, not just the water.
If 5.00 kJ of energy is absorbed by 500 g of water, the temperature rise is (c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹)
Equal masses of water (c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹) and ethanol (c = 2.44 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹) each absorb the same amount of energy. Which statement is correct?
The water has the larger temperature increase
Both have the same temperature increase
The ethanol has the larger temperature increase
Neither changes temperature because the energy is used in bonding
ΔT = q / (mc), so the liquid with the smaller specific heat capacity (ethanol) has the larger temperature rise.
A bomb calorimeter differs from a simple solution calorimeter because a bomb calorimeter
does not need to be calibrated
burns the sample in a sealed steel vessel with excess oxygen
The sealed, oxygen-filled 'bomb' ensures complete combustion and minimal heat loss; it still requires calibration.
Identify two sources of error in a spirit-burner experiment to measure the heat of combustion of ethanol, and state the effect of each on the calculated value.

Heat lost to the surroundings and the metal can, and incomplete combustion (soot on the can). Both mean less energy reaches the water, so the calculated heat of combustion is lower than the true value. Evaporation of ethanol from the wick before weighing would also make the calculated value too low.
Any two valid errors, each with its effect (value too low).
The main purpose of electrically calibrating a calorimeter is to
determine how much energy is needed to raise the temperature of the whole calorimeter and its contents by 1 °C
measure the specific heat capacity of pure water
remove the need to measure temperature changes
The calibration factor accounts for energy absorbed by the water, container, stirrer and thermometer together.
A 50.0 g block of metal absorbs 450 J of energy and its temperature rises by 20.0 °C. The specific heat capacity of the metal is
A bomb calorimeter with a calibration factor of 9.80 kJ °C⁻¹ is used to burn 0.320 g of methanol (M = 32.0 g mol⁻¹). The temperature rises by 0.740 °C. The experimental ΔcH of methanol is

50.0 mL of 1.00 M HCl is mixed with 50.0 mL of 1.00 M NaOH in a polystyrene cup and the temperature rises by 6.70 °C. Assuming the solution has a mass of 100 g and c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹, calculate ΔH for the neutralisation per mole of water formed.
n(HCl) = 1.00 × 0.0500 = 0.0500 mol; temperature rise means ΔH is negative.
A 2.00 g sample of a muesli bar is burnt and heats 100 g of water by 24.0 °C. Ignoring heat losses, the energy content of the bar is
In a solution calorimeter, the temperature of the solution rises during a reaction. Which statement is correct?
The reaction is exothermic and ΔH is negative
The reaction is endothermic and ΔH is negative
The reaction is exothermic and ΔH is positive
The reaction is endothermic and ΔH is positive
A temperature rise means energy was released by the reaction into the solution, so the reaction is exothermic with ΔH < 0.

A student's experiment gives the heat of combustion of ethanol as 820 kJ mol⁻¹, whereas the accepted value is 1364 kJ mol⁻¹. The percentage of the energy released that was captured by the water is closest to

0.200 g of methane (M = 16.0 g mol⁻¹, ΔcH = −890 kJ mol⁻¹) is burnt under a beaker containing 300 g of water. If only 70.0% of the energy released is absorbed by the water, calculate the temperature rise of the water.
Apply the efficiency before using ΔT = q / (mc).
Explain why a lid and a stirrer are used in a simple polystyrene-cup calorimeter.
The lid reduces heat loss (or gain) to the surroundings by convection and evaporation. The stirrer ensures the solution has a uniform temperature so the thermometer reads the true temperature change.
One clear purpose for each piece of equipment.
A solution calorimeter is calibrated by passing a current of 2.50 A at 6.00 V for 120 s. The temperature rises by 1.25 °C. The calibration factor is
E = VIt = 6.00 × 2.50 × 120 = 1800 J; CF = E ÷ ΔT = 1800 ÷ 1.25 = 1440 J °C⁻¹ (1.44 kJ °C⁻¹). 1800 J is the energy, not the calibration factor.
Why is electrical calibration of a calorimeter preferred over simply using mass × 4.18 × ΔT?
It accounts for energy absorbed by the calorimeter itself (container, thermometer, stirrer) and some heat loss.
It makes the reaction go faster.
It removes the need to measure temperature.
It increases the specific heat capacity of water.
The calibration factor measures the energy needed to raise the temperature of the whole calorimeter and its contents by 1 °C, so it includes the apparatus, not just the water.

A student burns 0.500 g of ethanol in a spirit burner under a can holding 150.0 g of water, and the water temperature rises by 18.5 °C. The experimental heat of combustion of ethanol (M = 46.0 g mol⁻¹) is closest to

q = 150.0 × 4.18 × 18.5 = 11.6 kJ; n = 0.500 ÷ 46.0 = 0.01087 mol; ΔH = −11.6 ÷ 0.01087 = −1.07 × 10³ kJ mol⁻¹. −1364 kJ mol⁻¹ is the data book value; the experimental value is smaller because of heat loss.
In a spirit burner experiment the experimental heat of combustion is much less than the data book value. Which is the most likely cause?
The thermometer was read too quickly.
The mass of fuel burnt was overestimated by weighing the burner with its cap on both times.
Heat was lost to the surroundings and the can, and some combustion was incomplete.
The water had a higher specific heat capacity than 4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹.

Spirit burner calorimeters are poorly insulated, so much of the energy heats the air and the can rather than the water; soot formation shows incomplete combustion. These are systematic errors that always lower the result.
A bomb calorimeter has a calibration factor of 8.62 kJ °C⁻¹. When 1.20 g of a fuel is burnt, the temperature rises by 5.80 °C. The heat of combustion of the fuel in kJ g⁻¹ is

A calorimeter with a calibration factor of 420 J °C⁻¹ contains 100.0 mL of 1.00 M HCl. 100.0 mL of 1.00 M NaOH is added and the temperature rises by 13.6 °C. Calculate ΔH for H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l). (3 marks)
Energy released = 420 × 13.6 = 5712 J = 5.71 kJ; n(H₂O) = n(H⁺) = 0.1000 L × 1.00 M = 0.100 mol; ΔH = −5.71 ÷ 0.100 = −57.1 kJ mol⁻¹ (negative sign because exothermic).
Explain why the calibration factor must be redetermined if the volume of water in a solution calorimeter is changed. (2 marks)

The calibration factor is the energy needed to raise the temperature of the calorimeter and its contents by 1 °C; changing the volume of water changes the total heat capacity, so the old calibration factor no longer applies.
A student's temperature–time graph for a calorimetry experiment shows the temperature peaking and then slowly falling. Describe how the student should determine ΔT and why. (2 marks)

Extrapolate the cooling section of the graph back to the time the reaction (or heating) began and take ΔT as the difference between this extrapolated temperature and the initial temperature; this corrects for heat lost to the surroundings while the temperature was rising.

Burning 0.500 g of ethanol (M = 46.0 g/mol) heats 100.0 g of water from 20.0 °C to 45.0 °C. Calculate the experimental molar enthalpy of combustion, and explain why its size is smaller than the data-book value (−1364 kJ/mol).
−961 kJ/mol; heat is lost to the surroundings and the container, and combustion may be incomplete.
chem-2-1: Using the electrochemical series, which species is the strongest oxidising agent?
The strongest oxidising agent is the species on the left-hand side with the highest E° value. Ag⁺/Ag (+0.80 V) is higher than Cu²⁺/Cu (+0.34 V). Zn(s) is a reducing agent.
A strip of nickel is placed in each of the following 1.0 M solutions. In which will a reaction occur?
A reaction occurs when the oxidising agent is higher on the series than the reducing agent. Pb²⁺/Pb (−0.13 V) is above Ni²⁺/Ni (−0.25 V), so Ni reduces Pb²⁺. Zn²⁺, Mg²⁺ and Al³⁺ are all below Ni²⁺.
Which metal would NOT react with 1.0 M hydrochloric acid at SLC?
Cu²⁺/Cu (+0.34 V) lies above 2H⁺/H₂ (0.00 V), so H⁺ cannot oxidise copper. Iron, zinc and magnesium all lie below H⁺ and release hydrogen gas.
A predicted reaction using the electrochemical series may not be observed in practice because
E° values change sign at higher temperatures.
the series predicts only whether a reaction is thermodynamically possible, not its rate; conditions may also differ from standard.
the series applies only to reactions involving gases.
reactions between metals and ions never occur in solution.

The electrochemical series is based on standard conditions and says nothing about rate; a predicted reaction may be too slow to observe, and non-standard concentrations or temperatures shift potentials.
Iron(II) ions can act as both an oxidising agent and a reducing agent. Which pair of half-equations shows this?
Fe²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → Fe(s) and Fe²⁺(aq) → Fe³⁺(aq) + e⁻
Fe³⁺(aq) + e⁻ → Fe²⁺(aq) and Fe(s) → Fe²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻
Fe²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → Fe(s) and Fe³⁺(aq) + e⁻ → Fe²⁺(aq)
As an oxidising agent Fe²⁺ gains electrons (reduced to Fe); as a reducing agent it loses an electron (oxidised to Fe³⁺). The other options do not show Fe²⁺ itself in both roles.
A student adds zinc powder to a blue copper(II) sulfate solution. Predict what is observed, and write the oxidation and reduction half-equations and the overall equation. (3 marks)

Blue colour fades and a brown/pink solid (copper) forms; zinc dissolves and the mixture warms; oxidation: Zn(s) → Zn²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻; reduction: Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → Cu(s); overall: Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s).

Three metals X, Y and Z are tested. X displaces Y from a solution of Y²⁺ ions; Z displaces X from a solution of X²⁺ ions; Y does not react with Z²⁺ ions. List the metals in order of increasing strength as reducing agents and justify. (2 marks)
Y < X < Z; X reduces Y²⁺ so X is a stronger reducing agent than Y; Z reduces X²⁺ so Z is stronger than X; consistent with Y not reducing Z²⁺.
Explain why bromine water can oxidise iodide ions but cannot oxidise chloride ions. Refer to E° values (Cl₂/Cl⁻ +1.36 V, Br₂/Br⁻ +1.09 V, I₂/I⁻ +0.54 V). (2 marks)

Br₂ is above I⁻ in the series (+1.09 V > +0.54 V), so Br₂ is a stronger oxidising agent than I₂ and reacts: Br₂(aq) + 2I⁻(aq) → 2Br⁻(aq) + I₂(aq); Br₂ is below Cl₂ (+1.09 V < +1.36 V), so it is not strong enough to oxidise Cl⁻.
Using the electrochemical series, which metal can reduce Fe³⁺(aq) to Fe²⁺(aq) but cannot reduce Fe²⁺(aq) to Fe(s)?
Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ is +0.77 V and Fe²⁺/Fe is −0.44 V. A metal reduces an oxidant listed above it: Cu²⁺/Cu (+0.34 V) lies between the two. Zinc and magnesium reduce both; silver (+0.80 V) reduces neither.
chem-2-2: chem34a1-gc-1
In a galvanic cell made from a Zn/Zn²⁺ half-cell and a Cu/Cu²⁺ half-cell under standard conditions, the cathode and the maximum cell voltage are
zinc, 1.10 V
zinc, 0.42 V
copper, 0.42 V
copper, 1.10 V
Cu²⁺ is the stronger oxidising agent and is reduced at the copper electrode, so copper is the cathode; E°cell = 0.34 − (−0.76) = 1.10 V.
chem34a1-gc-2
In a galvanic cell, electrons flow
from the cathode to the anode through the salt bridge.
from the anode to the cathode through the external circuit.
from the cathode to the anode through the external circuit.
from the anode to the cathode through the salt bridge.
Oxidation at the anode releases electrons, which flow through the wire to the cathode. The salt bridge carries ions, never electrons.
chem34a1-gc-3
A salt bridge soaked in KNO₃(aq) connects the half-cells of a galvanic cell. During operation,
K⁺ ions move toward the cathode half-cell and NO₃⁻ ions move toward the anode half-cell.
K⁺ ions move toward the anode half-cell and NO₃⁻ ions move toward the cathode half-cell.
electrons travel through the salt bridge.
the salt bridge supplies electrons to the cathode.
At the cathode positive ions are consumed (or negative ions formed), so cations migrate there to maintain electrical neutrality; anions move toward the anode where positive ions are being produced.
chem34a1-gc-4
A galvanic cell is built from an Ag/Ag⁺ half-cell and a Ni/Ni²⁺ half-cell. Which overall equation represents the cell reaction?
Ni²⁺(aq) + 2Ag(s) → Ni(s) + 2Ag⁺(aq)
Ag⁺(aq) + Ni(s) → Ag(s) + Ni²⁺(aq)
2Ag⁺(aq) + Ni(s) → 2Ag(s) + Ni²⁺(aq)
Ni(s) + Ag(s) → Ni²⁺(aq) + Ag⁺(aq)
Ag⁺ (+0.80 V) is reduced and Ni (−0.25 V) is oxidised; balancing electrons requires 2Ag⁺. Option B is not balanced for charge.
chem34a1-gc-5
A student builds a cell with Pb/Pb²⁺ and Fe/Fe²⁺ half-cells and measures 0.28 V instead of the predicted 0.31 V. The most likely reason is
the cell is producing electricity in the wrong direction.
the electrodes are made of the wrong metals.
the salt bridge is carrying electrons.
conditions were non-standard, e.g. the solutions were not 1.0 M or the temperature was not 25 °C.

E° values apply only under standard conditions (1 M, 25 °C, 100 kPa); real measurements differ because of concentration, temperature and internal resistance. The predicted value is −0.13 − (−0.44) = 0.31 V.
chem34a1-gc-6

A galvanic cell is built from a Mg/Mg²⁺ half-cell and an inert carbon electrode in a Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ solution. Identify the anode and its polarity, write the half-equation at each electrode, and calculate the standard cell potential. (Mg²⁺/Mg −2.37 V; Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ +0.77 V) (4 marks)
Anode: magnesium, negative electrode; anode: Mg(s) → Mg²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻; cathode (carbon, positive): Fe³⁺(aq) + e⁻ → Fe²⁺(aq); E°cell = 0.77 − (−2.37) = 3.14 V.
chem34a1-gc-7
Explain why the oxidising and reducing agents in a galvanic cell must be kept in separate half-cells. (2 marks)

If mixed, electrons would transfer directly between the reactants and the chemical energy would be released as heat; separating them forces electrons to travel through an external circuit, so chemical energy is converted into electrical energy.
chem34a1-gc-8
Over time in a Zn/Cu galvanic cell, describe what happens to the mass of each electrode and to the colour of the copper(II) sulfate solution. Explain. (3 marks)

The zinc anode loses mass because Zn is oxidised to Zn²⁺ which goes into solution; the copper cathode gains mass because Cu²⁺ is reduced and deposited as Cu; the blue colour of the Cu²⁺ solution fades as Cu²⁺ concentration decreases.
chem-2-2-c1
A galvanic cell is made from Zn(s)/Zn²⁺(aq) and Ag(s)/Ag⁺(aq) half-cells under standard conditions. The overall reaction and maximum voltage are:
Zn(s) + Ag⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Ag(s), 0.04 V
Zn(s) + 2Ag⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + 2Ag(s), 1.56 V
2Ag(s) + Zn²⁺(aq) → 2Ag⁺(aq) + Zn(s), 1.56 V
Zn(s) + 2Ag⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + 2Ag(s), 2.36 V
Ag⁺ (+0.80 V) is the stronger oxidant; Zn is the stronger reductant (−0.76 V). E = 0.80 − (−0.76) = 1.56 V. Balance electrons; do not double the voltage.
chem-2-3: In a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell with an acidic electrolyte, the half-equation at the cathode is
Oxygen is reduced at the cathode; in acid, H⁺ is available, so O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O. Option B applies to an alkaline electrolyte, and option A is the anode reaction.
Which feature distinguishes a fuel cell from a primary galvanic cell (non-rechargeable battery)?
Fuel cells produce electricity from a redox reaction.
Fuel cells have an anode and a cathode.
Fuel cells convert chemical energy into electrical energy.
Reactants are supplied continuously from outside the cell, so it does not run flat while fuel is supplied.

Both types are galvanic and convert chemical to electrical energy via redox, but fuel cells receive a continuous external supply of fuel and oxidant, whereas a battery contains a fixed amount of reactants.
In an alkaline hydrogen fuel cell, the anode half-equation is
Hydrogen is oxidised at the anode; in an alkaline electrolyte, OH⁻ ions combine with the H⁺ formed to give water. Option D is a reduction.
Fuel cell electrodes are usually porous and coated with a catalyst such as platinum. The main purpose is to
increase the surface area for reaction and lower the activation energy, increasing the rate of the electrode reactions.
increase the cell voltage above the E° difference.
prevent the electrolyte from conducting ions.
Porous electrodes allow gases, electrolyte and electrode to meet over a large surface area, and catalysts speed up the reactions. Catalysts do not change the thermodynamic cell voltage.
A direct methanol fuel cell with an acidic electrolyte has the overall reaction 2CH₃OH(l) + 3O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g) + 4H₂O(l). The anode half-equation is
Methanol is oxidised at the anode. Balance C, then O with H₂O, then H with H⁺, then charge with electrons: CH₃OH + H₂O → CO₂ + 6H⁺ + 6e⁻. Option D is not balanced for O or H.
Compare a hydrogen fuel cell with a coal-fired power station for producing electricity. Give two advantages and one disadvantage of the fuel cell. (3 marks)

Advantages: higher energy efficiency because chemical energy converts directly to electrical energy (avoiding heat → mechanical → electrical steps); only product is water, so no CO₂ or other pollutants at point of use; quiet with no moving parts; disadvantage: hydrogen is expensive and difficult to store/transport, catalysts such as platinum are costly, or most hydrogen is currently made from fossil fuels.
Write the anode and cathode half-equations for a methane fuel cell operating with an acidic electrolyte, and the overall equation. (3 marks)
Anode: CH₄(g) + 2H₂O(l) → CO₂(g) + 8H⁺(aq) + 8e⁻; cathode: O₂(g) + 4H⁺(aq) + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O(l) (×2); overall: CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l).
In an acidic hydrogen fuel cell, explain the direction of movement of H⁺ ions through the electrolyte and why this is necessary. (2 marks)

H⁺ ions are produced at the anode (H₂ → 2H⁺ + 2e⁻) and consumed at the cathode (O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O), so they migrate through the electrolyte from anode to cathode; this completes the circuit and maintains charge balance as electrons flow externally.
In a methanol fuel cell with an acidic electrolyte, the anode half-equation is:
Oxidation happens at the anode. Balance O with water, H with H⁺ (acidic), then charge with electrons. The OH⁻ version is for an alkaline electrolyte.
chem-2-4: chem34a1-ghs-1
Hydrogen produced by the electrolysis of water using electricity from solar or wind farms is described as
grey hydrogen.
blue hydrogen.
green hydrogen.
brown hydrogen.

Green hydrogen comes from electrolysis powered by renewable energy. Grey hydrogen is made from natural gas by steam methane reforming without carbon capture; blue hydrogen uses the same process with carbon capture and storage.
chem34a1-ghs-2
Most hydrogen produced today comes from steam methane reforming. Which equation represents the main reforming reaction?
CH₄(g) + H₂O(g) → CO(g) + 3H₂(g)
2H₂O(l) → 2H₂(g) + O₂(g)
CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(g)
C(s) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g)

Methane reacts with steam at high temperature over a nickel catalyst to form carbon monoxide and hydrogen; the CO is often converted to CO₂ by a further water–gas shift reaction, so the process emits CO₂.
chem34a1-ghs-3
Which green chemistry principle is best demonstrated by replacing a coal-fired power station with a solar farm that powers an electrolyser?
Design for degradation
Use of renewable feedstocks and energy
Catalysis
Real-time analysis for pollution prevention
Solar energy and water are renewable, replacing finite fossil fuels. The other principles relate to product breakdown, catalyst use and process monitoring.
chem34a1-ghs-4
A disadvantage of green hydrogen compared with grey hydrogen at present is that
green hydrogen releases CO₂ when used in a fuel cell.
green hydrogen is chemically different from grey hydrogen.
green hydrogen cannot be used in fuel cells.
green hydrogen is currently more expensive to produce and needs large amounts of renewable electricity.

Hydrogen is identical whichever way it is made; the difference is the emissions from production. Electrolysers and renewable electricity currently make green hydrogen costlier than reforming natural gas.
chem34a1-ghs-5
Australian projects plan to export hydrogen by converting it into ammonia. A key reason is that ammonia
is a liquid under mild pressure and stores more hydrogen per litre than compressed hydrogen gas.
is non-toxic and safe to handle.
releases CO₂ when converted back to hydrogen.
has a lower boiling point than hydrogen.

Ammonia liquefies at about −33 °C or under moderate pressure, making transport easier than hydrogen (boiling point −253 °C). Ammonia is toxic, so it is not 'safe' in that sense, and it contains no carbon.
chem34a1-ghs-6
Describe how green hydrogen is produced and write the overall equation for the process. Explain why this hydrogen can be described as a sustainable energy carrier. (3 marks)

Water is electrolysed using electricity from renewable sources such as solar or wind; 2H₂O(l) → 2H₂(g) + O₂(g); the process uses renewable energy and an abundant feedstock (water), produces no CO₂, and using the hydrogen in a fuel cell regenerates water, so the cycle does not deplete resources or add greenhouse gases.
chem34a1-ghs-7
Explain the difference between an energy source and an energy carrier, using hydrogen and solar energy as examples. (2 marks)

An energy source occurs naturally and can be harvested directly, e.g. solar energy from the Sun; an energy carrier stores and transports energy produced from a source, e.g. hydrogen must be manufactured (by electrolysis using solar power) and releases that energy later in a fuel cell.
chem34a1-ghs-8
Steam methane reforming with carbon capture and storage produces 'blue' hydrogen. Evaluate whether blue hydrogen is a sustainable alternative to green hydrogen. (3 marks)

Blue hydrogen lowers CO₂ emissions compared with grey hydrogen because much of the CO₂ is captured and stored underground; however, it still relies on a finite fossil fuel (natural gas), capture is not 100% efficient and methane leaks during extraction add greenhouse gases; therefore it is less sustainable than green hydrogen, though it may be a transitional option while renewable capacity grows.
chem-2-4-c1
Renewable electricity is stored by making hydrogen in an electrolyser (70% efficient) and later converting it back in a fuel cell (60% efficient). The overall efficiency is:
Efficiencies multiply: 0.70 × 0.60 = 0.42. This energy loss is a key argument in the hydrogen-storage debate.
chem-3-1: chem-3-1-1
According to collision theory, which conditions must be met for a collision between reactant particles to result in a reaction?
The particles must collide with the correct orientation, regardless of their energy
The particles must collide with energy at least equal to the activation energy and with the correct orientation
The particles must collide with energy exactly equal to the enthalpy change of the reaction
The particles must collide at least twice before bonds can break
A successful collision requires both sufficient energy (≥ Ea) to break bonds and an orientation that allows the reacting parts of the particles to come into contact.
chem-3-1-2
A student reacts magnesium ribbon with 0.50 M and then 2.0 M hydrochloric acid at the same temperature. The main reason the 2.0 M acid reacts faster is that:
the activation energy of the reaction is lowered at higher concentration
there are more acid particles per unit volume, so the frequency of collisions increases
a greater proportion of collisions have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy
each acid particle has a higher average kinetic energy
Increasing concentration increases the number of collisions per second; it does not change particle energies or the activation energy.
chem-3-1-3
Powdered calcium carbonate reacts faster with dilute hydrochloric acid than the same mass of marble chips because the powder:
has a lower activation energy for the reaction
produces a greater total amount of carbon dioxide
raises the temperature of the acid before reacting
has a larger surface area, increasing the frequency of collisions with acid particles
Smaller particles expose more surface for collisions; the same mass gives the same amount of CO₂ and Ea is unchanged.
chem-3-1-4
Using collision theory, explain why marble chips react faster with 2 M hydrochloric acid than with 1 M hydrochloric acid at the same temperature.

The 2 M acid has more H⁺ ions per unit volume, so collisions between H⁺ and the CaCO₃ surface occur more frequently. With more collisions per second, there are more successful collisions per second (the proportion of successful collisions is unchanged), so the rate is greater.
Full marks require linking concentration to collision frequency and to the number of successful collisions per unit time.
chem-3-1-5
The volume of a sealed vessel containing a gaseous reaction mixture is halved at constant temperature. The rate of reaction increases mainly because:
the activation energy of the reaction decreases
the average kinetic energy of the particles increases
the orientation of every collision becomes favourable
the frequency of collisions between reactant particles increases
Halving the volume doubles the concentration (partial pressure) of each gas, so particles collide more often.
chem-3-1-6
A 10 °C rise in temperature often roughly doubles the rate of a reaction. The main reason for this large increase is that:
the frequency of collisions doubles
the activation energy halves
a much greater proportion of collisions have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy
the enthalpy change of the reaction becomes more negative
The fraction of particles with energy ≥ Ea increases sharply with temperature; the collision frequency increases only by a few per cent.
chem-3-1-7
Which change would NOT increase the rate of reaction between zinc and dilute sulfuric acid?
Using larger lumps of zinc of the same total mass
Heating the acid to 40 °C
Using zinc powder instead of granules
Using a more concentrated sulfuric acid solution
Larger lumps reduce the surface area exposed to the acid, which lowers the collision frequency and slows the reaction.
chem-3-1-8
Explain why increasing temperature increases reaction rate by much more than the increase in collision frequency alone would predict.

At higher temperature particles have greater average kinetic energy, so collisions are slightly more frequent. More importantly, a much larger proportion of collisions now have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy, so the number of successful collisions per second increases greatly.
Students must identify the increased proportion of collisions with E ≥ Ea as the dominant factor.
chem-3-1-9
Calcium carbonate reacts with hydrochloric acid in an open conical flask sitting on an electronic balance. Which measurement is most suitable for following the rate of this reaction?
The increase in mass of the flask as carbon dioxide forms
The decrease in mass of the flask and contents over time
The melting point of the calcium chloride produced
The total volume of the conical flask
CO₂ gas escapes from the open flask, so the mass decreases at a rate that reflects the reaction rate.
The activation energy of a reaction is best described as:
the energy released when products form
the minimum energy colliding particles need for the collision to result in a reaction
the difference in energy between reactants and products
the average kinetic energy of the reactant particles
Ea is the energy barrier between reactants and the transition state that must be overcome in a collision.
An exothermic reaction has a forward activation energy of 50 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔH = −120 kJ mol⁻¹. What is the activation energy of the reverse reaction?
170 kJ mol⁻¹
70 kJ mol⁻¹
120 kJ mol⁻¹
50 kJ mol⁻¹
For an exothermic reaction, Ea(reverse) = Ea(forward) + |ΔH| = 50 + 120 = 170 kJ mol⁻¹.
The forward activation energy of a reaction is 185 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔH = −92 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate the activation energy of the reverse reaction.
Ea(reverse) = Ea(forward) + |ΔH| = 185 + 92 = 277 kJ mol⁻¹.
For an exothermic reaction the products sit lower than the reactants, so the reverse barrier is larger by |ΔH|.
An endothermic reaction has ΔH = +40 kJ mol⁻¹ and a forward activation energy of 90 kJ mol⁻¹. What is the activation energy of the reverse reaction?
130 kJ mol⁻¹
40 kJ mol⁻¹
90 kJ mol⁻¹
50 kJ mol⁻¹
For an endothermic reaction the products are higher in energy, so Ea(reverse) = Ea(forward) − ΔH = 90 − 40 = 50 kJ mol⁻¹.
The rate at which hydrogen gas is produced when magnesium reacts with excess hydrochloric acid slows down as the reaction proceeds. The best explanation is that:
the activation energy increases as products form
the concentration of acid and the surface area of magnesium decrease, so collisions become less frequent
the catalyst in the mixture is used up
the reaction becomes endothermic as it proceeds
As reactants are consumed, there are fewer reactant particles available to collide per unit time, so the rate falls.
Argon gas is injected into a sealed rigid vessel containing a gaseous reaction mixture at constant temperature. What is the effect on the rate of reaction?
The rate increases because the total pressure has increased
The rate decreases because argon lowers the activation energy
No change, because the concentrations of the reactant gases are unchanged
The rate increases because argon reacts with the reactants
At constant volume, adding an inert gas does not change the number of reactant particles per unit volume, so the frequency of reactant collisions is unchanged.
A 1.00 g marble chip (CaCO₃) reacts completely with excess hydrochloric acid in 120 s. Calculate the average rate of CO₂ production in mol s⁻¹.
CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂ gives a 1:1 mole ratio of CaCO₃ to CO₂.
A 0.0450 g sample of magnesium reacts completely with excess hydrochloric acid at SLC (25 °C, 100 kPa). What volume of hydrogen gas is produced? (Molar volume at SLC = 24.8 L mol⁻¹)
In a reaction producing carbon dioxide, 60.0 mL of gas is collected in the first 30 s and a further 20.0 mL in the next 30 s. What is the average rate of gas production over the first 60 s?
2.00 mL s⁻¹
0.667 mL s⁻¹
1.33 mL s⁻¹
1.00 mL s⁻¹
Average rate = total volume ÷ total time = 80.0 mL ÷ 60 s = 1.33 mL s⁻¹.
Milk stored in a refrigerator at 4 °C spoils more slowly than milk left on a kitchen bench in a Melbourne summer. The best explanation is that at the lower temperature:
fewer collisions between reacting particles have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy
the activation energy of the spoilage reactions is higher
the spoilage reactions become endothermic
the reacting particles collide with the correct orientation less often because they are larger
Lowering temperature reduces particle kinetic energies, so a smaller fraction of collisions are successful (and collisions are also slightly less frequent).
Describe two experimental methods that could be used to measure the rate of reaction between magnesium ribbon and hydrochloric acid.

1) Collect the hydrogen gas in a gas syringe (or inverted measuring cylinder) and record its volume at regular time intervals. 2) Measure the pH (or conductivity) of the solution over time as H⁺ is consumed, or time how long the magnesium takes to disappear completely.
Any two valid methods that track a reactant or product over time are acceptable; mass loss is possible but small because H₂ is very light.
Fine flour dust suspended in the air of a grain silo can explode if ignited, while a bag of flour burns slowly. This is mainly because the dust:
has an extremely large surface area in contact with oxygen
has a higher enthalpy of combustion than bagged flour
contains a catalyst that bagged flour does not
has a higher activation energy than bagged flour
Fine dispersion exposes an enormous surface area to oxygen, so the collision frequency and hence rate of combustion become extremely high.
Which change increases BOTH the frequency of collisions and the proportion of collisions that have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy?
Increasing the concentration of a reactant
Adding a catalyst
Increasing the temperature
Increasing the surface area of a solid reactant
Higher temperature makes particles move faster (more collisions) and gives more of them energy ≥ Ea; concentration and surface area only affect frequency.
Many collisions between reactant particles that have energy greater than the activation energy still do not produce products. The most likely reason is that:
the particles collided with an orientation that did not allow the required bonds to break and form
the particles had too much energy and bounced apart
the enthalpy change of the reaction is positive
the activation energy changes during each collision
Even energetic collisions are unsuccessful if the reacting atoms are not aligned correctly at the moment of collision.
A graph of volume of hydrogen collected against time for magnesium reacting with hydrochloric acid is steep at first, then becomes flatter and finally horizontal. Explain this shape.

Initially reactant concentrations are highest, so collision frequency and rate are greatest (steep slope). As magnesium and acid are used up, collisions become less frequent and the rate falls (flatter slope). The line becomes horizontal when the limiting reactant is fully consumed and no more gas is produced.
The gradient at any point represents the rate of reaction.
A student writes: 'Heating a reaction mixture increases the rate because it lowers the activation energy.' Correct this statement.

Heating does not change the activation energy. It increases the average kinetic energy of particles, so collisions are more frequent and a greater proportion of collisions have energy equal to or greater than the (unchanged) activation energy.
Only a catalyst lowers the activation energy, by providing an alternative pathway.
chem34a1-ctr-1
According to collision theory, for a reaction to occur, reactant particles must
collide with energy equal to or greater than the activation energy and with the correct orientation.
collide with any energy as long as they are moving.
be in the same physical state.
be at a temperature above 100 °C.
Collisions must be both sufficiently energetic (≥ Ea) and correctly oriented to break bonds and form new ones; most collisions do not meet both conditions.
chem34a1-ctr-2
Marble chips (CaCO₃) react with hydrochloric acid. Which change would NOT increase the initial rate of reaction?
Using powdered marble instead of chips
Using a larger volume of the same concentration of acid
Increasing the acid concentration
Warming the acid

Rate depends on concentration, not total volume; a larger volume of the same acid does not change the frequency of collisions per unit area. Powdering increases surface area; higher concentration and temperature increase collision frequency and energy.
chem34a1-ctr-3
Increasing the temperature by 10 °C often roughly doubles the rate of a reaction. The main reason is that
the activation energy is halved.
the number of collisions per second doubles.
particles become larger and collide more often.
a much greater proportion of collisions have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy.
Higher temperature slightly increases collision frequency, but the major effect is that a significantly larger fraction of particles have energy ≥ Ea. Temperature does not change Ea.
chem34a1-ctr-4
A student measures the mass of a flask as CaCO₃ chips react with excess HCl, and graphs mass lost against time. The gradient of the curve
is greatest at the start and decreases to zero as reactants are used up.
is zero at the start and increases over time.
remains constant until the reaction stops suddenly.
increases throughout because products catalyse the reaction.
The rate is greatest initially when reactant concentration is highest; as HCl is consumed and CaCO₃ surface shrinks, the rate decreases until the limiting reactant is used and the curve levels off.
chem34a1-ctr-5
Increasing the pressure of a gaseous reaction mixture by reducing its volume increases the rate because
the activation energy decreases.
the temperature of the gases always doubles.
the concentration of gas particles increases, so collisions occur more frequently.
the orientation of collisions becomes correct.
Compressing a gas increases the number of particles per unit volume, so collision frequency increases. Ea is unchanged.
chem34a1-ctr-6
Coal dust in an underground mine can explode, while a lump of coal burns slowly. Explain this using collision theory. (2 marks)

Coal dust has a much larger surface area exposed to oxygen than a lump of the same mass; this greatly increases the frequency of collisions between carbon and O₂ molecules, so the reaction rate is so high that energy is released almost instantly, producing an explosion.
chem34a1-ctr-7

Two experiments react 1.0 g magnesium ribbon with excess HCl: Experiment 1 uses 1.0 M HCl, Experiment 2 uses 2.0 M HCl. Describe how a graph of H₂ volume against time for Experiment 2 would compare with Experiment 1, and explain. (3 marks)

Experiment 2 has a steeper initial gradient (faster rate) because the higher HCl concentration increases collision frequency; it levels off sooner; it reaches the same final volume of H₂ because magnesium is the limiting reactant and the same amount is used in both.
chem34a1-ctr-8
Explain why food stored in a refrigerator spoils more slowly than food left on the bench. (2 marks)

Spoilage involves chemical (enzyme-catalysed and microbial) reactions; at lower temperature particles have less kinetic energy, so fewer collisions have energy ≥ activation energy and collisions are less frequent, so the rate of spoilage reactions decreases.
chem-3-1-c1
A 10 °C rise in temperature can double a reaction rate, although collision frequency rises only a few percent. The main reason is that:
The activation energy decreases, so collisions with less energy are now successful
Particles collide far more often, because they move much faster at a higher temperature
The equilibrium constant increases, so the forward reaction is pushed to go faster
A much larger proportion of collisions have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy
The high-energy tail of the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution grows sharply, so many more collisions are successful.
chem-3-2: chem-3-2-1
In a Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution curve for a gas, the total area under the curve represents:
the total energy released by the reaction
the total number of particles in the sample
the activation energy of the reaction
the number of particles with energy greater than the activation energy
The curve plots the number of particles at each kinetic energy, so the area under it equals the total number of particles.
chem-3-2-2
When the temperature of a gas sample is increased, its Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution curve:
becomes taller and narrower, with the peak moving to lower energy
shifts to higher energy and the total area increases
flattens and broadens, with the peak moving to higher energy and the area unchanged
stays the same, but the activation energy line moves to the left
At higher temperature more particles have high kinetic energies; the number of particles (area) is unchanged, so the peak must be lower.
chem-3-2-3
On a Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution, the area under the curve to the right of the activation energy line represents:
the number of particles with enough energy to react on collision
the number of particles that have already reacted
the enthalpy change of the reaction
the number of particles with the most probable energy
Only particles with kinetic energy ≥ Ea can react when they collide with correct orientation.
chem-3-2-4
Describe how the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution of a gas changes when the temperature is increased from 25 °C to 50 °C, and explain the effect on reaction rate.

The curve becomes flatter and broader, the peak shifts to a higher kinetic energy and is lower, and the total area stays the same. A greater area now lies beyond the activation energy, so more particles have energy ≥ Ea; more collisions are successful per second and the rate increases.
Award marks for: peak shift right and lower, same area, larger area beyond Ea, link to more successful collisions.
chem-3-2-5
How is the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution of a reaction mixture affected when a catalyst is added at constant temperature?
The curve shifts to higher energies and the activation energy is unchanged
The curve becomes taller and the activation energy increases
The curve is unchanged, but the activation energy is lower, so a larger area lies beyond it
The curve and the activation energy are both unchanged
A catalyst does not change the energy distribution of particles; it provides a lower-Ea pathway, so more particles have sufficient energy.
chem-3-2-6
A catalyst increases the rate of a reaction by:
increasing the kinetic energy of the reactant particles
increasing the enthalpy change of the reaction
increasing the concentration of the reactants
providing an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy
The catalysed pathway has a lower energy barrier, so a greater proportion of collisions are successful.
chem-3-2-7
What effect does adding a catalyst have on the enthalpy change, ΔH, of a reaction?
ΔH becomes more negative
ΔH becomes less negative
ΔH is unchanged
ΔH becomes zero
The reactants and products have the same energies with or without the catalyst; only the activation energy changes.
chem-3-2-8
With reference to a Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution, explain how a catalyst increases the rate of a reaction.

The catalyst provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy. The distribution curve itself is unchanged, but the Ea line moves to lower energy, so a larger proportion of particles have energy ≥ Ea and the frequency of successful collisions increases.
A common error is to say the curve shifts; for a catalyst only the position of Ea changes.
chem-3-2-9
A catalyst is added to a reaction mixture that is already at equilibrium. Which statement is correct?
The equilibrium shifts to the right, increasing the yield
The equilibrium shifts to the left, decreasing the yield
The rates of the forward and reverse reactions increase equally and the equilibrium position does not change
Only the forward reaction rate increases
A catalyst lowers the activation energies of both forward and reverse reactions, so it does not alter the equilibrium position or K.
The platinum, palladium and rhodium in a car's catalytic converter are best described as:
heterogeneous catalysts, because they are solids and the reactants are gases
homogeneous catalysts, because they are in the same phase as the exhaust gases
reactants that are consumed as exhaust gases pass over them
inhibitors that slow the formation of carbon monoxide
A heterogeneous catalyst is in a different phase from the reactants; the gases adsorb onto the solid metal surface.
The rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction falls sharply when the temperature is raised well above about 40 °C. The best explanation is that:
the activation energy of the reaction increases
the enzyme denatures, changing the shape of its active site
the reactant particles have less kinetic energy
the reaction becomes endothermic at high temperature
High temperatures disrupt the bonds that maintain the enzyme's tertiary structure, so substrates no longer fit the active site.
Distinguish between a homogeneous and a heterogeneous catalyst, giving an example of each.

A homogeneous catalyst is in the same phase as the reactants, e.g. concentrated H₂SO₄ in the esterification of ethanoic acid and ethanol. A heterogeneous catalyst is in a different phase from the reactants, e.g. solid iron catalysing the gaseous Haber process (or Pt/Pd/Rh in a catalytic converter).
Both a correct definition and a correct example are needed for each type.
Which feature of the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution of a fixed amount of gas does NOT change when the temperature increases?
The height of the peak
The total area under the curve
The position of the most probable kinetic energy
The proportion of particles with energy above the activation energy
The area represents the number of particles, which is constant for a fixed amount of gas.
