Compared with the distribution at 50 °C, the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution of the same gas sample at 10 °C has:
a lower peak at a higher kinetic energy
a taller peak at a higher kinetic energy
a taller peak at a lower kinetic energy
a smaller total area under the curve
At lower temperature particle energies are concentrated around a lower value, giving a taller, narrower peak with the same area.
When a catalyst is added to a reversible reaction, the rate of the reverse reaction:
increases, because the catalyst also lowers the activation energy of the reverse reaction
decreases, because the catalyst favours the forward reaction
is unchanged, because the catalyst only affects the forward reaction
becomes zero, because the reaction goes to completion
The catalysed pathway is shared by both directions, so both Ea values are lowered by the same amount.
Explain why adding a catalyst to a reversible reaction does not change the equilibrium yield of product.

A catalyst lowers the activation energy of both the forward and reverse reactions by the same amount, so both rates increase equally. Equilibrium is reached sooner, but the equilibrium position and the value of K are unchanged, so the yield is the same.
The key idea is that both directions are sped up equally.
Which of the following is an example of a homogeneous catalyst?
Iron in the Haber process
Concentrated sulfuric acid in the liquid-phase reaction between ethanoic acid and ethanol
Vanadium(V) oxide in the contact process
Platinum in a car's catalytic converter
In esterification the H₂SO₄ catalyst is in the same (liquid) phase as the reactants; the others are solids catalysing gas reactions.
Which statement best describes how a heterogeneous catalyst such as iron works in the Haber process?
The catalyst reacts permanently with nitrogen to form iron nitride as the product
The catalyst increases the temperature of the gases by absorbing heat
The catalyst dissolves in the gases to form a single phase
Reactant molecules adsorb onto the catalyst surface, weakening their bonds and allowing reaction at lower energy
Adsorption onto active sites weakens bonds and brings reactants together, then products desorb and the catalyst is regenerated.
The iron catalyst used in the Haber process is finely divided or porous. This is because:
finely divided iron has a higher activation energy
a larger surface area provides more active sites for reactant molecules to adsorb onto
finely divided iron shifts the equilibrium towards ammonia
finely divided iron absorbs heat, making the reaction endothermic
Heterogeneous catalysts act at their surfaces, so increasing surface area increases the catalysed rate.
Small amounts of lead or sulfur compounds in exhaust gases can 'poison' a catalytic converter. Explain what this means.
The poison binds strongly to the active sites on the metal catalyst surface and is not released. This blocks reactant molecules from adsorbing, so the catalyst's effectiveness decreases permanently.
Catalyst poisoning reduces the number of available active sites.
On an energy profile diagram, how does the pathway for a catalysed reaction compare with the uncatalysed pathway?
It has a higher peak, with the products at a lower energy
It has the same peak, but the products are at a higher energy
It has a lower peak, with the products at a lower energy
It has a lower peak, but the reactants and products are at the same energy levels
A catalyst lowers only the activation energy; ΔH is unchanged so reactant and product levels stay the same.

A catalyst lowers the forward activation energy of an exothermic reaction from 80 kJ mol⁻¹ to 50 kJ mol⁻¹. ΔH for the reaction is −30 kJ mol⁻¹. What is the activation energy of the catalysed reverse reaction?
80 kJ mol⁻¹
110 kJ mol⁻¹
20 kJ mol⁻¹
50 kJ mol⁻¹
Ea(reverse, catalysed) = Ea(forward, catalysed) + |ΔH| = 50 + 30 = 80 kJ mol⁻¹.

Raising the temperature of a gas from 25 °C to 35 °C increases the average kinetic energy of its particles by only about 3%, yet the reaction rate may double. Using the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution, this is explained by:
the activation energy line moving to a lower energy
the total area under the curve doubling
the peak of the curve becoming taller
a large relative increase in the number of particles in the high-energy tail beyond the activation energy
Because Ea lies in the tail of the distribution, a small shift in the curve greatly increases the area beyond Ea.

The uncatalysed oxidation of sulfur dioxide has Ea = 240 kJ mol⁻¹; with a V₂O₅ catalyst Ea = 140 kJ mol⁻¹. ΔH for 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2SO₃(g) is −196 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate the activation energy of the catalysed reverse reaction.
Ea(reverse, catalysed) = 140 + 196 = 336 kJ mol⁻¹.
For an exothermic reaction the reverse barrier equals the forward barrier plus |ΔH|.
Explain why a Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution curve starts at the origin and approaches, but never touches, the energy axis at high energies.

Very few particles have zero (or near-zero) kinetic energy, so the curve begins at the origin. A small number of particles have very high energies, and there is no fixed maximum energy, so the curve tails off towards the axis without reaching it.
The asymmetric shape reflects random collisions transferring energy between particles.
chem34a1-mbc-1
On a Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution curve, the area under the curve to the right of the activation energy represents
the total number of particles in the sample.
the activation energy of the reaction.
the number of particles with energy equal to or greater than the activation energy.
the average kinetic energy of the particles.
The total area represents all particles; the area beyond Ea is the fraction with enough energy to react on collision.
chem34a1-mbc-2
When the temperature of a gas sample is increased, its Maxwell–Boltzmann curve
becomes taller and narrower, with the peak shifting left.
flattens and broadens, with the peak shifting to higher energy, while the total area stays the same.
shifts to the right with the total area increasing.
stays the same but the activation energy decreases.
At higher temperature the average kinetic energy increases and the energies spread out; the number of particles is unchanged, so the area under the curve is constant.
chem34a1-mbc-3
A catalyst increases the rate of a reaction by
increasing the average kinetic energy of the reactant particles.
increasing the enthalpy change of the reaction.
shifting the Maxwell–Boltzmann curve to higher energies.
providing an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy.
A catalyst lowers Ea by providing a different mechanism, so on the Maxwell–Boltzmann curve the Ea line moves left and more particles have sufficient energy. The curve itself and ΔH are unchanged.
chem34a1-mbc-4
Which statement about a catalyst in a reversible reaction is correct?
It increases the rate of the forward reaction only.
It changes ΔH for the reaction.
It increases the rates of both forward and reverse reactions by lowering the activation energy of each.
It is consumed during the reaction.
The catalysed pathway is shared by both directions, so Ea is lowered for forward and reverse reactions equally (by the same amount). A catalyst is regenerated and does not change ΔH.
chem34a1-mbc-5
Platinum and rhodium in a car's catalytic converter speed up the conversion of CO and NO into CO₂ and N₂. These metals are best described as
heterogeneous catalysts that provide a surface where gas molecules adsorb and react.
homogeneous catalysts in the same phase as the gases.
reactants that are slowly used up.
enzymes that denature at high temperature.
The solid metals are in a different phase from the gaseous reactants, so they are heterogeneous catalysts; gases adsorb onto the surface, bonds weaken, and products desorb.
chem34a1-mbc-6
Describe (in words) a Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution for a gas at temperature T₁ and the same gas at a higher temperature T₂. Use it to explain why reaction rate increases with temperature. (3 marks)

Axes: number of particles (vertical) against kinetic energy (horizontal); curve starts at origin, rises to a peak and has a long tail that approaches but never reaches zero; the T₂ curve is lower and broader with its peak shifted to the right, with the same area; with Ea marked, the area to the right of Ea is much larger at T₂, so a greater proportion of collisions are successful and the rate increases.
chem34a1-mbc-7
On a Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution, show how adding a catalyst changes the proportion of particles able to react. Explain why the curve itself does not change. (2 marks)

A catalyst lowers the activation energy, so the Ea line moves to the left and the area under the curve beyond Ea increases, meaning more particles can react; the curve depends only on temperature (the energy distribution of the particles), which a catalyst does not change.
chem34a1-mbc-8

Hydrogen peroxide decomposes slowly: 2H₂O₂(aq) → 2H₂O(l) + O₂(g). Adding manganese(IV) oxide powder causes rapid bubbling, and the MnO₂ can be recovered unchanged in mass. Explain these observations and identify the type of catalyst. (3 marks)

MnO₂ is a catalyst that provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy, so more collisions are successful and O₂ is produced rapidly (bubbling); because it is regenerated at the end of the reaction, its mass is unchanged; it is a heterogeneous catalyst (solid catalyst with aqueous reactant).
chem-3-2-c1
Adding a catalyst to a reaction mixture changes a Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution diagram by:
Shifting the peak of the curve to the right, so that more particles have high energy
Making the curve taller and narrower, while the activation-energy line stays fixed
Leaving the curve unchanged and moving the activation-energy line to a lower energy
Leaving the curve unchanged and moving the activation-energy line to a higher energy
A catalyst provides a pathway with lower activation energy. The particles' energies (the curve) depend only on temperature.
chem-3-3: Which is the correct equilibrium expression for N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g)?
Kc = products over reactants, each concentration raised to the power of its coefficient in the balanced equation.
What are the units of Kc for N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g)?
For 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g), the equilibrium constant is K. What is the equilibrium constant for 2SO₃(g) ⇌ 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) at the same temperature?
Reversing an equation inverts the equilibrium expression, so the new constant is the reciprocal.
Write the equilibrium expression, including units, for 2NO(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g).
For 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g), the equilibrium constant is K. What is the equilibrium constant for SO₂(g) + ½O₂(g) ⇌ SO₃(g) at the same temperature?
Halving all coefficients halves every power in the expression, so the new constant is K^(1/2).
A reaction has Kc = 1 × 10²⁰ at 25 °C. Which statement is correct?
The reaction must occur very rapidly
At equilibrium the mixture consists almost entirely of reactants
At equilibrium the mixture consists almost entirely of products
A very large K means the equilibrium position lies far to the right; K says nothing about rate.
At 450 °C, an equilibrium mixture for H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g) contains [H₂] = 0.100 M, [I₂] = 0.100 M and [HI] = 0.700 M. What is the value of Kc?
0.500 mol of H₂ and 0.500 mol of I₂ are placed in a 5.00 L vessel. Kc for H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g) is 64.0 at this temperature. Calculate the equilibrium concentration of HI.
For a reaction mixture that is not at equilibrium, the reaction quotient Q is found to be less than K. What will happen?
The net reaction proceeds in the forward direction until Q = K
The net reaction proceeds in the reverse direction until Q = K
The value of K decreases until it equals Q
No change occurs because the system is already at equilibrium
Q < K means the ratio of products to reactants is too small, so more products form.
For N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g), Kc = 4.6 × 10⁻³ M at 25 °C. A mixture at 25 °C has [N₂O₄] = 0.50 M and [NO₂] = 0.020 M. Which statement is correct?
Q = 0.040, so the net reaction proceeds in reverse, producing more N₂O₄
Q = 8.0 × 10⁻⁴, so the net reaction proceeds in reverse, producing more N₂O₄
Q = Kc, so the mixture is at equilibrium
Q = 8.0 × 10⁻⁴, so the net reaction proceeds forward, producing more NO₂
Q = (0.020)² ÷ 0.50 = 8.0 × 10⁻⁴, which is less than Kc, so the forward reaction is favoured.
Which change will alter the value of the equilibrium constant for a reaction?
Increasing the concentration of a reactant
Decreasing the volume of the container
K depends only on temperature for a given equation; other changes shift the position but leave K unchanged.

For 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g), Kc = 280 M⁻¹ at a certain temperature. A mixture contains [SO₂] = 0.10 M, [O₂] = 0.050 M and [SO₃] = 0.50 M. Determine whether the mixture is at equilibrium and, if not, the direction of net reaction.
Q = (0.50)² ÷ ((0.10)² × 0.050) = 0.25 ÷ 0.00050 = 500 M⁻¹. Q > Kc, so the mixture is not at equilibrium and the net reaction proceeds in the reverse direction (forming more SO₂ and O₂).
When Q > K there are too many products relative to reactants.
The temperature of an exothermic equilibrium reaction is increased. What happens to the value of Kc?
Raising the temperature favours the endothermic (reverse) direction, lowering the product-to-reactant ratio and therefore Kc.
2.00 mol of PCl₅ is placed in a 1.00 L flask and allowed to reach equilibrium: PCl₅(g) ⇌ PCl₃(g) + Cl₂(g). At equilibrium, 0.40 mol of PCl₃ is present. What is the value of Kc?
At equilibrium [PCl₅] = 1.60 M and [PCl₃] = [Cl₂] = 0.40 M; Kc = (0.40 × 0.40) ÷ 1.60 = 0.10 M.
1.00 mol of N₂ and 3.00 mol of H₂ are placed in a 2.00 L vessel. At equilibrium, 0.400 mol of NH₃ has formed. What is the value of Kc for N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g)?
At equilibrium n(N₂) = 0.800, n(H₂) = 2.40, n(NH₃) = 0.400 mol, so concentrations are 0.400, 1.20 and 0.200 M; Kc = 0.0400 ÷ (0.400 × 1.728) = 0.0579 M⁻².
Explain why the value of Kc does not change when extra reactant is added to an equilibrium mixture at constant temperature.

Adding reactant makes Q smaller than K, so the forward reaction is temporarily favoured. Concentrations then adjust until the ratio of products to reactants again equals K. K depends only on temperature, which has not changed.
Distinguish between the equilibrium position (which shifts) and the equilibrium constant (which does not).
For the reaction X(g) ⇌ Y(g), Kc = 4.0 at a certain temperature. If 1.00 M of X is initially present with no Y, what is the equilibrium concentration of Y?
For 2A(g) ⇌ B(g), Kc = 2.5 × 10⁻³ M⁻¹. What is the value of Kc for 2B(g) ⇌ 4A(g) at the same temperature?
Reversing gives 1/K = 400; doubling the coefficients squares this: 400² = 1.6 × 10⁵ M².
What are the units of Kc for CH₃COOH(l) + C₂H₅OH(l) ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅(l) + H₂O(l), treating all species as being in the same solution?
There are two concentration terms on top and two on the bottom, so the units cancel.
For A(g) + B(g) ⇌ C(g), Kc = 2.0 M⁻¹. Determine the value and units of Kc for 2C(g) ⇌ 2A(g) + 2B(g) at the same temperature.
Reversing gives 1/2.0 = 0.50 M; doubling the coefficients squares this: (0.50)² = 0.25 M².
Which statement is true for a chemical system at dynamic equilibrium?
The concentrations of reactants and products are equal
Both the forward and reverse reactions have stopped
The value of Kc is always equal to 1
The rates of the forward and reverse reactions are equal and non-zero
At dynamic equilibrium both reactions continue at equal rates, so concentrations stay constant (but are not necessarily equal).
At a certain temperature, Kc for N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g) is 4.6 × 10⁻³ M. What is Kc for 2NO₂(g) ⇌ N₂O₄(g) at the same temperature?
Reversing the equation gives the reciprocal: 1 ÷ (4.6 × 10⁻³) = 217 M⁻¹.
For which reaction would the units of Kc be M?
For PCl₅ decomposition, units = (M × M) ÷ M = M; the others give no units, M⁻¹ and M⁻² respectively.
Explain what is meant by the term 'dynamic equilibrium'.

In a closed system, the forward and reverse reactions continue to occur at equal rates, so there is no net change in the concentrations of reactants and products, even though particles are still reacting.
Both 'equal rates' and 'reactions still occurring' must be stated.
0.800 mol of NO₂ is placed in a 2.00 L vessel. At equilibrium for 2NO₂(g) ⇌ N₂O₄(g), 0.200 mol of N₂O₄ is present. Calculate Kc.
NO₂ reacted = 2 × 0.200 = 0.400 mol, so 0.400 mol NO₂ remains. [NO₂] = 0.200 M and [N₂O₄] = 0.100 M. Kc = 0.100 ÷ (0.200)² = 2.50 M⁻¹.
Remember to use the 2:1 mole ratio and convert moles to concentrations before substituting.
Which expression is the equilibrium constant, K, for the reaction N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g)?

K is products over reactants, each concentration raised to the power of its coefficient in the balanced equation: [NH₃]²/([N₂][H₂]³). The inverse expression is K for the reverse reaction, and coefficients are never used as multipliers or sums.
What are the units of K for the reaction 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g)?
K = [SO₃]²/([SO₂]²[O₂]), so the units are M²/(M² × M) = M⁻¹, i.e. L mol⁻¹. K only has no units when total moles of gas are equal on both sides.
At a particular temperature, K for the reaction A(g) ⇌ B(g) is 4.0. What is the value of K for 2B(g) ⇌ 2A(g) at the same temperature?
Reversing the equation inverts K (1/4.0 = 0.25), and doubling the coefficients squares it: (0.25)² = 0.0625. 0.25 only accounts for the reversal; 16 only accounts for doubling.
A reaction mixture in a closed vessel has a reaction quotient Q = 2.5 × 10⁻³, while K at that temperature is 1.8 × 10⁻². Which statement is correct?
The net reaction will proceed in the reverse direction until Q decreases to K.
The net reaction will proceed in the forward direction until Q increases to K.
K will decrease until it equals Q.
Q < K means there are relatively too few products, so the forward reaction is favoured until Q rises to equal K. K is fixed at a given temperature; only Q changes.
A reaction has K = 3 × 10¹⁵ at 25 °C. What can be concluded from this value alone?
The reaction is very fast at 25 °C.
At equilibrium, the mixture contains mainly products.
The reaction goes to completion almost instantly once a catalyst is added.
A very large K means the equilibrium position lies far to the right, so products dominate. K gives no information about rate (kinetics) or the sign of ΔH.
0.500 mol of H₂(g) and 0.500 mol of I₂(g) were placed in a sealed 2.00 L vessel at 450 °C. At equilibrium, 0.780 mol of HI(g) was present. H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g). Calculate K at 450 °C. (3 marks)

n(H₂) reacted = n(I₂) reacted = 0.780/2 = 0.390 mol, so 0.110 mol of each remains; equilibrium concentrations: [H₂] = [I₂] = 0.110/2.00 = 0.0550 M, [HI] = 0.780/2.00 = 0.390 M; K = [HI]²/([H₂][I₂]) = 0.390²/(0.0550 × 0.0550) = 50.3 (no units, as the mole totals on each side are equal).

For 2NO₂(g) ⇌ N₂O₄(g), K = 6.0 M⁻¹ at a certain temperature. A mixture at this temperature contains [NO₂] = 0.20 M and [N₂O₄] = 0.50 M. Determine whether the mixture is at equilibrium and, if not, predict how [NO₂] will change. (3 marks)
Q = [N₂O₄]/[NO₂]² = 0.50/(0.20)² = 12.5 M⁻¹; Q > K (12.5 > 6.0), so the system is not at equilibrium; net reverse reaction occurs, so [NO₂] increases (and [N₂O₄] decreases) until Q = K.
Explain what is meant by 'dynamic equilibrium' and state the only factor that changes the value of K for a given reaction. (2 marks)

In a closed system the forward and reverse reactions continue to occur at equal rates, so the concentrations of reactants and products stay constant (no net change), even though particles are still reacting; only a change in temperature changes the value of K.
0.100 mol of N₂O₄ is placed in a sealed 1.00 L flask: N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g). At equilibrium, [NO₂] = 0.060 M. Calculate K.
NO₂ formed = 0.060 mol, so N₂O₄ reacted = 0.030 mol and 0.070 mol remains. K = [NO₂]²/[N₂O₄] = 0.060² ÷ 0.070 = 0.051 M.
chem-3-4: chem-3-4-1
For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), ΔH = −92 kJ mol⁻¹, the volume of the vessel is decreased at constant temperature. How does the system respond?
The equilibrium shifts to the left, because there are more gas particles on the reactant side
There is no shift, because pressure does not affect gaseous equilibria
The equilibrium shifts to the right, because the reaction is exothermic
The equilibrium shifts to the right, because there are fewer gas particles on the product side
Increasing pressure favours the side with fewer moles of gas (2 vs 4), partially opposing the increase.
chem-3-4-2
The temperature of an equilibrium mixture of N₂, H₂ and NH₃ (ΔH = −92 kJ mol⁻¹) is increased. Which statement is correct?
The rate and the equilibrium yield of ammonia both increase
The rate decreases but the equilibrium yield of ammonia increases
The rate increases but the equilibrium yield of ammonia decreases
The rate increases and the yield of ammonia is unchanged
Higher temperature speeds up both reactions but favours the endothermic reverse reaction, reducing the yield.
chem-3-4-3
The Haber process is typically run at about 400–450 °C, even though lower temperatures give a higher equilibrium yield. This is because:
the reaction is endothermic, so high temperatures increase yield
the iron catalyst only increases the yield at high temperatures
ammonia decomposes completely below 400 °C
a moderate temperature gives an acceptable yield at a fast enough rate (a compromise)
At low temperatures the rate is uneconomically slow; ~450 °C balances rate against yield.
chem-3-4-4
Using Le Chatelier's principle, explain why increasing pressure increases the equilibrium yield of ammonia in N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g).

Increasing pressure (by decreasing volume) increases the concentration of all gases. The system partially opposes this by shifting to the side with fewer gas particles; there are 4 mol of gas on the left and 2 mol on the right, so the equilibrium shifts right, increasing the yield of ammonia.
Reference to the mole ratio of gas particles (4:2) is required.
chem-3-4-5
A catalyst is added to an equilibrium mixture of N₂, H₂ and NH₃. What happens to the amount of ammonia?
It increases
It decreases
It does not change
It increases, then returns to its original amount
A catalyst increases forward and reverse rates equally, so the equilibrium position is unaffected.
chem-3-4-6
Argon is added to an equilibrium mixture of N₂, H₂ and NH₃ in a rigid sealed vessel at constant temperature. What happens to the equilibrium position?
It shifts to the right because the total pressure increases
It shifts to the left because argon reacts with ammonia
It shifts to the right because argon acts as a catalyst
It does not shift
At constant volume the concentrations (partial pressures) of the reacting gases are unchanged, so Q still equals K.
chem-3-4-7
In an industrial ammonia plant, ammonia is continuously removed by condensing it. The effect of this is to:
shift the equilibrium to the left, regenerating nitrogen and hydrogen
increase the value of Kc
lower the activation energy of the reaction
shift the equilibrium to the right, increasing the overall conversion of reactants
Removing a product lowers Q below K, so the forward reaction is favoured to replace it.
chem-3-4-8
The Haber process (ΔH = −92 kJ mol⁻¹) is operated at about 450 °C. Explain this choice in terms of both rate and yield.

Because the reaction is exothermic, lower temperatures give a higher equilibrium yield. However, at low temperatures the rate is too slow to be economical. About 450 °C (with an iron catalyst) is a compromise that gives an acceptable yield at a fast enough rate.
Both the yield argument and the rate argument must be addressed.
chem-3-4-9
Fe³⁺(aq) + SCN⁻(aq) ⇌ FeSCN²⁺(aq) is an equilibrium in which FeSCN²⁺ is deep red. A few crystals of KSCN are dissolved in the mixture. What is observed?
The solution becomes a deeper red
The solution becomes paler red
The colour does not change
The solution becomes colourless
Adding SCN⁻ shifts the equilibrium right, forming more red FeSCN²⁺.
For Fe³⁺(aq) + SCN⁻(aq) ⇌ FeSCN²⁺(aq) (deep red), a few drops of AgNO₃ solution are added, precipitating AgSCN. What is observed?
The red colour becomes paler
The red colour deepens
The colour does not change
The solution turns blue
Removing SCN⁻ as a precipitate shifts the equilibrium left, reducing the concentration of FeSCN²⁺.
2NO₂(g) ⇌ N₂O₄(g), ΔH = −57 kJ mol⁻¹. NO₂ is brown and N₂O₄ is colourless. A sealed flask of the equilibrium mixture is placed in hot water. What is observed?
The mixture becomes paler
The colour does not change
The mixture becomes darker brown
The mixture becomes colourless
Heating favours the endothermic reverse reaction, producing more brown NO₂.
A syringe contains an equilibrium mixture of 2NO₂(g) (brown) ⇌ N₂O₄(g) (colourless). The plunger is pushed in and held. Describe and explain the colour changes observed.

The colour immediately becomes darker because [NO₂] increases when the volume decreases. The system then shifts right, towards fewer gas particles, converting some NO₂ to N₂O₄, so the colour lightens. The final colour is still darker than the original because [NO₂] is only partially restored.
Both the immediate effect and the subsequent shift must be explained.
A gas syringe containing an equilibrium mixture of brown NO₂ and colourless N₂O₄ (2NO₂ ⇌ N₂O₄) is quickly compressed to half its volume. What is observed?
The colour lightens immediately and stays lighter than originally
The colour darkens and stays at that darker shade with no further change
There is no colour change because the number of molecules is unchanged
The colour darkens immediately, then lightens somewhat but remains darker than originally
Compression instantly doubles [NO₂]; the system then shifts right (fewer gas particles), partially but not fully reducing [NO₂].
For H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g), the pressure is increased by decreasing the volume. What is the effect on the equilibrium position?
It shifts right, because the products have fewer gas particles
No shift occurs, because there are equal numbers of gas particles on each side
It shifts left, because the reactants have fewer gas particles
It shifts right, because the reaction is exothermic
With 2 mol of gas on each side, changing volume changes Q and K by the same factor, so there is no net shift.
In the contact process, 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g), ΔH = −197 kJ mol⁻¹. Which conditions would give the highest equilibrium yield of SO₃?
Low temperature and high pressure
High temperature and high pressure
Low temperature and low pressure
High temperature and low pressure
The forward reaction is exothermic and reduces the number of gas particles (3 → 2).
For CH₄(g) + H₂O(g) ⇌ CO(g) + 3H₂(g), ΔH = +206 kJ mol⁻¹, predict the effect of increasing the temperature on the value of Kc and on the yield of hydrogen. Explain.

Kc increases and the yield of hydrogen increases. The forward reaction is endothermic, so increasing temperature favours the forward direction to partially absorb the added heat, increasing the product concentrations relative to reactants.
Temperature is the only factor that changes K.
The contact process is usually operated at only slightly above atmospheric pressure, even though high pressure would increase yield. The main reason is that:
high pressure would decrease the yield of SO₃
high pressure would poison the V₂O₅ catalyst
the conversion to SO₃ is already very high at low pressure, so the extra cost of high pressure is not justified
the reaction cannot occur above atmospheric pressure
Conversions of about 99% are achieved at modest pressure, so expensive high-pressure equipment is unnecessary.
Water is added to dilute an equilibrium mixture of Fe³⁺(aq) + SCN⁻(aq) ⇌ FeSCN²⁺(aq). How does the equilibrium respond?
It shifts to the left, the side with more dissolved particles
It shifts to the right, the side with fewer dissolved particles
It does not shift, because all species are diluted equally
It shifts to the right, because water is a product
Dilution lowers the total concentration of particles; the system partially opposes this by favouring the side with more particles (Q > K after dilution).
Extra H₂ is added to the Haber equilibrium mixture at constant volume and temperature. Once equilibrium is re-established, how does [N₂] compare with its value before the H₂ was added?
It is lower
It is higher
It is the same
It is zero
The added H₂ shifts the equilibrium right, consuming some N₂ to form NH₃.
Explain why adding a catalyst does not increase the yield of an equilibrium reaction, yet catalysts are still essential in industrial processes such as the Haber process.

A catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally, so the equilibrium position and yield are unchanged. However, equilibrium is reached much faster, and a reasonable rate can be achieved at a lower temperature, where the equilibrium yield is higher, saving time and energy costs.
Award a mark for the rate benefit and one for enabling lower operating temperature.
Steam reforming of methane is CH₄(g) + H₂O(g) ⇌ CO(g) + 3H₂(g), ΔH = +206 kJ mol⁻¹. Which conditions favour the highest equilibrium yield of hydrogen?
Low temperature and high pressure
High temperature and low pressure
High temperature and high pressure
Low temperature and low pressure
The forward reaction is endothermic and increases the number of gas particles (2 → 4).
Which statement best expresses Le Chatelier's principle?
If an equilibrium system is subjected to a change, the system adjusts to completely reverse that change
If an equilibrium system is subjected to a change, the system adjusts to partially oppose the effect of that change
An equilibrium system always shifts towards the products when disturbed
The value of K changes to oppose any change made to an equilibrium system
The system shifts to partially counteract the change; it cannot fully restore the original conditions.
The temperature of an equilibrium mixture for an endothermic reaction is increased. Which statement is correct once equilibrium is re-established?
The value of K has decreased and the yield of products is smaller
The value of K has increased and the yield of products is greater
The value of K is unchanged but the yield of products is greater
The value of K has increased but the yield of products is smaller
Raising temperature favours the endothermic forward direction, increasing both the product concentrations and K.
For the esterification CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O, suggest two ways to increase the yield of ethyl ethanoate and explain each.

1) Use an excess of ethanol (or ethanoic acid): increasing a reactant concentration shifts the equilibrium right. 2) Remove a product as it forms, e.g. by distilling off the ester or using concentrated H₂SO₄ to absorb water: lowering product concentration shifts the equilibrium right.
Any two valid methods with a Le Chatelier explanation are acceptable; a catalyst alone does not increase yield.

Extra O₂ is added at constant volume and temperature to an equilibrium mixture of 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g). Describe how [O₂], [SO₂], [SO₃] and Kc compare with their original values once equilibrium is re-established.
[O₂] is higher than originally (but lower than immediately after the addition); [SO₂] is lower; [SO₃] is higher; Kc is unchanged because the temperature is constant.
The system only partially opposes the addition of O₂, so [O₂] remains above its original value.
chem34a2-lc-1
N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g), ΔH = +58 kJ mol⁻¹. N₂O₄ is colourless and NO₂ is brown. A sealed syringe of the equilibrium mixture is placed in hot water. Which observation and explanation are correct?
The mixture becomes paler because the reverse reaction is endothermic.
The mixture becomes browner and the value of K increases.
The mixture becomes browner but the value of K is unchanged.
No colour change occurs because temperature only affects rate.

Increasing temperature favours the endothermic (forward) direction to partially absorb the added energy, producing more brown NO₂. For an endothermic reaction, K increases with temperature, so K does change.
chem34a2-lc-2
A catalyst is added to a system already at equilibrium. Which statement is correct?
The equilibrium position shifts to the right.
The value of K increases.
The forward rate increases more than the reverse rate.
The forward and reverse rates increase equally, so the position does not change.

A catalyst lowers the activation energy for both the forward and reverse reactions by the same amount, so both rates increase equally. Equilibrium is reached faster, but the position and K are unchanged.
chem34a2-lc-3
The volume of a vessel containing H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g) at equilibrium is suddenly halved at constant temperature. I₂ is purple. What is observed?
The colour becomes darker and the equilibrium position does not shift.
The colour becomes darker and then fades as the equilibrium shifts right.
The colour becomes paler because the reaction shifts right.
There is no change in colour or concentrations.
Halving the volume doubles every concentration, so [I₂] increases and the colour darkens. Both sides have 2 mol of gas, so Q still equals K and there is no shift.
chem34a2-lc-4
Argon gas is added to an equilibrium mixture of 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g) in a rigid, sealed container at constant temperature. What happens?
The equilibrium shifts right because total pressure increased.
The equilibrium shifts left because argon reacts with SO₃.
The equilibrium position does not change.
K increases because total pressure increased.

At constant volume, adding an inert gas does not change the concentrations (partial pressures) of the reacting species, so Q stays equal to K and nothing shifts. A total pressure rise alone is not a disturbance to the equilibrium.
chem34a2-lc-5

A concentration–time graph for 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g) shows that at time t, [SO₃] jumps up vertically and then gradually decreases, while [SO₂] and [O₂] gradually increase from t until new constant values. What change was made at time t?
The temperature was increased.
Some SO₃ was added to the vessel.
The volume of the vessel was decreased.
A catalyst was added.

Only [SO₃] shows an instantaneous jump, which indicates SO₃ was added. A volume change would make all concentrations jump at once; a temperature change produces only gradual changes; a catalyst causes no change at all once at equilibrium.
chem34a2-lc-6

Methanol is made by CO(g) + 2H₂(g) ⇌ CH₃OH(g), ΔH = −91 kJ mol⁻¹. Explain the effect of increasing pressure, by decreasing the volume at constant temperature, on the equilibrium yield of methanol and on K. (3 marks)

Decreasing volume increases the concentrations of all gases (increases pressure); by Le Chatelier's principle the system partially opposes this by shifting to the side with fewer gas particles, i.e. forward (3 mol → 1 mol); so the yield of methanol increases; K is unchanged because temperature is constant.
chem34a2-lc-7

Fe³⁺(aq) + SCN⁻(aq) ⇌ FeSCN²⁺(aq). FeSCN²⁺ is deep red. Water is added to double the volume of an equilibrium mixture. Using the reaction quotient, explain the direction of the shift and the colour change observed. (3 marks)

Dilution halves every concentration, so Q = [FeSCN²⁺]/([Fe³⁺][SCN⁻]) becomes (½)/(½ × ½) = 2 × the original value, i.e. Q > K; the net reverse reaction occurs (towards the side with more particles in solution) until Q = K; the solution becomes paler red, both due to dilution and to some FeSCN²⁺ converting back to Fe³⁺ and SCN⁻.
chem34a2-lc-8

For the exothermic reaction N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), the temperature of an equilibrium mixture is increased at constant volume. Describe the changes you would see on a concentration–time graph for all three species, and state the effect on K. (3 marks)

There is no sudden vertical jump in any concentration at the moment of change; [NH₃] gradually decreases while [N₂] and [H₂] gradually increase (the changes in N₂ : H₂ : NH₃ are in the ratio 1 : 3 : 2) until new constant (horizontal) values are reached; K decreases because the reverse (endothermic) reaction is favoured at higher temperature.
chem34a2-ind-1
The Haber process (N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), ΔH = −92 kJ mol⁻¹) operates at about 400–450 °C. Why is a lower temperature not used?
Lower temperatures would decrease the equilibrium yield of ammonia.
The iron catalyst only works below 200 °C.
Lower temperatures would give a higher yield, but the rate would be too slow to be economical.
Ammonia decomposes at temperatures below 400 °C.

Because the forward reaction is exothermic, lower temperatures favour a higher equilibrium yield. However, fewer particles would have energy ≥ Ea, so the rate would be uneconomically slow; ~400–450 °C is a compromise between rate and yield.
chem34a2-ind-2
Which statement best describes the role of the iron catalyst in the Haber process?
It increases the rate of reaction without changing the equilibrium yield.
It increases the equilibrium yield by shifting the position to the right.
It increases the value of K.
It makes the reaction more exothermic.
A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy, so equilibrium is reached faster. It does not alter ΔH, K or the equilibrium yield.
chem34a2-ind-3
In the Haber process, the gas mixture leaving the reactor is cooled so that ammonia condenses and is removed; the unreacted N₂ and H₂ are recycled. What is the main effect of this?
It increases K for the reaction.
It increases the overall conversion of N₂ and H₂ into ammonia.
It increases the rate by raising the temperature of the reactor.
It reduces the need for high pressure to zero.
Removing NH₃ and recycling unreacted gases means reactants pass through the reactor repeatedly, so nearly all N₂ and H₂ are eventually converted. K depends only on temperature and is not changed.
chem34a2-ind-4
In the contact process, 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g) is exothermic and has fewer gas particles on the product side, yet it is run at only slightly above atmospheric pressure. What is the best reason?
High pressure would decrease the yield of SO₃.
The V₂O₅ catalyst is destroyed at high pressure.
Pressure has no effect on this equilibrium.
Conversion is already very high (about 99%) at low pressure, so the extra cost of high-pressure equipment is not justified.

Le Chatelier's principle predicts higher pressure would increase yield, but with a V₂O₅ catalyst, moderate temperature and multiple catalyst beds the conversion is already near-complete, so the cost and safety risks of high pressure are not worthwhile.
chem34a2-ind-5
An engineer proposes raising the temperature of an exothermic equilibrium reaction in an industrial reactor. Which pair of effects is expected?
Rate increases; equilibrium yield increases.
Rate decreases; equilibrium yield increases.
Rate increases; equilibrium yield decreases.
Rate is unchanged; equilibrium yield decreases.

Higher temperature increases the proportion of successful collisions, so rate increases. For an exothermic forward reaction, higher temperature favours the reverse reaction, so K and the equilibrium yield decrease.
chem34a2-ind-6
Methanol is manufactured by CO(g) + 2H₂(g) ⇌ CH₃OH(g), ΔH = −91 kJ mol⁻¹, at about 250 °C and 50–100 atm with a Cu/ZnO catalyst. Explain why these conditions are a compromise. (3 marks)

Lower temperature would favour a higher equilibrium yield (exothermic forward reaction) but the rate would be too slow, so a moderate temperature with a catalyst gives an acceptable rate; high pressure increases both rate (more frequent collisions) and yield (shift to fewer gas particles, 3 mol → 1 mol); pressure is not raised further because of the energy cost of compression and the cost and safety risk of stronger equipment.
chem34a2-ind-7
A Haber process plant uses 10.0 tonnes of N₂ in excess H₂ and collects 2.50 tonnes of NH₃ in a single pass. Calculate the percentage yield. (3 marks)
chem34a2-ind-8
Explain how the use of a catalyst in an industrial process supports the green chemistry principle of energy efficiency. (2 marks)

A catalyst lowers the activation energy, so an acceptable rate can be reached at a lower temperature; this means less energy (often from fossil fuels) is needed for heating, reducing costs and CO₂ emissions; a catalyst is also not consumed, so it can be reused.
chem-3-4-c1
Argon is added to an equilibrium mixture of N₂, H₂ and NH₃ in a rigid container at constant temperature. The equilibrium position:
Shifts right, because the total pressure increases and the right side has fewer particles

Shifts left, because argon dilutes the mixture and the left side has more particles
Shifts right, because adding an inert gas increases the value of K
Total pressure rises, but in a fixed volume each reacting gas keeps the same concentration, so the reaction quotient still equals K.

In an electrolytic cell, oxidation occurs at the

cathode, which is connected to the negative terminal of the power supply
anode, which is connected to the negative terminal of the power supply
cathode, which is connected to the positive terminal of the power supply
Oxidation always occurs at the anode; in an electrolytic cell the anode is the positive electrode because the power supply draws electrons away from it.

Which energy transformation occurs in an electrolytic cell?
Chemical energy to electrical energy
Electrical energy to chemical energy

An external power supply forces a non-spontaneous reaction to occur, storing electrical energy as chemical energy in the products.

With no water present, the only species that can be reduced is Na⁺, giving Na(l) at the cathode.

Anode: 2Br⁻(l) → Br₂(g) + 2e⁻. Cathode: K⁺(l) + e⁻ → K(l).

Molten sodium chloride is electrolysed using inert electrodes. The product at the anode is

oxygen gas
hydrogen gas
chlorine gas
Cl⁻ is the only species available to be oxidised in the melt: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻.

Hydrogen gas and hydroxide ions
Sodium metal
Chlorine gas

Water (E° = −0.83 V) is a far stronger oxidant than Na⁺ (E° = −2.71 V), so 2H₂O + 2e⁻ → H₂ + 2OH⁻ occurs.
chem-4-1-7
Dilute aqueous sodium sulfate is electrolysed with platinum electrodes. The ratio of the volume of gas at the cathode to that at the anode (same conditions) is
Water is electrolysed: 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂, so hydrogen (cathode) and oxygen (anode) form in a 2 : 1 mole and volume ratio.
chem-4-1-8
Explain why sodium metal is not produced when dilute aqueous sodium chloride is electrolysed.
Water is a stronger oxidant than Na⁺ (E° −0.83 V compared with −2.71 V), so water is reduced at the cathode to H₂ and OH⁻ instead of Na⁺ being reduced to Na.
Refer to relative oxidant strengths using the electrochemical series.
chem-4-1-9
During electrolysis of aqueous copper(II) sulfate with graphite electrodes, which observation is expected over time?
The blue colour deepens and the solution becomes basic
The solution colour stays constant and the pH stays constant
The blue colour fades and the solution becomes more acidic
A green gas forms at the anode
Cu²⁺ is removed as copper at the cathode (colour fades) while water is oxidised at the anode producing O₂ and H⁺ (pH falls).
Aqueous copper(II) sulfate is electrolysed using copper electrodes. Which statement is correct?
Oxygen gas forms at the anode and the solution becomes acidic
Hydrogen gas forms at the cathode
The concentration of Cu²⁺ decreases steadily
The anode is oxidised to Cu²⁺ and the concentration of Cu²⁺ in solution stays approximately constant
Copper metal is a stronger reductant than water, so the anode dissolves at the same rate Cu²⁺ is deposited at the cathode.
In the industrial electrolysis of concentrated brine, chlorine rather than oxygen is the main anode product. This is mainly because
the high Cl⁻ concentration and the large overpotential for O₂ formation favour oxidation of Cl⁻
Cl⁻ is a stronger reductant than water under standard conditions
oxygen cannot be formed in any aqueous electrolysis
sodium ions block water from reaching the anode
Under standard conditions water (1.23 V) would be oxidised before Cl⁻ (1.36 V), but high [Cl⁻] and the overpotential for O₂ make Cl₂ the main product.
Write the overall equation for the electrolysis of dilute sulfuric acid using platinum electrodes.
2H₂O(l) → 2H₂(g) + O₂(g)
Cathode: 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂; anode: 2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻; H⁺ cancels, leaving decomposition of water.
Aqueous potassium iodide is electrolysed with inert electrodes. The products at the anode and cathode respectively are
oxygen and potassium
iodine and hydrogen
iodine and potassium
oxygen and hydrogen
I⁻ (E° 0.54 V) is a stronger reductant than water (1.23 V) so it is oxidised to I₂; water is reduced to H₂ in preference to K⁺.
Aluminium is produced by electrolysing alumina dissolved in molten cryolite rather than an aqueous solution because
Al³⁺ is a stronger oxidant than water
aluminium compounds are insoluble in all solvents
water would be reduced in preference to Al³⁺
molten electrolytes do not conduct electricity
Al³⁺ (E° = −1.66 V) is a much weaker oxidant than water (−0.83 V), so in water only H₂ would form at the cathode.
Using standard electrode potentials (Cu²⁺/Cu = +0.34 V, O₂/H₂O = +1.23 V), the theoretical minimum voltage to electrolyse aqueous CuSO₄ with inert electrodes is
Minimum voltage = E°(anode reaction couple) − E°(cathode reaction couple) = 1.23 − 0.34 = 0.89 V.
Aqueous nickel(II) sulfate is electrolysed with inert electrodes. Write the overall equation.
2Ni²⁺(aq) + 2H₂O(l) → 2Ni(s) + O₂(g) + 4H⁺(aq)
Ni²⁺ (−0.23 V) is a stronger oxidant than water (−0.83 V), so Ni deposits; sulfate is not oxidised so water is oxidised to O₂.
In an electrolytic cell, electrons in the external circuit flow
from the anode to the positive terminal of the power supply, and from the negative terminal to the cathode
from the cathode to the anode through the electrolyte
from the cathode through the power supply to the anode
through the electrolyte from anode to cathode
Electrons are released at the anode, pumped by the power supply and delivered to the cathode; ions, not electrons, carry charge through the electrolyte.
In an electrolytic cell, cations in the electrolyte migrate towards the
anode, which is negative
cathode, which is negative
cathode, which is positive
anode, which is positive
Positive ions are attracted to the negative electrode, which in an electrolytic cell is the cathode where reduction occurs.
Aqueous silver nitrate is electrolysed using platinum electrodes. The products are
hydrogen at the cathode and oxygen at the anode
silver at the cathode and nitrogen dioxide at the anode
silver at the cathode and oxygen at the anode

Ag⁺ (0.80 V) is a stronger oxidant than water so silver deposits; NO₃⁻ is not oxidised, so water is oxidised to O₂.
Using E°(I₂/I⁻) = +0.54 V and E°(H₂O/H₂) = −0.83 V, calculate the minimum theoretical voltage needed to electrolyse aqueous potassium iodide.
The applied voltage must at least equal the difference between the oxidation and reduction couples; in practice more is needed because of resistance and overpotential.
During electrolysis of aqueous sodium chloride, the pH of the solution near the cathode
decreases
stays at 7
first increases and then returns to 7 immediately
increases
Reduction of water at the cathode produces OH⁻ ions, raising the local pH.
In the Downs cell for producing sodium from molten NaCl, calcium chloride is added mainly to
lower the melting point of the electrolyte and reduce energy costs
act as a catalyst for chlorine formation
increase the melting point so sodium does not boil
provide calcium ions to be reduced instead of sodium
The NaCl/CaCl₂ mixture melts at about 600 °C rather than 801 °C, saving energy.
In the Downs cell, the sodium and chlorine products must be kept separated mainly because
chlorine dissolves in liquid sodium without reacting
they would react together to re-form sodium chloride
sodium is a gas at the operating temperature
chlorine would be reduced back to Cl⁻ at the anode
Sodium is a powerful reductant and chlorine a powerful oxidant; if they mix they react vigorously, reversing the electrolysis.
Explain why an electrolytic cell requires an external power supply.

The reaction in an electrolytic cell is non-spontaneous (the strongest oxidant present lies below the strongest reductant in the electrochemical series), so electrical energy must be supplied to force electrons from the anode to the cathode.
Mention non-spontaneity and that the supply drives electron flow.
Explain why graphite or platinum is often chosen as the electrode material in electrolysis.
They are inert: they conduct electricity but do not react themselves, so the products depend only on the species in the electrolyte.
A reactive anode, such as copper, would itself be oxidised and change the products.
chem34a2-ely-1
Which statement about an electrolytic cell is correct?
Oxidation occurs at the anode, which is the positive electrode.
Oxidation occurs at the anode, which is the negative electrode.
Reduction occurs at the anode, which is the positive electrode.
Reduction occurs at the cathode, which is the positive electrode.

In all cells oxidation occurs at the anode. In an electrolytic cell the anode is connected to the positive terminal of the power supply, which draws electrons away from it. (In a galvanic cell the anode is negative.)
chem34a2-ely-2
Molten sodium chloride is electrolysed using inert electrodes. What are the products at the cathode and anode?
Cathode: H₂(g); anode: Cl₂(g)
Cathode: Na(l); anode: Cl₂(g)
Cathode: Cl₂(g); anode: Na(l)
Cathode: Na(l); anode: O₂(g)
In the molten salt the only species are Na⁺ and Cl⁻ (no water). Na⁺ is reduced at the cathode: Na⁺(l) + e⁻ → Na(l); Cl⁻ is oxidised at the anode: 2Cl⁻(l) → Cl₂(g) + 2e⁻.
chem34a2-ely-3
A 1.0 M Na₂SO₄(aq) solution is electrolysed using platinum electrodes. Which products form?
Na(s) at the cathode and SO₂(g) at the anode
Na(s) at the cathode and O₂(g) at the anode
H₂(g) at the anode and O₂(g) at the cathode
H₂(g) at the cathode and O₂(g) at the anode, in a 2 : 1 volume ratio
Water is a stronger oxidant than Na⁺ (−0.83 V vs −2.71 V), so 2H₂O + 2e⁻ → H₂ + 2OH⁻ at the cathode. SO₄²⁻ is not oxidised; water is: 2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻. Balancing electrons gives 2 H₂ : 1 O₂.
chem34a2-ely-4
CuSO₄(aq) is electrolysed using copper electrodes. Which statement is correct?
Oxygen gas forms at the anode and [Cu²⁺] decreases.
Copper dissolves from the cathode and deposits on the anode.
The anode loses mass, the cathode gains mass, and [Cu²⁺] stays approximately constant.
Hydrogen forms at the cathode and the solution becomes basic.

Cu(s) is a stronger reductant than water, so the copper anode is oxidised: Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻. Cu²⁺ is reduced at the cathode. Cu²⁺ enters and leaves at the same rate, so its concentration stays about constant (the basis of copper refining).
chem34a2-ely-5
Which statement correctly compares an electrolytic cell with a galvanic cell?
An electrolytic cell converts chemical energy into electrical energy.
An electrolytic cell uses electrical energy to drive a non-spontaneous redox reaction.
Both cells require a salt bridge to function.
In both cells the cathode is the negative electrode.

An electrolytic cell converts electrical energy into chemical energy, forcing a reaction that would not occur spontaneously. A galvanic cell does the reverse. Electrolytic cells often have a single electrolyte container with no salt bridge, and their cathode is negative while a galvanic cathode is positive.
chem34a2-ely-6

1.0 M KI(aq) is electrolysed with inert graphite electrodes. Using the electrochemical series, write the half-equations at each electrode, the overall equation, and one observation at each electrode. (4 marks)

Cathode: 2H₂O(l) + 2e⁻ → H₂(g) + 2OH⁻(aq) (water, −0.83 V, is a stronger oxidant than K⁺, −2.93 V); anode: 2I⁻(aq) → I₂(aq) + 2e⁻ (I⁻ is a stronger reductant than H₂O, since I₂/I⁻ at +0.54 V is below O₂/H₂O at +1.23 V); overall: 2I⁻(aq) + 2H₂O(l) → I₂(aq) + H₂(g) + 2OH⁻(aq); observations: bubbles of colourless gas at the cathode (pH rises there), brown/yellow colour forming around the anode.
chem34a2-ely-7
Explain why sodium metal is produced industrially by electrolysis of molten NaCl rather than aqueous NaCl. (2 marks)

In aqueous solution water is a much stronger oxidant than Na⁺ (E° −0.83 V vs −2.71 V), so water would be reduced to H₂ at the cathode instead of Na⁺; in addition, any sodium formed would react vigorously with water; in molten NaCl there is no water, so Na⁺ is the only species that can be reduced.
chem34a2-ely-8
A steel spoon is to be electroplated with silver. Describe the setup (electrode materials, polarity and electrolyte) and write the half-equations at each electrode. (3 marks)

The spoon is the cathode, connected to the negative terminal; a silver anode is connected to the positive terminal, with AgNO₃(aq) (a solution of Ag⁺) as the electrolyte; cathode: Ag⁺(aq) + e⁻ → Ag(s); anode: Ag(s) → Ag⁺(aq) + e⁻, which replaces the Ag⁺ removed so [Ag⁺] stays constant.
chem-4-1-c1
Dilute aqueous potassium iodide is electrolysed with inert electrodes. The main products at the cathode and the anode are:
Potassium at the cathode; iodine at the anode
Hydrogen gas at the cathode; oxygen gas at the anode
Hydrogen gas at the cathode; iodine at the anode
Iodine at the cathode; hydrogen gas at the anode
Water (−0.83 V) is a stronger oxidant than K⁺ (−2.93 V), so water is reduced to H₂. I⁻ (I₂/I⁻ +0.54 V) is a stronger reductant than water (+1.23 V), so I₂ forms.

independent of the time of electrolysis

Q = It = 2.00 A × (10.0 × 60) s = 1.20 × 10³ C. 20.0 C results from forgetting to convert minutes to seconds; 1.24 × 10⁻² is the amount of electrons in mol, not the charge.

The mass of product is inversely proportional to the current.
The amount of product formed is independent of the charge on the ion.
To deposit one mole of a metal, the number of moles of electrons required equals the charge on the metal ion.

a galvanic cell
a fuel cell
a primary cell

The discharge products remain in contact with the electrodes so the reaction can be reversed

becomes the cathode and is connected to the positive terminal
becomes the cathode and is connected to the negative terminal of the charger

Pb²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → Pb(s)

from the graphite electrode to the metal oxide electrode

has a low molar mass and a very low reduction potential, giving a high voltage and energy density
is the most abundant metal in the Earth's crust

Li⁺ + C₆ + e⁻ → LiC₆

The electrolyte in a lithium-ion battery is non-aqueous because
water would not conduct electricity
lithium reacts with water
lithium salts are insoluble in water
water would make the battery too heavy

To recharge a battery, the positive terminal of the charger must be connected to
the negative electrode of the battery, which becomes the anode
the positive electrode of the battery, which becomes the cathode
the positive electrode of the battery, which becomes the anode during recharging
either electrode, as polarity does not matter
Like terminals are connected so the charger forces electrons out of the positive electrode, oxidising the discharge product there.
A rechargeable battery gradually loses capacity after hundreds of cycles. A likely reason is
the Faraday constant changes with use
the battery becomes a primary cell
the electrolyte becomes a stronger oxidant over time
side reactions and physical changes to the electrodes reduce the amount of reactant that can be regenerated
Examples include large PbSO₄ crystals forming (sulfation), dendrite growth and electrode material breaking down.
Explain why the charger voltage must be greater than the battery's voltage during recharging.
The recharge reaction is non-spontaneous, so the applied voltage must exceed the cell's EMF to push electrons in the reverse direction and also overcome internal resistance.
Mention reversing the spontaneous reaction and resistance/overpotential losses.
Overcharging a lead–acid battery can produce gases. These gases are
hydrogen and oxygen
chlorine and hydrogen
sulfur dioxide and oxygen
carbon dioxide and hydrogen
Once PbSO₄ is used up, the applied voltage electrolyses water in the electrolyte, giving H₂ at the cathode and O₂ at the anode.
In a nickel–metal hydride (NiMH) cell, the half-equation at the anode during discharge is
M + H₂O + e⁻ → MH + OH⁻
MH + OH⁻ → M + H₂O + e⁻
NiOOH + H₂O + e⁻ → Ni(OH)₂ + OH⁻
Ni²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Ni
The metal hydride is oxidised in the alkaline electrolyte; NiOOH is reduced at the cathode.
Which equation represents the overall reaction when a lead–acid battery is recharged?
Pb + PbO₂ + 4H⁺ + 2SO₄²⁻ → 2PbSO₄ + 2H₂O
2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂
2PbSO₄ + 2H₂O → Pb + PbO₂ + 4H⁺ + 2SO₄²⁻
Pb + SO₄²⁻ → PbSO₄ + 2e⁻
Recharging is the reverse of discharge, regenerating Pb, PbO₂ and sulfuric acid.
Explain how the labels anode/cathode and the polarity of each electrode change when a rechargeable battery switches from discharge to recharge.

The polarity of each electrode stays the same (negative stays negative), but the labels swap: the negative electrode is the anode on discharge and the cathode on recharge, and the positive electrode is the cathode on discharge and the anode on recharge.
Anode is always the site of oxidation; polarity is fixed by how the charger is connected.
In a lithium-ion cell with a LiCoO₂ cathode, what is reduced at the cathode during discharge?
Lithium, from +1 to 0
Oxygen, from −2 to −1
Carbon in the graphite
Cobalt, from the +4 to the +3 oxidation state
Li⁺ + CoO₂ + e⁻ → LiCoO₂: cobalt's oxidation number falls from +4 to +3; Li stays +1.
Which of the following is a primary (non-rechargeable) cell?
Alkaline zinc–manganese dioxide cell
Lead–acid cell
Lithium-ion cell
Nickel–metal hydride cell
Standard alkaline cells are designed for single use; the others are common secondary cells.
During discharge of a lead–acid battery, the oxidation number of lead at the positive electrode changes from
0 to +2
+2 to 0
PbO₂ (Pb +4) is reduced to PbSO₄ (Pb +2).
A standard car battery is labelled 12 V. Each lead–acid cell produces about 2 V. Explain how the battery achieves 12 V.
Six cells of about 2 V each are connected in series, so their voltages add to about 12 V.
Voltages add for cells in series.
Give one advantage and one disadvantage of lithium-ion batteries for electric vehicles in Australia.

Advantage: high energy density and low mass give a long driving range and many recharge cycles. Disadvantage: risk of thermal runaway/fire, high cost, or environmental impacts of mining lithium and cobalt.
Any one valid advantage and disadvantage.
chem34a2-bat-1
When a rechargeable (secondary) cell is being recharged, which statement is correct?
It operates as a galvanic cell, and the electrode polarities reverse.
The electrode that was the anode during discharge becomes the cathode.
The negative terminal of the charger is connected to the positive electrode of the cell.
The spontaneous discharge reaction runs faster.

During recharging the cell operates as an electrolytic cell and the discharge reaction is reversed. The electrode that was oxidised (anode) on discharge is now reduced (cathode). The charger's negative terminal connects to the cell's negative electrode, and the polarities themselves stay the same.
chem34a2-bat-2
Why can a lead–acid car battery be recharged, while a standard alkaline cell is not designed to be?
The lead–acid battery has a higher voltage.
The discharge products in a lead–acid battery are gases that can be recaptured.
The discharge product PbSO₄(s) stays in contact with the electrodes, so it can be converted back into reactants.
Lead is a stronger oxidant than zinc.

For a cell to be recharged, its discharge products must stay in contact with the electrodes so the reaction can be reversed. In the lead–acid battery solid PbSO₄ forms on both electrodes. If products diffused or escaped as gas, recharging would not regenerate the reactants.
chem34a2-bat-3
Overall discharge reaction of a lead–acid battery: Pb(s) + PbO₂(s) + 4H⁺(aq) + 2SO₄²⁻(aq) → 2PbSO₄(s) + 2H₂O(l). As the battery discharges, what happens to the electrolyte?
Its pH decreases and its density increases.
Its sulfuric acid concentration increases.
It turns blue as Pb²⁺ ions accumulate.
Its sulfuric acid concentration and density decrease.

H⁺ and SO₄²⁻ are consumed and water is produced, so [H₂SO₄] falls, the pH rises, and the density of the electrolyte decreases. PbSO₄ is an insoluble white solid, so Pb²⁺ does not build up in solution.
chem34a2-bat-4
During discharge of a lithium-ion battery, which describes the movement of lithium ions?
Li⁺ ions move from the graphite anode through the electrolyte to the metal oxide cathode.
Li⁺ ions move from the metal oxide cathode to the graphite anode.
Li⁺ ions move through the external circuit with the electrons.
Li atoms move through the separator to the anode.

On discharge, lithium in the graphite is oxidised (LiC₆ → C₆ + Li⁺ + e⁻), and Li⁺ travels through the non-aqueous electrolyte to the cathode, where it is inserted into the metal oxide. Electrons travel through the external circuit, not ions. The direction reverses on recharge.
chem34a2-bat-5
Which factor best explains why a rechargeable battery gradually loses its capacity after many charge–discharge cycles?
The electrolyte is converted into electrons.
Side reactions and physical degradation of the electrodes mean that not all products are reconverted into reactants.
The value of E° for each half-cell steadily increases.
The battery runs as a fuel cell after many cycles.

Over many cycles, unwanted side reactions (e.g. electrolyte breakdown) and changes to the electrode structure (e.g. crystals forming, cracking) mean that some material can no longer take part in the reversible reaction, so capacity falls.
chem34a2-bat-6

A lithium-ion cell discharges according to: anode LiC₆(s) → C₆(s) + Li⁺ + e⁻; cathode CoO₂(s) + Li⁺ + e⁻ → LiCoO₂(s). (a) Write the half-equation occurring at the graphite electrode during recharging. (b) State which terminal of the charger the graphite electrode is connected to, and explain. (3 marks)

(a) C₆(s) + Li⁺ + e⁻ → LiC₆(s); (b) the negative terminal of the charger; during recharge reduction occurs at the graphite electrode (it is the cathode), so it must be supplied with electrons from the negative terminal (it remains the negative electrode of the cell).
chem34a2-bat-7
Write the overall equation for recharging a lead–acid battery, and identify the species oxidised and the species reduced during recharging. (3 marks)
2PbSO₄(s) + 2H₂O(l) → Pb(s) + PbO₂(s) + 4H⁺(aq) + 2SO₄²⁻(aq); PbSO₄ at the positive electrode is oxidised (Pb from +2 to +4 in PbO₂); PbSO₄ at the negative electrode is reduced (Pb from +2 to 0).
chem34a2-bat-8
Explain why lithium-ion batteries use a non-aqueous electrolyte, and give one safety concern associated with them. (2 marks)

Lithium is a very strong reductant (Li⁺/Li E° = −3.04 V) and would react with water to produce H₂ gas, and water would be reduced/oxidised in preference at the high cell voltage; safety concern: the organic electrolyte is flammable, so overcharging, damage or overheating can lead to thermal runaway and fire.
chem-4-3-c1
The electrode that acts as the anode while a rechargeable cell discharges becomes, during recharging:
The cathode, connected to the negative terminal of the charger
The anode, connected to the positive terminal of the charger
The cathode, connected to the positive terminal of the charger
Inactive, because only one electrode reacts during recharging
Recharging reverses the reactions: oxidation becomes reduction at that electrode, so it is now the cathode. The negative terminal of the charger supplies its electrons.
chem-4-4: chem-4-4-1
To electroplate a brass key with silver, the key should be
the cathode, connected to the negative terminal
the anode, connected to the positive terminal
the cathode, connected to the positive terminal
the anode, connected to the negative terminal
Ag⁺ ions are reduced to silver on the object, so the object must be the cathode (negative electrode).
chem-4-4-2
In silver plating, the anode is usually made of
graphite
pure silver
the object being plated
platinum
A silver anode is oxidised to Ag⁺, replacing the ions deposited at the cathode.
chem-4-4-3
A suitable electrolyte for silver electroplating is a solution containing
sodium chloride
copper(II) sulfate
silver ions, such as silver nitrate
dilute sulfuric acid only
The electrolyte must contain the ions of the metal to be deposited.
chem-4-4-4
Describe how a steel spoon could be electroplated with nickel. Include the electrodes, electrolyte and half-equations.
The spoon is the cathode (negative terminal) and a nickel bar is the anode (positive terminal), both in NiSO₄(aq), connected to a DC supply. Cathode: Ni²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Ni; anode: Ni → Ni²⁺ + 2e⁻.
Must identify object as cathode, nickel anode, Ni²⁺ electrolyte and both half-equations.
chem-4-4-5
When an object is copper-plated using a copper anode and CuSO₄(aq) electrolyte, the concentration of Cu²⁺(aq)
decreases steadily
increases steadily
falls to zero
remains approximately constant
Copper dissolves from the anode at the same rate as it is deposited at the cathode.
chem-4-4-6
In electrolytic refining of copper, silver and gold impurities in the impure anode
fall to the bottom of the cell as anode sludge
are deposited on the pure copper cathode
are oxidised and remain dissolved in solution
form gases at the anode
Ag and Au are weaker reductants than Cu so they are not oxidised; they drop off as the anode dissolves.
chem-4-4-7
In copper refining, zinc impurities in the anode
fall to the bottom as sludge
are oxidised to Zn²⁺ but are not reduced at the cathode
are deposited at the cathode with copper
are reduced to zinc at the anode
Zn is a stronger reductant than Cu so it is oxidised, but Zn²⁺ is a weaker oxidant than Cu²⁺ so it stays in solution.
chem-4-4-8
A watch is gold-plated from a solution containing Au(I) ions using 0.200 A for 15.0 minutes. Calculate the mass of gold deposited.
Au⁺ + e⁻ → Au, a 1:1 ratio.
chem-4-4-9
Which statement correctly compares the anode in galvanic and electrolytic cells?
The anode is positive in both cells
The anode is negative in both cells
The anode is negative in a galvanic cell and positive in an electrolytic cell
The anode is positive in a galvanic cell and negative in an electrolytic cell
Oxidation occurs at the anode in both, but polarity depends on whether electrons are released spontaneously or withdrawn by a power supply.
Which statement about spontaneity is correct?
Both types of cell involve spontaneous reactions
Electrolytic cell reactions are spontaneous; galvanic cell reactions are non-spontaneous
Neither type of cell involves redox reactions
Galvanic cell reactions are spontaneous; electrolytic cell reactions are non-spontaneous
Galvanic cells release energy from a spontaneous redox reaction; electrolytic cells need energy input.
A feature common to both galvanic and electrolytic cells is that
reduction occurs at the cathode
the cathode is positive
an external power supply is required
a salt bridge is always required
In every electrochemical cell, oxidation is at the anode and reduction is at the cathode.
Compare galvanic and electrolytic cells in terms of energy conversion and the polarity of the anode.
Galvanic: chemical → electrical energy, anode negative. Electrolytic: electrical → chemical energy, anode positive.
Both points are needed for full marks.
The energy transformation in a galvanic cell is
electrical energy to chemical energy
chemical energy to electrical energy
electrical energy to light energy
thermal energy to chemical energy
A galvanic cell converts the chemical energy of a spontaneous redox reaction into electrical energy.
Why does a typical electrolytic cell not need a salt bridge, whereas a galvanic cell does?
Electrolytic cells do not need ions to move
Salt bridges only work with molten electrolytes
In a galvanic cell the half-cells are separated to stop direct reaction, so a salt bridge completes the circuit; electrolytic electrodes usually share one electrolyte
Galvanic cells have no electrolyte
Separating the oxidant and reductant in a galvanic cell forces electrons through the wire; the salt bridge balances charge.
An object is being chrome-plated from a Cr³⁺ solution. The half-equation at the object is
Cr(s) → Cr³⁺(aq) + 3e⁻
2H₂O(l) → O₂(g) + 4H⁺(aq) + 4e⁻
Cr³⁺(aq) → Cr⁶⁺(aq) + 3e⁻
Cr³⁺(aq) + 3e⁻ → Cr(s)
The object is the cathode, where chromium ions are reduced to chromium metal.
Explain why the copper deposited at the cathode in electrolytic refining is purer than the anode.
Only Cu²⁺, the strongest oxidant present, is reduced at the cathode; more reactive impurities such as Zn and Fe remain in solution as ions, and less reactive Ag and Au fall as sludge.
Refer to relative oxidant/reductant strengths.
Before nickel plating, the steel object is thoroughly cleaned. The main reason is to
ensure the plated metal adheres evenly to the surface
increase the voltage of the cell
make the object the anode
prevent nickel ions forming
Grease or oxide layers prevent a uniform, well-bonded coating forming.
In ideal silver plating using a silver anode, how does the mass lost by the anode compare with the mass gained by the cathode?
The anode loses twice the mass gained by the cathode
They are equal
The cathode gains twice the mass lost by the anode
The anode does not lose mass
The same number of electrons flow at each electrode, so equal moles (and mass) of silver dissolve and deposit.
For the electrolysis of a solution to occur, the applied voltage must be
less than the cell's E° difference
exactly zero
greater than the difference between the E° values of the couples involved
equal to the Faraday constant
The reaction is non-spontaneous, so at least the E° difference (plus overpotential and resistance losses) must be supplied.
Explain why an inert graphite anode is not used when copper-plating an object from CuSO₄(aq).

Water rather than copper would be oxidised at the anode, producing O₂ and H⁺, so Cu²⁺ would not be replenished; its concentration would fall and the solution would become acidic, slowing and changing plating.
A copper anode maintains [Cu²⁺].
Steel sheet can be electroplated with zinc. Zinc continues to protect the steel even when the coating is scratched because
zinc is a weaker reductant than iron
zinc does not react with water or oxygen
iron is plated over the zinc
zinc is a stronger reductant than iron and is oxidised in preference
Zinc acts as a sacrificial anode, being oxidised instead of iron.
Which change would increase the rate at which metal is deposited in an electroplating cell (assuming no side reactions)?
Increasing the current
Decreasing the current
Using a larger anode at the same current
Adding more water to dilute the electrolyte
Rate of deposition is proportional to current, since mass ∝ It.
In both galvanic and electrolytic cells, anions in the electrolyte migrate towards the
cathode
anode
power supply
salt bridge only in electrolytic cells
Anions move towards the anode to balance the positive charge building up from oxidation (or the electron loss) there.
A plate with surface area 50.0 cm² is silver-plated using 2.00 A for 30.0 minutes. Given the density of silver is 10.5 g cm⁻³, calculate the thickness of the silver layer in micrometres.
1 cm = 10⁴ µm.
State the polarity of the cathode in a galvanic cell and in an electrolytic cell, and explain the difference.

Galvanic cathode is positive; electrolytic cathode is negative. In a galvanic cell electrons are consumed spontaneously at the cathode leaving it relatively positive; in an electrolytic cell the power supply pushes electrons onto the cathode, making it negative.
Reduction occurs at the cathode in both cells.
chem-4-4-c1
A spoon is silver-plated using a silver anode and an AgNO₃ electrolyte. Why does [Ag⁺] stay almost constant?
Ag⁺ ions take no part in either reaction; only water is oxidised and reduced
Silver atoms are oxidised at the anode at the same rate as Ag⁺ ions are reduced at the cathode
Nitrate ions are reduced at the cathode, which releases Ag⁺ ions back into the solution
Water is oxidised at the anode, and this reaction produces new Ag⁺ ions
Each electron through the circuit removes one Ag⁺ at the cathode and adds one Ag⁺ at the anode.
chem-5-1: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂CH₂OH?
Three-carbon chain (prop-) with an –OH on carbon 1 gives propan-1-ol.
What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH(OH)CH₃?
The longest chain has three carbons and the –OH is on the middle carbon, carbon 2.
What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂COOH?
The carboxyl carbon is counted in the chain, giving three carbons: propanoic acid.
What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂CHO?
A –CHO group at the end of a three-carbon chain is an aldehyde, propanal.
What is the IUPAC name of CH₃COCH₂CH₃?
Four carbons with a C=O on carbon 2 (not at the chain end) is the ketone butan-2-one.
What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH=CHCH₃?
Four carbons with the double bond starting at carbon 2 is but-2-ene.
What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃?
The longest chain is four carbons with a methyl branch; numbering from the nearer end gives locant 2.
What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂Cl?
A four-carbon chain with Cl on the end carbon; lowest locant is 1.
What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂NH₂?
A two-carbon chain bearing an amino (–NH₂) group is the amine ethanamine.
What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CONH₂?
The –CONH₂ amide group includes the carbonyl carbon, so the two-carbon amide is ethanamide.
What is the IUPAC name of CH₃COOCH₂CH₃?
CH₃COO– is the ethanoate part (from ethanoic acid) and –CH₂CH₃ is the ethyl part (from ethanol).
Which functional group is characteristic of all alcohols?
Alcohols contain an –OH group bonded to a saturated carbon atom.
Which of the following compounds contains a carbonyl (C=O) functional group?
Propanone, CH₃COCH₃, is a ketone containing C=O; the others have no carbonyl group.
Butan-2-ol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃, is classified as which type of alcohol?
The carbon bearing the –OH is bonded to two other carbon atoms, making it a secondary alcohol.
2-Methylpropan-2-ol, (CH₃)₃COH, is classified as which type of alcohol?
The –OH carbon is bonded to three other carbon atoms, so it is a tertiary alcohol.
What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂CH(CH₃)CH₂OH?
The longest chain containing the –OH carbon has four carbons; numbering from the –OH end puts the methyl on carbon 2.
Which general formula represents the alkane homologous series?
Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons with general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, e.g. C₃H₈.
What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CHClCH₂CH₃?
Four-carbon chain with Cl on carbon 2; numbering from the nearer end gives 2 rather than 3.
Give the IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₂OH.
Write the condensed structural formula of 3-methylpentane.
A five-carbon chain with a methyl branch on the middle (third) carbon.
A student names a compound '3-methylbutane'. Explain why this name is incorrect and give the correct name.
The chain should be numbered from the end nearer the branch to give the lowest locant, so the correct name is 2-methylbutane.
IUPAC rules require the lowest possible locants for substituents.
Give the IUPAC name of HCOOCH₃.
HCOO– comes from methanoic acid and –CH₃ from methanol; the alkyl (alcohol) part is named first.
Lactic acid, found in sour milk and fatigued muscles, has the formula CH₃CH(OH)COOH. Identify its two functional groups and give its IUPAC name.
Hydroxyl (–OH) and carboxyl (–COOH) groups; IUPAC name 2-hydroxypropanoic acid.
The carboxyl carbon is carbon 1, so the –OH is on carbon 2 of a three-carbon acid.
Give the molecular formula of heptan-1-ol.
Alcohols follow CₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH; with n = 7 this is C₇H₁₅OH.
Ethanol (M = 46 g/mol) boils at 78 °C, whereas propane (M = 44 g/mol) boils at –42 °C. Explain the difference.
Ethanol molecules form hydrogen bonds between their –OH groups as well as dispersion forces, whereas propane has only weak dispersion forces; more energy is needed to separate ethanol molecules.
Molar masses are similar, so dispersion forces are similar; the difference is due to hydrogen bonding.
What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃?

The longest carbon chain has 4 carbons (butane), with a methyl branch on carbon 2 when numbered to give the lowest locant. '3-methylbutane' numbers from the wrong end; '2-ethylpropane' does not use the longest chain.
What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CH₃?
The parent chain has 4 carbons and the –OH is on carbon 2 when numbered to give it the lowest locant, so butan-2-ol. Numbering from the other end gives the incorrect butan-3-ol.
What is the IUPAC name of CH₃COOCH₂CH₃?
The acid-derived part, CH₃COO–, has 2 carbons (ethanoate); the alcohol-derived part, –CH₂CH₃, is ethyl. The ester is named alkyl (from the alcohol) then alkanoate (from the acid): ethyl ethanoate.
What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH(NH₂)CH₃?
The amine group is on the middle carbon of a 3-carbon chain, so propan-2-amine. Propan-1-amine would be CH₃CH₂CH₂NH₂.
What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH=C(CH₃)CH₃?

The longest chain containing the double bond has 4 carbons. Numbering from the right gives the double bond locant 2 either way, so the tie is broken by giving the methyl group the lowest locant (2): 2-methylbut-2-ene.
Write the semi-structural (condensed) formula for (a) 3-methylpentanoic acid and (b) 1,2-dichloropropane. (2 marks)
(a) CH₃CH₂CH(CH₃)CH₂COOH (carbon 1 is the carboxyl carbon, methyl on carbon 3); (b) CH₂ClCHClCH₃.
A student named a compound '2-ethylbutane'. Explain why this name is incorrect and give the correct IUPAC name. (2 marks)

The name does not use the longest carbon chain: an ethyl group on carbon 2 of butane extends the main chain to 5 carbons; drawing it as CH₃CH(CH₂CH₃)CH₂CH₃ shows the longest chain is 5 carbons with a methyl on carbon 3, so the correct name is 3-methylpentane.
Propan-1-ol reacts with butanoic acid. Name the ester produced and write its semi-structural formula. (2 marks)
The IUPAC name of CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH(OH)CH₃ is:
The longest chain containing the OH has 5 carbons. Number from the end nearer the OH: OH on C2, methyl on C4.
chem-5-2: How many structural isomers have the molecular formula C₄H₁₀?
Butane and 2-methylpropane are the only two arrangements of four carbons.
How many structural isomers have the molecular formula C₅H₁₂?
How many structural isomers have the molecular formula C₆H₁₄?
Which pair of compounds are structural isomers?
Both are C₄H₁₀O but with different arrangements of atoms; the other pairs have different molecular formulas.
Which compound is a structural isomer of ethyl ethanoate (C₄H₈O₂)?
Butanoic acid, CH₃CH₂CH₂COOH, is also C₄H₈O₂.
Which compound is a structural isomer of propanal?
Propanal and propanone both have the formula C₃H₆O.
How many structural isomers have the formula C₃H₇Cl?
How many structural isomers have the formula C₄H₉Br?
Structural isomers are compounds that have
the same structural formula but different molecular formulas
the same molecular formula and the same arrangement of atoms
the same molecular formula but different structural formulas
different molecular formulas but the same molar mass
Isomers share a molecular formula; structural isomers differ in how the atoms are bonded.
Pentane and 2,2-dimethylpropane are best described as
Both are C₅H₁₂ and differ only in the branching of the carbon chain.
Propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol are best described as
Same carbon chain and functional group, but the –OH is in a different position.
Propanal and propanone are best described as
Both are C₃H₆O, but one is an aldehyde and the other a ketone.
Which isomer of C₄H₁₀O is a tertiary alcohol?
