In 2-methylpropan-2-ol the –OH carbon is bonded to three other carbons.
How many alcohols have the molecular formula C₄H₁₀O?
Which isomer of C₅H₁₂ has the lowest boiling point?
They all boil at the same temperature as they have the same molar mass
The most branched, compact isomer has the smallest contact area and weakest dispersion forces.
Ignoring stereoisomers, how many alkenes have the molecular formula C₄H₈?
Which compound is NOT a structural isomer of hexane?
2-Methylhexane has seven carbons (C₇H₁₆), so it is not C₆H₁₄.
How many carboxylic acids have the molecular formula C₄H₈O₂?
Name the three structural isomers of C₅H₁₂.
All three are C₅H₁₂ with different degrees of branching.
Name the two esters with the molecular formula C₃H₆O₂.
Propanoic acid is also C₃H₆O₂ but is a carboxylic acid, not an ester.
Explain why pentane (36 °C) has a higher boiling point than its isomer 2,2-dimethylpropane (10 °C).
Pentane is an unbranched chain, so its molecules have a larger surface area of contact and stronger dispersion forces; the compact, branched 2,2-dimethylpropane has weaker dispersion forces.
Award the mark only if dispersion forces are linked to molecular shape/contact area.
Give the condensed structural formulas and names of the two alcohols with formula C₃H₈O.
Explain why but-1-ene and butane are not isomers.
They have different molecular formulas: but-1-ene is C₄H₈ and butane is C₄H₁₀.
Isomers must have the same molecular formula.
Give the name of the positional isomer of 1-chloropentane in which the chlorine is on the middle carbon.
The middle carbon of a five-carbon chain is carbon 3.
Butanal and 2-methylpropanal are two carbonyl compounds with the formula C₄H₈O. Name the ketone that is also an isomer of these.
It is the only ketone with four carbons; a C=O on carbon 2 is the only possible ketone position.
How many structural isomers have the molecular formula C₄H₁₀?
There are two: butane (straight chain) and 2-methylpropane (branched). Bending a chain or drawing it differently on paper does not create a new isomer.
Which compound can exist as cis and trans isomers?

Cis–trans isomerism needs restricted rotation about C=C and two different groups on each carbon of the double bond. In but-2-ene each double-bond carbon has H and CH₃. But-1-ene and 2-methylpropene each have one carbon bearing two identical groups.
Which molecule contains a chiral carbon atom?
In butan-2-ol, carbon 2 is bonded to four different groups: H, OH, CH₃ and CH₂CH₃. In propan-2-ol carbon 2 has two identical CH₃ groups, so it is not chiral.
Two enantiomers of a compound are compared. In which property would they differ?
Their interaction with plane-polarised light or with other chiral molecules, such as enzymes

Enantiomers are non-superimposable mirror images with identical physical properties in a non-chiral environment. They rotate plane-polarised light in opposite directions and can interact differently with chiral biological molecules such as enzymes and receptors.
How many structural isomers have the formula C₃H₇Cl?
Chlorine can be on an end carbon (1-chloropropane) or the middle carbon (2-chloropropane). 3-chloropropane is the same molecule as 1-chloropropane.
Explain why but-2-ene exists as cis and trans isomers, but propene (CH₂=CHCH₃) does not. (3 marks)

There is no rotation about a carbon–carbon double bond, so groups attached to the double-bond carbons are fixed in position; in but-2-ene each double-bond carbon has two different groups (H and CH₃), so the CH₃ groups can be on the same side (cis) or opposite sides (trans); in propene one double-bond carbon has two identical H atoms, so swapping them gives the same molecule and no cis–trans isomers exist.
Name the four structural isomers of C₄H₉OH that are alcohols, and identify which one is chiral. (3 marks)
Butan-1-ol, butan-2-ol, 2-methylpropan-1-ol and 2-methylpropan-2-ol; butan-2-ol is chiral because carbon 2 is bonded to four different groups (H, OH, CH₃, C₂H₅).
Many medicines contain a chiral carbon. Explain why pharmaceutical companies may need to produce a single enantiomer rather than a mixture of both. (2 marks)

Biological receptors and enzymes are themselves chiral, so only one enantiomer may fit the active site and produce the desired effect; the other enantiomer may be inactive (wasting material) or cause harmful side effects, as in the case of thalidomide.
How many structural isomers have the formula C₄H₉Cl, and how many of them have a chiral carbon?
1-chlorobutane, 2-chlorobutane, 1-chloro-2-methylpropane and 2-chloro-2-methylpropane. Only C2 of 2-chlorobutane has four different groups (H, Cl, CH₃, CH₂CH₃).
chem-5-3: Ethene reacts with steam in the presence of a phosphoric acid catalyst. What is the organic product?
Addition of H₂O across the C=C double bond produces ethanol.
What type of reaction occurs when ethene reacts with bromine?
Br₂ adds across the double bond to form 1,2-dibromoethane.
Propene reacts with hydrogen chloride. Which of the following is a possible organic product?
HCl adds across the C=C, giving a chloropropane (2-chloropropane and/or 1-chloropropane).
Which catalyst is commonly used for the addition of hydrogen to an alkene?
Hydrogenation of alkenes uses a metal catalyst such as Ni, Pt or Pd.
Chloroethane reacts with aqueous sodium hydroxide to form ethanol. This reaction is classified as
The –Cl atom is replaced by an –OH group.
Chloroethane reacts with ammonia. What is the organic product?
NH₃ substitutes for the Cl atom, producing ethanamine (CH₃CH₂NH₂) and HCl.
Propan-1-ol is heated under reflux with excess acidified potassium dichromate. What is the final organic product?
A primary alcohol is fully oxidised under reflux, via propanal, to the carboxylic acid.
Propan-2-ol is heated with acidified potassium permanganate. What is the organic product?
Secondary alcohols are oxidised to ketones.
2-Methylpropan-2-ol is warmed with acidified potassium dichromate. What is observed?
no reaction occurs and the solution stays orange
2-methylpropanal forms and the solution turns green
2-methylpropanoic acid forms and the solution turns green
butan-2-one forms and the solution turns green
Tertiary alcohols have no H on the –OH carbon, so they are not oxidised by dichromate.
When acidified potassium dichromate oxidises an alcohol, the colour change observed is
Orange Cr₂O₇²⁻ is reduced to green Cr³⁺.
When acidified potassium permanganate oxidises an alcohol, the colour change observed is
Purple MnO₄⁻ is reduced to almost colourless Mn²⁺.
Ethanoic acid reacts with ethanol in the presence of concentrated sulfuric acid. This reaction is classified as
Two molecules join to form an ester with the loss of a water molecule.
What is the main role of concentrated sulfuric acid in an esterification reaction?
H₂SO₄ speeds up the reaction without being consumed (it also absorbs water).
N-methylethanamide, CH₃CONHCH₃, is hydrolysed in acidic solution. What are the products?
Hydrolysis breaks the C–N amide bond, giving the carboxylic acid and the amine.
Which statement best describes a condensation reaction?
a molecule is split by reaction with water
atoms are added across a double bond
two molecules join together with the loss of a small molecule such as water
one atom or group is replaced by another
Esterification and amide formation are examples of condensation.
What small molecule is eliminated when an ester forms from a carboxylic acid and an alcohol?
–OH from the acid and H from the alcohol combine as H₂O.
Ethyl ethanoate is heated with aqueous sodium hydroxide. What are the products?
Base hydrolysis gives the alcohol and the salt of the carboxylic acid.
Methane reacts with chlorine in UV light to form chloromethane and hydrogen chloride. This reaction is classified as
A hydrogen atom on the alkane is replaced by a chlorine atom.
Write a balanced equation for the reaction of ethene with steam and state the catalyst and reaction type.
C₂H₄(g) + H₂O(g) → CH₃CH₂OH(g); phosphoric acid (H₃PO₄) catalyst; addition reaction.
States are optional for the equation mark; the catalyst and reaction type must be given.
Write a balanced equation for the reaction of 1-bromopropane with aqueous sodium hydroxide.
CH₃CH₂CH₂Br + NaOH → CH₃CH₂CH₂OH + NaBr (or CH₃CH₂CH₂Br + OH⁻ → CH₃CH₂CH₂OH + Br⁻).
This is a substitution producing propan-1-ol.
Explain why alkenes undergo addition reactions but alkanes do not.
Alkenes are unsaturated, containing a C=C double bond that can open to bond to added atoms; alkanes are saturated with only single bonds, so they can only undergo substitution.
Reference to the C=C double bond/unsaturation is essential.
Explain how the conditions of oxidising ethanol with acidified dichromate determine whether ethanal or ethanoic acid is the main product.
Distilling the ethanal off as it forms (limited oxidant) stops further oxidation, giving ethanal; heating under reflux with excess oxidant oxidises it fully to ethanoic acid.
Ethanal is an intermediate in the oxidation of a primary alcohol.
What is the atom economy for producing ethanol by the hydration of ethene? Explain.
100%, because it is an addition reaction in which all reactant atoms end up in the single desired product.
Atom economy = mass of desired product ÷ total mass of reactants × 100.
Calculate the atom economy for producing ethanol from chloroethane and sodium hydroxide: C₂H₅Cl + NaOH → C₂H₅OH + NaCl. (M: C₂H₅Cl 64.5, NaOH 40.0, C₂H₅OH 46.0 g/mol)
The NaCl by-product lowers the atom economy compared with hydration of ethene.
Describe a simple chemical test to distinguish hexene from hexane.
Add bromine water: hexene rapidly decolourises it (orange/brown to colourless) by addition across the C=C; hexane does not decolourise it quickly.
Alkanes only react with bromine slowly in UV light.
Ethene reacts with steam at about 300 °C with a phosphoric acid catalyst. What is the product and type of reaction?
H₂O adds across the C=C double bond (hydration), giving CH₃CH₂OH. It is an addition reaction because two reactants join to form one product and the double bond is lost.
Which reaction is a substitution reaction?
In the first reaction the Cl atom of chloroethane is replaced by an –OH group. The two alkene reactions are additions, and the last is combustion.
Propan-1-ol is heated with excess acidified potassium dichromate solution. Which observation and product are correct?
The solution changes from green to orange; propanoic acid forms.
The solution changes from orange to green; propanoic acid forms.
The solution changes from purple to colourless; propene forms.
No colour change; propyl propanoate forms.

Cr₂O₇²⁻ (orange) is reduced to Cr³⁺ (green) as the primary alcohol is oxidised to the carboxylic acid CH₃CH₂COOH. The purple-to-colourless change is seen with acidified permanganate, and propene is not an oxidation product.
Which statement about the formation of an ester from a carboxylic acid and an alcohol is correct?
It is an addition reaction that needs UV light.
It requires a strong base such as NaOH as a catalyst.
It is a condensation reaction catalysed by concentrated H₂SO₄, and water is a by-product.
Esterification joins the acid and alcohol with the loss of a small molecule (H₂O), so it is a condensation reaction. It is reversible and catalysed by concentrated sulfuric acid under heat (reflux).
Ethane is mixed with chlorine gas and exposed to UV light. Which equation shows the first product formed?

Alkanes are saturated, so they undergo substitution, not addition: one H atom is replaced by Cl, with HCl as the other product. C₂H₆Cl₂ is not possible because carbon cannot form more than four bonds.
Write a balanced equation, using semi-structural formulas, for the reaction between ethanoic acid and methanol. Name the organic product and state the conditions required. (3 marks)
CH₃COOH(l) + CH₃OH(l) ⇌ CH₃COOCH₃(l) + H₂O(l); product is methyl ethanoate; conditions: a few drops of concentrated H₂SO₄ as a catalyst and heating under reflux.
Chloroethane reacts with ammonia to form an amine. Write the balanced equation, name the organic product and identify the type of reaction. (3 marks)
CH₃CH₂Cl + NH₃ → CH₃CH₂NH₂ + HCl; the product is ethanamine; this is a substitution reaction (the Cl atom is replaced by –NH₂).
Bromine water is added to propene and to propane in separate test tubes. Describe and explain the observations, including an equation for any reaction. (3 marks)

Propene decolourises the orange/brown bromine water quickly; Br₂ adds across the C=C double bond: CH₂=CHCH₃ + Br₂ → CH₂BrCHBrCH₃ (1,2-dibromopropane); propane is saturated and does not react (without UV light), so the orange colour remains.
Which alkene gives only one product when it reacts with HCl?
But-2-ene is symmetrical, so Cl adding to either carbon gives 2-chlorobutane. The others can each form two different chloroalkanes.
chem-5-4: chem-5-4-1
Which two-step pathway converts ethene into ethanoic acid?
react with HCl, then heat with NaOH(aq)
react with H₂ (Ni catalyst), then heat with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇
react with steam (H₃PO₄ catalyst), then heat under reflux with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇
react with steam (H₃PO₄ catalyst), then heat with concentrated H₂SO₄ and methanol
Hydration gives ethanol, which is oxidised to ethanoic acid.
chem-5-4-2
Which pair of reactants produces ethyl propanoate?
propan-1-ol and ethanoic acid
ethanol and ethanoic acid
propan-1-ol and propanoic acid
ethanol and propanoic acid
The '-ethyl' part comes from the alcohol and 'propanoate' from the carboxylic acid.
chem-5-4-3
What is the name of the ester formed from methanol and butanoic acid?
methyl butanoate
butyl methanoate
methyl propanoate
propyl methanoate
The alcohol gives the alkyl name (methyl) and the acid gives the -oate name (butanoate).
chem-5-4-4
Propyl ethanoate, CH₃COOCH₂CH₂CH₃, is formed from which reactants?
ethanol and propanoic acid
propan-1-ol and ethanoic acid
propan-2-ol and ethanoic acid
propanoic acid and propan-1-ol
The propyl group comes from propan-1-ol and the ethanoate from ethanoic acid.
chem-5-4-5
What is the molecular formula of ethyl ethanoate?
C₄H₁₀O₂
C₃H₆O₂
C₄H₈O₂
C₄H₈O
CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ contains 4 C, 8 H and 2 O atoms.
chem-5-4-6
Which pathway converts chloroethane into ethanoic acid?
heat with NH₃, then heat with acidified KMnO₄
react with H₂O and H₃PO₄, then react with H₂ and Ni
heat with acidified KMnO₄, then heat with NaOH(aq)
heat with NaOH(aq), then heat under reflux with acidified KMnO₄
Substitution gives ethanol, which is then oxidised to ethanoic acid.
chem-5-4-7
Which two-step pathway produces ethanamine from ethene?
add HCl, then react the chloroethane with NH₃
add H₂O, then react the ethanol with NH₃
add H₂, then react the ethane with NH₃
add HCl, then react the chloroethane with NaOH(aq)
Addition gives chloroethane; substitution of Cl by NH₃ gives ethanamine.
chem-5-4-8
Why does ethyl ethanoate (77 °C) have a lower boiling point than butanoic acid (164 °C), even though they are isomers?
ethyl ethanoate has a smaller molar mass
ester molecules cannot form hydrogen bonds with each other, whereas carboxylic acid molecules can
ethyl ethanoate has stronger dispersion forces
esters are ionic compounds
Esters lack an O–H group, so only dipole–dipole and dispersion forces act between their molecules.
chem-5-4-9
A student reacted 12.0 g of ethanoic acid (M = 60.0 g/mol) with excess ethanol and obtained 14.1 g of ethyl ethanoate (M = 88.0 g/mol). What is the percentage yield?
A two-step synthesis has a yield of 80% for step 1 and 75% for step 2. What is the overall percentage yield?
Biodiesel is made by reacting a triglyceride (vegetable oil) with methanol using a KOH catalyst. The products are
fatty acid methyl esters and glycerol
fatty acids and methanol
glycerol and water
methyl ethanoate and fatty acids
Transesterification swaps glycerol for methanol, forming methyl esters (biodiesel) and glycerol.
Which reagents convert ethanol directly into ethyl ethanoate in one step?
acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ under reflux
ethanoic acid with a concentrated H₂SO₄ catalyst
NaOH(aq)
steam with an H₃PO₄ catalyst
Esterification of ethanol with ethanoic acid produces ethyl ethanoate.
Methyl propanoate is hydrolysed in dilute acid. What are the products?
propan-1-ol and methanoic acid
methanol and propanal
methanol and propanoic acid
ethanol and ethanoic acid
Hydrolysis reverses esterification, giving back the alcohol and carboxylic acid.
Which group of atoms is characteristic of an ester?
–COOH
–CONH–
–OH
–COO– (ester linkage)
Esters contain a carbonyl carbon bonded to an oxygen that links to an alkyl group.
What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂COOCH₂CH₂CH₃?
propyl propanoate
ethyl propanoate
propyl ethanoate
propyl butanoate
CH₃CH₂COO– is propanoate and –CH₂CH₂CH₃ is propyl.
2-Chloropropane is heated with NaOH(aq), and the organic product is then heated with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇. What is the final organic product?
propanal
propanone
propanoic acid
propan-1-ol
Substitution gives propan-2-ol, a secondary alcohol, which oxidises to the ketone propanone.
Calculate the atom economy for making ethyl ethanoate: CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH → CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O. (M: CH₃COOH 60.0, C₂H₅OH 46.0, CH₃COOC₂H₅ 88.0 g/mol)
Pentyl ethanoate has a banana-like odour. Which reactants form it?
ethanol and pentanoic acid
pentan-1-ol and methanoic acid
butan-1-ol and ethanoic acid
pentan-1-ol and ethanoic acid
The pentyl group comes from pentan-1-ol and the ethanoate from ethanoic acid.
Outline a reaction pathway to make ethyl ethanoate using ethene as the only organic starting material. Give reagents for each step.

1) Ethene + steam with H₃PO₄ catalyst → ethanol. 2) Oxidise some ethanol with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ (or KMnO₄) under reflux → ethanoic acid. 3) React ethanol with ethanoic acid using concentrated H₂SO₄ catalyst → ethyl ethanoate + water.
Both the alcohol and acid parts can be made from the ethanol produced in step 1.
Write a balanced equation for the formation of methyl ethanoate.
CH₃COOH + CH₃OH ⇌ CH₃COOCH₃ + H₂O (concentrated H₂SO₄ catalyst).
Esterification is a reversible condensation reaction.
23.0 g of ethanol (M = 46.0 g/mol) reacts with excess ethanoic acid. If the yield is 65.0%, what mass of ethyl ethanoate (M = 88.0 g/mol) is obtained?
The mole ratio of ethanol to ester is 1:1.
Name CH₃CH₂COOCH₂CH₃ and the products of its acid hydrolysis.
Ethyl propanoate; hydrolysis gives propanoic acid and ethanol.
Hydrolysis breaks the ester linkage, adding water.
Give a two-step pathway, with reagents, to convert chloroethane into ethanoic acid.
1) Heat with NaOH(aq) (substitution) → ethanol. 2) Heat under reflux with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ or KMnO₄ (oxidation) → ethanoic acid.
Both reagents and the intermediate (ethanol) should be stated.
Name the ester formed from ethanol and methanoic acid and give its condensed formula.
Ethyl methanoate, HCOOCH₂CH₃.
Ethyl from ethanol; methanoate from methanoic acid.
A three-step synthesis has yields of 90%, 80% and 75%. Calculate the overall percentage yield.
Multiply the fractional yields of each step.
chem34a2-syn-1
Which reagents would convert ethene into ethanoic acid in two steps?
Step 1: H₂/Ni; Step 2: Cl₂/UV light
Step 1: H₂O(g)/H₃PO₄; Step 2: H⁺/Cr₂O₇²⁻
Step 1: HCl; Step 2: NaOH(aq)
Step 1: H⁺/Cr₂O₇²⁻; Step 2: H₂O(g)/H₃PO₄

Hydration of ethene gives ethanol, and acidified dichromate then oxidises the primary alcohol to ethanoic acid. The reverse order fails because dichromate does not convert ethene to an alcohol. HCl then NaOH only gives ethanol.
chem34a2-syn-2
What is the atom economy for the production of ethanol by the reaction CH₂=CH₂(g) + H₂O(g) → CH₃CH₂OH(g)?
Cannot be determined without the percentage yield

Atom economy = (molar mass of desired product / total molar mass of reactants) × 100. All atoms in the reactants end up in ethanol (28.0 + 18.0 = 46.0), so atom economy is 100%. Atom economy is independent of percentage yield.
chem34a2-syn-3
Ethanol can also be made by CH₃CH₂Cl + NaOH → CH₃CH₂OH + NaCl. What is the atom economy for ethanol? (M: C₂H₅Cl = 64.5, NaOH = 40.0, C₂H₅OH = 46.0 g mol⁻¹)
Atom economy = 46.0/(64.5 + 40.0) × 100 = 46.0/104.5 × 100 = 44.0%. 71.3% uses only chloroethane as the reactant mass; the NaCl by-product represents wasted atoms.
chem34a2-syn-4
A three-step synthesis has step yields of 80%, 70% and 90%. What is the overall percentage yield?
Overall yield is the product of the step yields: 0.80 × 0.70 × 0.90 = 0.504, about 50%. The yields are multiplied, not averaged or added.
chem34a2-syn-5
A reaction has a percentage yield of 95% but an atom economy of 30%. Which statement is correct?
Most of the reactant atoms end up in the desired product.
The reaction is close to completion, but most of the reactant atoms end up in by-products.
The yield must be wrong because it cannot be higher than the atom economy.
The reaction produces no waste.

Percentage yield compares actual with theoretical product. Atom economy measures what fraction of the reactant mass can ever become the desired product. A process can run almost to completion yet still produce mostly unwanted by-products.
chem34a2-syn-6
12.0 g of ethanoic acid was heated under reflux with excess ethanol and concentrated H₂SO₄. 11.0 g of ethyl ethanoate was obtained. Calculate the percentage yield. (3 marks)
n(CH₃COOH) = 12.0/60.0 = 0.200 mol; 1 : 1 ratio, so theoretical n(CH₃COOCH₂CH₃) = 0.200 mol, mass = 0.200 × 88.0 = 17.6 g; percentage yield = 11.0/17.6 × 100 = 62.5%.
chem34a2-syn-7
Outline a synthetic pathway to produce ethyl ethanoate using ethene as the only organic starting material. Include the reagents and conditions for each step. (3 marks)

Step 1: ethene + steam with H₃PO₄ catalyst (about 300 °C) → ethanol; step 2: oxidise part of the ethanol with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ (or KMnO₄), heated, → ethanoic acid; step 3: react ethanoic acid with the remaining ethanol, heated under reflux with concentrated H₂SO₄ as a catalyst → ethyl ethanoate + water.
chem34a2-syn-8

Calculate the atom economy for producing ethyl ethanoate by CH₃COOH + CH₃CH₂OH ⇌ CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ + H₂O, and suggest one way the percentage yield of this equilibrium reaction could be increased. (3 marks)

Molar masses: CH₃COOH 60.0, C₂H₅OH 46.0, ester 88.0 g mol⁻¹; atom economy = 88.0/(60.0 + 46.0) × 100 = 83.0%; yield could be increased by using an excess of one reactant (e.g. ethanol) or by removing the ester or water as it forms, shifting the equilibrium to the right.
chem-5-4-c1
10.0 g of ethanol reacts with excess propanoic acid. The yield of ethyl propanoate (M = 102.0 g/mol) is 65%. What mass of ester is obtained?
n(ethanol) = 10.0 ÷ 46.0 = 0.2174 mol = n(ester) in theory. Theoretical mass = 0.2174 × 102.0 = 22.2 g; 65% of that is 14.4 g.
chem-5-5: chem34a2-phys-1
Which compound has the highest boiling point?
Butane, C₄H₁₀
Methyl methanoate, HCOOCH₃
Propan-1-ol, C₃H₇OH
Ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH

All have similar molar masses (58–60 g mol⁻¹). Ethanoic acid forms two hydrogen bonds between pairs of molecules (dimers) via both the C=O and O–H, giving stronger intermolecular forces than propan-1-ol. The ester cannot hydrogen bond between its own molecules, and butane has only dispersion forces.
chem34a2-phys-2
Why do boiling points increase from methane to octane in the alkane homologous series?
Hydrogen bonding increases with chain length.
Longer molecules have more electrons and greater surface area, so dispersion forces are stronger.
The C–C covalent bonds become stronger.
Longer alkanes are more polar.
Alkanes are non-polar, so their only intermolecular forces are dispersion forces, which strengthen as molecular size and contact area increase. Boiling does not break covalent bonds.
chem34a2-phys-3
Pentane boils at 36 °C and its isomer 2,2-dimethylpropane boils at 10 °C. What is the best explanation?
2,2-dimethylpropane has a lower molar mass.
Pentane can form hydrogen bonds.
The compact, branched shape of 2,2-dimethylpropane gives less surface contact, so its dispersion forces are weaker.
Branching makes the C–H bonds weaker.

Isomers have the same molar mass. The straight-chain pentane molecules can lie close together over a large area, giving stronger dispersion forces. The near-spherical branched isomer has a smaller contact area.
chem34a2-phys-4
Which statement explains why the solubility of alcohols in water decreases from methanol to hexan-1-ol?
The longer non-polar hydrocarbon chain disrupts hydrogen bonding with water and cannot itself interact strongly with water.
The –OH group becomes less polar as the chain gets longer.
Larger alcohols react with water.
Larger alcohols have fewer hydrogen atoms.

Each alcohol has one –OH group that can hydrogen bond with water, but as the non-polar alkyl chain lengthens, an increasing part of the molecule only has dispersion forces, which do not compensate for disrupting water's hydrogen-bond network.
chem34a2-phys-5
Moving from hexane to decane in the alkane series, how do viscosity and flash point change?
Viscosity decreases; flash point decreases.
Viscosity increases; flash point decreases.
Viscosity decreases; flash point increases.
Viscosity increases; flash point increases.

Longer chains have stronger dispersion forces and can tangle, so they flow less easily (higher viscosity). They are also less volatile, so a higher temperature is needed before enough vapour forms to ignite (higher flash point).
chem34a2-phys-6
Ethanol (M = 46 g mol⁻¹) boils at 78 °C, while propane (M = 44 g mol⁻¹) boils at −42 °C. Explain this difference with reference to intermolecular forces. (3 marks)

The two molecules have similar molar masses, so their dispersion forces are of similar strength; ethanol has an –OH group (H bonded to highly electronegative O), so hydrogen bonds form between ethanol molecules; propane is non-polar with only dispersion forces, so much less energy is needed to separate its molecules, giving a much lower boiling point.
chem34a2-phys-7
Methyl ethanoate (CH₃COOCH₃) and propanoic acid (CH₃CH₂COOH) are isomers. Explain why methyl ethanoate has a much lower boiling point. (2 marks)

Propanoic acid has an O–H group, so it can form hydrogen bonds between its molecules (including dimers); methyl ethanoate has no H atom bonded to O, so it cannot form hydrogen bonds between its own molecules and has only weaker dipole–dipole and dispersion forces, which need less energy to overcome.
chem34a2-phys-8

Propan-1-amine (CH₃CH₂CH₂NH₂) boils at 48 °C and propan-1-ol boils at 97 °C. Explain why both have higher boiling points than butane (−1 °C), but the amine boils at a lower temperature than the alcohol. (3 marks)

Both the amine (N–H) and the alcohol (O–H) can form hydrogen bonds between molecules, whereas butane has only dispersion forces, so they boil higher; N is less electronegative than O, so the N–H bond is less polar and the hydrogen bonds in the amine are weaker; therefore less energy is needed to separate amine molecules than alcohol molecules.
chem-5-5-c1
Propan-1-ol (M = 60), propanal (M = 58) and butane (M = 58) have similar molar masses. Their boiling points in decreasing order are:
Propan-1-ol > propanal > butane
Butane > propanal > propan-1-ol
Propanal > propan-1-ol > butane
All about the same, because their molar masses are similar
Propan-1-ol has hydrogen bonding; propanal has dipole–dipole attraction; butane has only dispersion forces.
chem-6-1: chem-6-1-1
In a mass spectrum, the molecular ion peak (M⁺) corresponds to:
the ion formed when a whole molecule loses one electron
the most abundant ion detected in the spectrum
the smallest fragment ion produced
the ion formed when a molecule gains one electron
The molecular ion is the intact molecule minus one electron, so its m/z equals the molecular mass of the compound.
chem-6-1-2
The base peak in a mass spectrum is best described as the peak:
with the highest m/z value
produced by the most abundant ion, assigned a relative intensity of 100%
due to the molecular ion
with the lowest m/z value
The base peak is the tallest peak; all other intensities are expressed relative to it. It is not necessarily the molecular ion.
chem-6-1-3
The mass spectrum of chloromethane shows peaks at m/z 50 and 52 with relative heights of about 3:1. This is because:
carbon exists as ¹²C and ¹³C in about a 3:1 ratio
the molecule loses either one or three hydrogen atoms
chlorine exists naturally as ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl in about a 3:1 ratio
the m/z 52 peak is a fragment containing two hydrogen atoms more
The M and M+2 peaks reflect the two natural isotopes of chlorine, ³⁵Cl (about 75%) and ³⁷Cl (about 25%).
chem-6-1-4
The mass spectrum of bromoethane (CH₃CH₂Br) would be expected to show molecular ion peaks at:
m/z 108 and 110 in a 3:1 ratio
m/z 109 only
m/z 29 and 79 of equal height
m/z 108 and 110 of almost equal height
C₂H₅ has mass 29, so with ⁷⁹Br and ⁸¹Br (roughly 1:1 abundance) the molecular ions appear at 108 and 110 with similar heights.
chem-6-1-5
A peak at m/z 15 in the mass spectrum of an organic compound is most likely due to:
CH₃⁺
NH⁺
CH₂⁺
OH⁺
CH₃⁺ has mass 12 + 3 = 15. OH⁺ is 17 and CH₂⁺ is 14.
chem-6-1-6
The difference between the molecular ion peak and a fragment peak is 15 m/z units. This suggests the molecule lost:
an ethyl group (C₂H₅)
a methyl group (CH₃)
a hydroxyl group (OH)
a water molecule (H₂O)
A mass loss of 15 corresponds to CH₃ (12 + 3). Loss of OH would be 17, H₂O 18 and C₂H₅ 29.
chem-6-1-7
What is the m/z of the molecular ion of ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH?
C₂H₆O: 2(12) + 6(1) + 16 = 46. The peak at 31 is the CH₂OH⁺ fragment.
chem-6-1-8
Primary alcohols such as propan-1-ol commonly show a fragment peak at m/z 31. This fragment is:
CH₃O⁻
C₂H₇⁺
CH₃CH₂⁺
CH₂OH⁺
CH₂OH⁺ has mass 12 + 2 + 16 + 1 = 31 and forms when the C–C bond next to the CH₂OH group breaks.
chem-6-1-9
In the mass spectrum of butane (M = 58), a large peak at m/z 43 is due to:
C₃H₇⁺ formed by loss of a CH₃ radical
C₂H₅⁺ formed by loss of a C₂H₅ radical
C₄H₁₀⁺ formed by ionisation
C₃H₇⁺ formed by loss of a CH₄ molecule
58 − 15 = 43, which corresponds to C₃H₇⁺ (36 + 7) after a methyl radical breaks away.
Only positively charged fragments appear in a mass spectrum because:
neutral fragments are too heavy to be detected
only ions are accelerated, deflected and detected; neutral radicals are not
negative ions are destroyed by the magnetic field
radicals always recombine to reform the molecular ion
The instrument manipulates charged particles. Neutral radicals formed during fragmentation are not accelerated or deflected, so they are never detected.
The base peak in the mass spectrum of propanone (CH₃COCH₃) is at m/z 43. The ion responsible is:
C₃H₆O⁺
CH₃⁺
CH₃CO⁺
C₂H₃⁺
Loss of a methyl radical from the molecular ion (58 − 15) gives the acylium ion CH₃CO⁺, mass 12 + 3 + 12 + 16 = 43.
A small peak at one m/z unit above the molecular ion (the M+1 peak) in organic compounds is mainly due to:
the presence of the ³⁷Cl isotope
a molecule gaining a hydrogen atom in the instrument
a doubly charged molecular ion
the presence of the ¹³C isotope
About 1.1% of carbon atoms are ¹³C, so a small fraction of molecules have a mass one unit higher than the main molecular ion.
An organic compound containing C, H and O shows a molecular ion peak at m/z 60. Which compound could it be?
propan-1-ol
propanal
butane
ethyl ethanoate
Propan-1-ol, C₃H₈O, has M = 36 + 8 + 16 = 60. Propanal and butane are 58; ethyl ethanoate is 88.
A ketone with molecular ion at m/z 86 shows its base peak at m/z 57. Which ketone is most consistent with this?
pentan-2-one
pentan-3-one
propanone
butanone
Pentan-3-one (CH₃CH₂COCH₂CH₃) loses an ethyl radical (29) to give CH₃CH₂CO⁺ at m/z 57. Pentan-2-one gives CH₃CO⁺ at 43 instead; propanone and butanone have different M values.
Which equation correctly represents a fragmentation that occurs in a mass spectrometer?
[CH₃CH₂OH]⁺ → CH₂OH⁺ + CH₃⁺
CH₃CH₂OH → CH₂OH⁺ + CH₃•
[CH₃CH₂OH]⁺ → CH₂OH⁺ + CH₃•
[CH₃CH₂OH]⁺ → CH₂OH• + CH₃•
The molecular ion splits into one cation and one neutral radical; charge is conserved, so only one fragment carries the positive charge.
A peak at m/z 45 in the mass spectrum of an organic acid is most likely due to:
C₂H₅⁺
CH₂OH⁺
CH₃CO⁺
COOH⁺
COOH⁺ has mass 12 + 32 + 1 = 45. C₂H₅⁺ is 29, CH₂OH⁺ is 31 and CH₃CO⁺ is 43.
A compound has a molecular ion at m/z 74 and fragment peaks at m/z 45 and 29. The compound is most likely:
propanoic acid
ethanoic acid
propan-1-ol
butanoic acid
Propanoic acid (C₂H₅COOH) has M = 74 and splits into COOH⁺ (45) and C₂H₅⁺ (29). The other compounds have molecular masses of 60, 60 and 88.
Why is it often difficult to distinguish structural isomers such as propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol by their molecular ion peak alone?
isomers never form molecular ions
isomers have the same molecular formula and therefore the same molecular ion m/z
isomers always produce identical fragment patterns
isomers contain different isotopes
Structural isomers share a molecular formula, so M⁺ is the same (60 here). Differences only show up in the fragmentation pattern.
Explain why the molecular ion peak of some organic compounds, such as certain alcohols, is very small or missing from the mass spectrum.
The molecular ion is unstable and fragments readily before it reaches the detector, so very few intact molecular ions are detected.
Credit the idea that M⁺ breaks apart quickly into more stable fragment ions and radicals.
Calculate the m/z value of the fragment ion CH₃CH₂CH₂⁺ and name a compound in whose mass spectrum it would be expected.
m/z = 3(12) + 7(1) = 43. It would be expected in the spectrum of butane (or propan-1-ol, 1-chloropropane, etc.).
Any compound that contains a propyl group and could lose the rest of the molecule is acceptable.
The mass spectrum of propane has a large peak at m/z 29. Identify the ion responsible and write an equation for its formation from the molecular ion.
C₂H₅⁺ (CH₃CH₂⁺). [CH₃CH₂CH₃]⁺ → CH₃CH₂⁺ + CH₃•
44 − 15 = 29. The equation must show the fragment cation and a neutral methyl radical.
Chloroethane, C₂H₅Cl, shows two molecular ion peaks. State their m/z values and the approximate ratio of their heights, and explain the pattern.
m/z 64 and 66 in about a 3:1 ratio, because chlorine occurs naturally as ³⁵Cl (about 75%) and ³⁷Cl (about 25%).
The mass spectrum of ethanal (CH₃CHO) shows a significant peak at m/z 29. Identify the ion and the neutral species lost.
The ion is CHO⁺ (m/z 29), formed when the molecular ion (m/z 44) loses a methyl radical, CH₃• (mass 15).
The mass spectrum of butanone (CH₃COCH₂CH₃, M = 72) shows peaks at m/z 57 and 43. Identify the ion causing each peak.
m/z 57: CH₃CH₂CO⁺ (loss of CH₃•, 72 − 15). m/z 43: CH₃CO⁺ (loss of C₂H₅•, 72 − 29).
Both are acylium ions from breaking a C–C bond either side of the carbonyl group.
Outline the main steps that occur inside a mass spectrometer, from the sample entering to the spectrum being produced.

The sample is vaporised and ionised (an electron is knocked off to form positive ions, some of which fragment). The ions are accelerated, then deflected by a magnetic field according to their mass-to-charge ratio, and detected; the detector records relative abundance against m/z.
Award for vaporisation/ionisation, acceleration, deflection by m/z and detection.
chem34a3-ms-1
In the mass spectrum of an organic compound, the molecular ion peak (M⁺) is best described as the peak that
is always the tallest peak in the spectrum
corresponds to the whole molecule that has lost one electron
corresponds to the most stable fragment cation formed
appears at m/z = 1 more than the molar mass because of ¹³C

The molecular ion forms when the intact molecule loses one electron, so its m/z equals the relative molecular mass. The tallest peak is the base peak, which is often a fragment, not M⁺. A small M+1 peak arises from ¹³C, but that is a separate peak.
chem34a3-ms-2
A mass spectrum of a haloalkane shows two molecular ion peaks at m/z = 64 and m/z = 66, with relative heights of about 3 : 1. The compound is most likely
bromomethane
chloromethane
chloroethane
fluoroethane

Chlorine occurs as ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl in about a 3 : 1 ratio, giving M and M+2 peaks in that ratio. C₂H₅³⁵Cl has M = 24 + 5 + 35 = 64. Chloromethane would give peaks at 50 and 52; bromomethane would give peaks at 94 and 96 in a 1 : 1 ratio.
chem34a3-ms-3
The base peak in the mass spectrum of butanone, CH₃COCH₂CH₃, occurs at m/z = 43. Which species is responsible for this peak?
CH₃CO⁺
CH₃CO•
C₂H₅⁺
CH₃CH₂CO⁺

Only charged species are deflected and detected, so the peak must be a cation. CH₃CO⁺ has m/z = 12 + 3 + 12 + 16 = 43. CH₃CO• is a neutral radical and is not detected; C₂H₅⁺ is at 29 and CH₃CH₂CO⁺ is at 57.
chem34a3-ms-4
A student notices a very small peak at m/z = 47 in the mass spectrum of ethanol (M = 46). The best explanation for this peak is
the presence of an impurity with a higher molar mass
a fragment ion that has gained a hydrogen atom
the presence of molecules containing one ¹³C atom
a doubly charged ion of a fragment with mass 94

About 1.1% of carbon atoms are ¹³C, so a small fraction of molecular ions has a mass 1 unit higher, producing a small M+1 peak. It is not evidence of an impurity, and there is no species of mass 94 in ethanol.
chem34a3-ms-5
An unknown compound has its molecular ion at m/z = 60 and prominent peaks at m/z = 45 and m/z = 15. Which compound is consistent with these data?
propan-1-ol
ethanoic acid
methyl methanoate
propanal

Ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH, has M = 60. Loss of CH₃ gives COOH⁺ (m/z = 45) and the CH₃⁺ fragment gives m/z = 15. Propan-1-ol also has M = 60 but would be expected to show a strong peak at 31 (CH₂OH⁺) rather than 45 as COOH⁺; propanal has M = 58.
chem34a3-ms-6
Explain why the m/z value of the molecular ion peak can be used to find the relative molecular mass of a compound, and state one reason why a molecular ion peak may be very small or absent. (2 marks)

The molecular ion is the whole molecule with one electron removed (charge 1+), so its m/z equals its mass, which is the relative molecular mass (the lost electron has negligible mass); the molecular ion may be unstable and fragment almost completely before reaching the detector, so the M⁺ peak is small or missing.
chem34a3-ms-7

Bromoethane, CH₃CH₂Br, is analysed by mass spectrometry. Bromine exists as ⁷⁹Br and ⁸¹Br in roughly equal amounts. (a) Predict the m/z values and relative heights of the molecular ion peaks. (b) Identify the cation responsible for a peak at m/z = 29. (3 marks)

(a) Peaks at m/z = 108 (CH₃CH₂⁷⁹Br⁺) and m/z = 110 (CH₃CH₂⁸¹Br⁺); approximately equal heights (1 : 1) because the two isotopes are about equally abundant; (b) m/z = 29 is CH₃CH₂⁺ (C₂H₅⁺), formed by loss of a Br atom from the molecular ion.
chem34a3-ms-8

A compound containing only C, H and O has a molecular ion at m/z = 58 and a base peak at m/z = 43. A peak at m/z = 15 is also present, but there is no peak at m/z = 29. Suggest the identity of the compound and justify using the fragments. (3 marks)

Propanone, CH₃COCH₃ (M = 58); the base peak at 43 is CH₃CO⁺ formed by loss of a CH₃ group (58 − 15 = 43); the peak at 15 is CH₃⁺; the absence of a peak at 29 (C₂H₅⁺ or CHO⁺) argues against propanal, CH₃CH₂CHO, which has the same molar mass.
chem-6-1-c1
A mass spectrum shows peaks at m/z 78 and 80 in an intensity ratio of about 3 : 1. This suggests the molecule:
Contains one bromine atom
Contains one chlorine atom
Contains two chlorine atoms
Has a molar mass of 79 g/mol
³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl occur in about a 3 : 1 ratio, giving M and M + 2 peaks. Bromine gives a 1 : 1 pair. C₃H₇Cl fits (78 with ³⁵Cl).
chem-6-2: chem-6-2-1
A broad absorption between 3200 and 3600 cm⁻¹ in an infrared spectrum indicates the presence of:
a C=O bond in a ketone
a C–H bond in an alkane
an O–H bond in an alcohol
a C=C bond in an alkene
The O–H stretch of alcohols appears around 3200–3600 cm⁻¹ and is broadened by hydrogen bonding.
chem-6-2-2
A bond will absorb infrared radiation only if its vibration:
breaks the bond
causes an electron to move to a higher energy level
involves a carbon atom
causes a change in the dipole moment of the molecule
IR activity requires the vibration to change the molecular dipole; that change lets the bond interact with the oscillating electric field of IR radiation.
chem-6-2-3
A strong, sharp absorption at about 1715 cm⁻¹ is most characteristic of:
a C=O bond
an O–H bond
an N–H bond
a C–O bond
Carbonyl (C=O) stretches absorb strongly in the 1670–1750 cm⁻¹ range.
chem-6-2-4
How can IR spectroscopy distinguish ethanoic acid from ethanol?
ethanol shows a C=O absorption near 1700 cm⁻¹ but ethanoic acid does not
ethanoic acid shows a C=O absorption near 1700 cm⁻¹ and a very broad O–H absorption around 2500–3000 cm⁻¹
only ethanol shows C–H absorptions near 3000 cm⁻¹
ethanoic acid has no O–H absorption at all
Carboxylic acids contain both C=O and an O–H that absorbs very broadly at lower wavenumber than an alcohol O–H. Ethanol has no C=O.
chem-6-2-5
The fingerprint region of an IR spectrum (below about 1500 cm⁻¹) is most useful for:
identifying O–H groups
determining molecular mass
confirming the identity of a compound by matching against a reference spectrum
counting hydrogen environments
The fingerprint region contains many overlapping absorptions unique to each molecule, so it is compared with database spectra.
chem-6-2-6
In IR spectroscopy, absorptions are reported as wavenumbers in cm⁻¹. A higher wavenumber corresponds to:
longer wavelength radiation
lower frequency radiation
lower energy radiation
higher energy radiation
Wavenumber is 1/λ, so a larger wavenumber means shorter wavelength, higher frequency and higher energy.
chem-6-2-7
When an organic molecule absorbs infrared radiation, the energy is used to:
increase the vibrational energy of its bonds
ionise the molecule
change the spin state of its nuclei
promote electrons to higher energy levels
IR photons match the energy gaps between quantised vibrational levels, causing bonds to stretch and bend more strongly.
chem-6-2-8
Propan-1-ol is oxidised with excess acidified dichromate. Which change in the IR spectrum confirms that propanoic acid has formed?
all absorptions above 2500 cm⁻¹ disappear
a new strong absorption appears near 1700 cm⁻¹ and the O–H band becomes very broad around 2500–3000 cm⁻¹
a new absorption appears around 3350–3500 cm⁻¹ due to N–H
the C–H absorption near 3000 cm⁻¹ disappears
Propanoic acid contains a C=O group and a carboxylic acid O–H, which produce these characteristic absorptions.
chem-6-2-9
Which of these molecules does NOT absorb infrared radiation?
CO₂
H₂O
N₂
CO
The N≡N stretch in a symmetric diatomic molecule produces no change in dipole moment, so N₂ is IR inactive. CO₂ absorbs through its asymmetric stretch and bending.
An IR spectrum shows absorptions at about 1650 cm⁻¹ and in the 2850–3300 cm⁻¹ region, with no absorptions above 3300 cm⁻¹ or near 1700 cm⁻¹. The compound is most likely:
propan-1-ol
propanal
propanoic acid
propene
The 1650 cm⁻¹ peak suggests C=C and the others are C–H. The absence of O–H and C=O bands rules out the other options.
How could IR spectroscopy distinguish ethyl ethanoate from butanoic acid?
both show C=O near 1700 cm⁻¹, but only butanoic acid shows a broad O–H absorption at 2500–3000 cm⁻¹
only ethyl ethanoate shows a C=O absorption
only butanoic acid shows C–H absorptions
the two compounds would give identical IR spectra
Esters and carboxylic acids both contain C=O, but only acids have an O–H group.
An absorption in the 3350–3500 cm⁻¹ region in the spectrum of a compound containing nitrogen most likely indicates:
a C≡N bond
an N–H bond
a C=O bond
a C–N bond
N–H stretches in amines and amides absorb at about 3350–3500 cm⁻¹.
On a typical IR spectrum with percentage transmittance on the vertical axis, an absorption appears as:
an upward peak where more radiation is transmitted
a horizontal line at 100% transmittance
a downward dip where less radiation is transmitted
a shift of the whole baseline to the left
Absorbed radiation is not transmitted, so transmittance falls and the absorption appears as a trough.
The C=O bond absorbs at a higher wavenumber (about 1700 cm⁻¹) than the C–O bond (about 1000–1300 cm⁻¹) mainly because:
the C=O bond contains heavier atoms
the C–O bond is more polar
single bonds do not absorb infrared radiation
the double bond is stronger, so it vibrates at a higher frequency
Stronger bonds behave like stiffer springs and vibrate at higher frequencies, so they absorb higher-energy IR radiation.
How would the IR spectrum of propanone differ from that of propan-2-ol?
propanone shows a strong absorption near 1700 cm⁻¹ and no broad band at 3200–3600 cm⁻¹
propanone shows a broad band at 3200–3600 cm⁻¹ and no absorption near 1700 cm⁻¹
propanone shows no C–H absorptions
the spectra would be identical because both contain three carbon atoms
Propanone is a ketone (C=O present, no O–H), while propan-2-ol is an alcohol (O–H present, no C=O).
Propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol have very similar IR spectra above 1500 cm⁻¹. The best way to tell them apart using IR is to:
look for a C=O absorption
compare their fingerprint regions with reference spectra
measure the height of the O–H band
look for an absorption at 2500–3000 cm⁻¹
The two isomers contain the same functional groups, but their fingerprint regions differ and can be matched to known spectra.
Absorptions in the 2850–3300 cm⁻¹ region appear in the IR spectra of almost all organic compounds. They are due to:
C–C bonds
C=O bonds
C–H bonds
O–H bonds in water
Almost every organic molecule contains C–H bonds, which stretch at about 2850–3300 cm⁻¹.
A sample of ethyl ethanoate is hydrolysed completely in acidic solution. Compared with the spectrum of pure ethyl ethanoate, the IR spectrum of the product mixture would show:
the loss of all C–H absorptions
the loss of all absorptions near 1700 cm⁻¹
a new N–H absorption
new broad O–H absorptions from ethanol and ethanoic acid
Hydrolysis produces ethanol and ethanoic acid, which both contain O–H groups. Ethanoic acid still has a C=O.
Explain why the O–H absorption in the IR spectrum of a carboxylic acid is very broad.

Carboxylic acid molecules form strong hydrogen bonds with each other (often as dimers). This gives a range of O–H bond strengths, so the O–H absorbs over a wide range of wavenumbers (about 2500–3000 cm⁻¹).
The key idea is that hydrogen bonding produces a spread of O–H vibrational energies.
Describe how IR spectroscopy could be used to distinguish butan-1-ol from butanal.
Butan-1-ol shows a broad O–H absorption at about 3200–3600 cm⁻¹ and no C=O peak. Butanal shows a strong, sharp C=O absorption at about 1700 cm⁻¹ and no broad O–H band.
Both functional-group differences should be stated.
Carbon dioxide is a non-polar molecule, yet it absorbs infrared radiation. Explain why.
Although the molecule has no overall dipole, its asymmetric stretching and bending vibrations create a temporary change in dipole moment, so those vibrations absorb IR radiation.
IR activity depends on a change in dipole during the vibration, not on a permanent dipole.
Explain how the fingerprint region of an IR spectrum is used in chemical analysis.

The region below about 1500 cm⁻¹ contains complex absorptions from bending and skeletal vibrations that are unique to each compound. Matching a sample's fingerprint region to a reference spectrum confirms its identity.
Mention that the pattern is unique and is compared with a database or known spectrum.
Propan-2-ol is heated with acidified potassium dichromate. Name the organic product and describe two changes in the IR spectrum showing the reaction has occurred.
Propanone forms. A strong C=O absorption appears at about 1700 cm⁻¹ and the broad alcohol O–H absorption at 3200–3600 cm⁻¹ disappears.
A secondary alcohol is oxidised to a ketone, which cannot be oxidised further to an acid.
State one limitation of using IR spectroscopy alone to determine the structure of an unknown organic compound.
IR mainly identifies the functional groups present; it does not give the molecular mass, the number of carbon atoms or how the carbon skeleton is arranged, so isomers can be hard to tell apart.
Any valid limitation is acceptable, for example that it cannot give molecular mass or connectivity.
Explain why a given bond absorbs infrared radiation only at particular wavenumbers rather than across the whole IR range.

Vibrational energy levels are quantised. A bond absorbs only photons whose energy exactly matches the gap between its vibrational levels, and that gap depends on bond strength and the masses of the atoms.
Link quantised energy levels to specific absorption wavenumbers.
chem34a3-ir-1
Absorption of infrared radiation by an organic molecule causes
electrons to move to higher energy levels
bonds to vibrate with greater energy (stretching or bending)
nuclei to flip their spin in a magnetic field
the molecule to ionise and fragment

IR radiation has the right energy to increase the vibrational energy of bonds. Electron transitions need UV–visible radiation, spin flips relate to NMR (radio waves), and ionisation is used in mass spectrometry.
chem34a3-ir-2
An IR spectrum shows a very broad absorption from about 2500 to 3300 cm⁻¹ and a strong, sharp absorption near 1710 cm⁻¹. The compound is most likely
butan-1-ol
butanal
butanoic acid
butan-1-amine

A very broad O–H band spanning roughly 2500–3300 cm⁻¹ is typical of the hydrogen-bonded O–H in carboxylic acids, and the absorption near 1710 cm⁻¹ is a C=O stretch. Butanal has C=O but no O–H; butan-1-ol has a broad O–H centred higher (about 3200–3600 cm⁻¹) and no C=O.
chem34a3-ir-3
Propan-1-ol is oxidised by acidified potassium dichromate and the product is analysed by IR. Which change in the spectrum would confirm that some propanal has formed while some propan-1-ol remains?
The O–H band disappears and a C=O band appears
A C=O band appears near 1730 cm⁻¹ while a broad band near 3200–3600 cm⁻¹ is still present
A C≡N band appears near 2250 cm⁻¹
Only the C–H band near 2900 cm⁻¹ is present

Formation of the aldehyde introduces a C=O absorption; remaining alcohol still shows its broad O–H stretch. If the O–H band disappeared completely, all the alcohol would have reacted (assuming no acid formed).
chem34a3-ir-4
The region of an IR spectrum below about 1500 cm⁻¹ is called the fingerprint region because
it only contains absorptions from O–H bonds
its complex pattern of absorptions is unique to a particular compound
it is the only region where C=O bonds absorb
no absorptions occur there for organic compounds

The fingerprint region contains many overlapping bending and single-bond absorptions; the overall pattern is characteristic of one compound and can be matched against a reference spectrum. O–H and C=O absorb above 1500 cm⁻¹.
chem34a3-ir-5
Which pair of compounds would be most difficult to distinguish using only the absorptions above 1500 cm⁻¹ in their IR spectra?
ethanol and ethanoic acid
propanone and propan-2-ol
pentan-2-one and pentan-3-one
ethyl ethanoate and ethanol

Pentan-2-one and pentan-3-one are both ketones with the same functional groups (C=O and C–H), so their absorptions above 1500 cm⁻¹ are nearly identical; they differ only in the fingerprint region. Each of the other pairs differs in the presence of O–H and/or C=O.
chem34a3-ir-6
A bottle is labelled either propanal, propan-1-ol or propanoic acid. Describe how IR spectroscopy could identify which compound it contains, referring to specific absorptions. (3 marks)

Propan-1-ol: broad O–H (alcohol) absorption around 3200–3600 cm⁻¹ and no C=O absorption; propanal: strong C=O absorption around 1700–1740 cm⁻¹ and no broad O–H band; propanoic acid: both a C=O absorption near 1700 cm⁻¹ and a very broad O–H (acid) absorption from about 2500–3300 cm⁻¹ overlapping the C–H region.
chem34a3-ir-7
Explain why the O–H absorption in the IR spectrum of a liquid alcohol is broad rather than sharp. (2 marks)

Alcohol molecules are hydrogen bonded to each other in the liquid; the strength of these hydrogen bonds varies between molecules, so O–H bonds vibrate over a range of frequencies (wavenumbers), producing a broad absorption band.
chem34a3-ir-8

An ester, ethyl ethanoate, is made from ethanol and ethanoic acid. A student says the IR spectrum of the purified product should contain no absorption between 3200 and 3600 cm⁻¹. Explain whether the student is correct and identify one absorption that should be present. (2 marks)

The student is correct: the ester has no O–H group, so a pure sample shows no broad O–H absorption (a band there would indicate unreacted ethanol, ethanoic acid or water); a strong C=O absorption around 1735–1750 cm⁻¹ should be present (C–O and C–H absorptions are also acceptable).
chem-6-2-c1
An IR spectrum shows a very broad absorption from 2500 to 3300 cm⁻¹ and a strong sharp absorption near 1710 cm⁻¹. The compound is most likely:
An alcohol
A carboxylic acid
An ester
An alkene
The very broad band is the hydrogen-bonded O–H of an acid, and 1710 cm⁻¹ is C=O. An alcohol has no C=O; an ester has no broad O–H.
chem-6-3: chem-6-3-1
Tetramethylsilane (TMS) is used as the reference in NMR spectroscopy because it:
gives a single strong signal from 12 equivalent hydrogens and is chemically inert
contains no hydrogen atoms
has many different hydrogen environments to compare with
reacts with the sample to produce sharper peaks
TMS, Si(CH₃)₄, has 12 equivalent ¹H (and 4 equivalent ¹³C), is unreactive and volatile, and its signal is defined as 0 ppm.
chem-6-3-2
How many different hydrogen environments are there in ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH?
The CH₃, CH₂ and OH hydrogens are each in a different environment.
chem-6-3-3
In the high-resolution ¹H NMR spectrum of chloroethane (CH₃CH₂Cl), the CH₃ signal is split into a:
quartet
doublet
triplet
singlet
The CH₃ hydrogens have 2 neighbouring H on the adjacent carbon, so by the n + 1 rule they give 2 + 1 = 3 peaks.
chem-6-3-4
How many peaks would appear in the ¹³C NMR spectrum of propan-2-ol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₃?
The two CH₃ carbons are equivalent by symmetry, and the CH carbon is different, giving two carbon environments.
chem-6-3-5
How many peaks would appear in the ¹³C NMR spectrum of butanone, CH₃COCH₂CH₃?
Every carbon is in a different environment: CH₃ next to C=O, the C=O carbon, the CH₂ and the terminal CH₃.
chem-6-3-6
What is the ratio of peak areas in the ¹H NMR spectrum of ethyl ethanoate, CH₃COOCH₂CH₃?
There are three environments: CH₃ attached to C=O (3H), OCH₂ (2H) and the terminal CH₃ (3H).
chem-6-3-7
Deuterated solvents such as CDCl₃ are used in ¹H NMR spectroscopy because:
they react with the sample to make it more soluble
they increase the splitting of peaks
they contain no ¹H atoms, so they produce no interfering signals
they act as the 0 ppm reference
Replacing H with deuterium stops the solvent producing a large ¹H signal that would swamp the sample's peaks.
chem-6-3-8
Which compound shows only one signal in its ¹H NMR spectrum?
propanal, CH₃CH₂CHO
propan-1-ol, CH₃CH₂CH₂OH
ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH
propanone, CH₃COCH₃
The two CH₃ groups in propanone are equivalent, so all six hydrogens share one environment.
chem-6-3-9
In the ¹H NMR spectrum of 2-methylpropane, (CH₃)₃CH, the signal for the CH₃ hydrogens is a:
doublet with a relative area of 9
singlet with a relative area of 9
doublet with a relative area of 3
decet with a relative area of 1
The nine equivalent CH₃ hydrogens each have 1 neighbouring H (on the CH), giving 1 + 1 = 2 peaks, a doublet.
Hydrogen atoms near an electronegative atom such as oxygen or chlorine appear at higher chemical shifts because they are:
shielded by extra electron density
deshielded, as electron density is drawn away from them
not affected by the magnetic field
coupled to more neighbouring hydrogens
Less electron density around the nucleus means less shielding from the applied field, so the signal moves downfield to a higher ppm.
A ¹H NMR signal at about 9.7 ppm is most likely due to a hydrogen in:
an alkane (R–CH₃)
a methyl group next to a ketone C=O
an aldehyde group (–CHO)
the TMS reference
Aldehyde hydrogens are strongly deshielded and appear at about 9.4–10 ppm.
How many peaks would appear in the ¹³C NMR spectrum of pentan-3-one, CH₃CH₂COCH₂CH₃?
Symmetry makes the two CH₃ carbons equivalent and the two CH₂ carbons equivalent, and the C=O carbon is unique.
In the high-resolution ¹H NMR spectrum of 1-chloropropane (CH₃CH₂CH₂Cl), the signal for the middle CH₂ group is a:
sextet
triplet
quartet
quintet
The middle CH₂ has 3 + 2 = 5 neighbouring hydrogens, so the n + 1 rule gives 6 peaks.
In VCE-level ¹H NMR analysis, the signal from the hydrogen of an alcohol O–H group is usually treated as a:
triplet
singlet, because the O–H proton exchanges rapidly and does not split
quartet
doublet
Rapid exchange of the hydroxyl proton between molecules means it normally neither splits nor is split by neighbouring hydrogens.
NMR spectroscopy involves the absorption of which type of electromagnetic radiation?
infrared radiation
ultraviolet radiation
radio waves
X-rays
In a strong magnetic field, nuclei with spin absorb low-energy radiofrequency radiation as they flip between spin states.
Which statement correctly describes how ¹³C NMR distinguishes propan-1-ol from propan-2-ol?
propan-1-ol gives 2 peaks and propan-2-ol gives 3 peaks
both give 3 peaks
both give 1 peak
propan-1-ol gives 3 peaks and propan-2-ol gives 2 peaks
All three carbons in propan-1-ol are different, but propan-2-ol has two equivalent CH₃ carbons.
A compound with formula C₂H₄O₂ has a ¹H NMR spectrum with two singlets in a 3 : 1 ratio at 2.1 ppm and 11.5 ppm. The compound is:
ethanoic acid
methyl methanoate
ethane-1,2-diol
ethanal
The singlet at 11.5 ppm is typical of a carboxylic acid –COOH hydrogen, and the 3H singlet is a CH₃ next to C=O. Methyl methanoate's HCOO hydrogen would appear near 8 ppm.
How many hydrogen environments are there in methyl propanoate, CH₃CH₂COOCH₃?
The environments are CH₃ of the ethyl group, CH₂ next to C=O, and the OCH₃.
Predict the number of signals, their splitting patterns and their relative areas in the high-resolution ¹H NMR spectrum of chloroethane, CH₃CH₂Cl.
Two signals: the CH₃ signal is a triplet (area 3) and the CH₂ signal is a quartet (area 2), with the CH₂ at the higher chemical shift because it is next to Cl.
Apply n + 1: CH₃ has 2 neighbours and CH₂ has 3 neighbours.
State two reasons why tetramethylsilane (TMS) is a suitable reference substance for NMR spectroscopy.

Any two of: it gives one strong signal because all 12 H (and 4 C) are equivalent; its signal sits away from most organic signals (defined as 0 ppm); it is chemically inert; it is volatile, so it is easily removed; it is non-toxic.
Award one mark for each valid reason.
How many peaks would be observed in the ¹³C NMR spectrum of butan-2-ol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃? Explain.
Four peaks. Each of the four carbon atoms is in a different chemical environment because the molecule has no symmetry that makes any two carbons equivalent.
The two CH₃ groups differ: one is bonded to CH(OH), the other to CH₂.
A ¹H NMR spectrum shows a triplet with area 3 and a quartet with area 2. What structural feature does this pattern indicate? Explain.
An ethyl group (–CH₂CH₃). The CH₃ is split into a triplet by the 2 neighbouring CH₂ hydrogens, and the CH₂ is split into a quartet by the 3 neighbouring CH₃ hydrogens.
Link each splitting to the n + 1 rule.
A compound with formula C₃H₆O shows only one signal (a singlet) in its ¹H NMR spectrum. Identify the compound and explain your reasoning.
Propanone, CH₃COCH₃. All six hydrogens are equivalent (two identical CH₃ groups on either side of the C=O) and have no non-equivalent neighbouring hydrogens, so they give one singlet.
Propanal would give three signals.
A compound C₃H₈O shows 2 peaks in its ¹³C NMR spectrum. Identify it and describe its expected high-resolution ¹H NMR spectrum (ignore chemical shift values).
Propan-2-ol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₃. ¹H NMR: a doublet (6H) for the two equivalent CH₃ groups, a septet (1H) for the CH, and a singlet (1H) for the OH.
CH₃ groups have 1 neighbour (doublet); the CH has 6 neighbours (7 peaks); OH is treated as a singlet.
Explain how the ratio of peak areas in a ¹H NMR spectrum helps determine the structure of an organic compound.

The area under each signal is proportional to the number of hydrogen atoms in that environment. The area ratio therefore shows how many H are in each environment, for example 3 : 2 suggests CH₃ and CH₂ groups.
Mention that relative areas (integration) give the relative number of H in each environment.
chem34a3-nmr-1
Tetramethylsilane (TMS) is used as the reference in NMR spectroscopy. Which property is NOT a reason for choosing TMS?
All its hydrogen atoms are in the same environment, giving a single peak
It is chemically inert and easily removed because it is volatile
Its signal appears at a higher chemical shift than most organic compounds
It gives a strong signal from a small amount

TMS is defined as 0 ppm and its signal appears at a lower chemical shift (more upfield) than almost all organic protons and carbons, so it does not overlap their signals. The other three statements are genuine reasons for using TMS.
chem34a3-nmr-2
How many peaks would appear in the ¹³C NMR spectrum of pentan-3-one, CH₃CH₂COCH₂CH₃?
The molecule is symmetrical about the C=O carbon. The two CH₃ carbons are equivalent, the two CH₂ carbons are equivalent, and the C=O carbon is unique, giving 3 carbon environments.
chem34a3-nmr-3
In the high-resolution ¹H NMR spectrum of 1-chloropropane, CH₃CH₂CH₂Cl, the signal for the middle CH₂ group would be split into a
triplet
quartet
quintet
sextet
The middle CH₂ has 3 + 2 = 5 hydrogens on neighbouring carbons. By the n + 1 rule it is split into 6 lines, a sextet.
chem34a3-nmr-4
A compound with molecular formula C₂H₄O₂ gives a ¹H NMR spectrum with two singlets, at about 2.1 ppm and about 11.5 ppm, in the area ratio 3 : 1. The compound is
methyl methanoate
ethanoic acid
2-hydroxyethanal
ethane-1,2-diol

Ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH, has two H environments: CH₃ (3H, singlet near 2.1 ppm, no neighbouring H) and COOH (1H, singlet at about 9–13 ppm). Methyl methanoate, HCOOCH₃, also gives two singlets but in a 1 : 3 ratio with the methyl at about 3.7 ppm and the HCOO proton near 8 ppm, not 11.5 ppm.
chem34a3-nmr-5
The relative areas under the peaks in a ¹H NMR spectrum indicate the
number of neighbouring hydrogen atoms for each environment
relative number of hydrogen atoms in each environment
number of carbon atoms bonded to each hydrogen
electronegativity of the atoms near each hydrogen

Peak area (integration) is proportional to the number of hydrogen atoms producing that signal. The number of neighbouring hydrogens is shown by splitting, and electronegative neighbours affect chemical shift.
chem34a3-nmr-6

Predict the high-resolution ¹H NMR spectrum of ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH. For each signal give the splitting pattern and relative peak area. Assume the O–H hydrogen does not couple with other hydrogens. (3 marks)

Three signals (three H environments); CH₃: triplet (split by 2 H on CH₂), relative area 3, about 1.2 ppm; CH₂: quartet (split by 3 H on CH₃), relative area 2, about 3.6 ppm (shifted downfield by the O); OH: singlet, relative area 1, variable shift (about 2–5 ppm).
chem34a3-nmr-7
Ethyl ethanoate (CH₃COOCH₂CH₃) and methyl propanoate (CH₃CH₂COOCH₃) are isomers. Describe two differences in their ¹H NMR spectra that would allow them to be distinguished. (2 marks)

Ethyl ethanoate has a CH₃ singlet near 2.0 ppm (CH₃ next to C=O), whereas methyl propanoate has a CH₃ singlet near 3.7 ppm (CH₃ bonded to O); in ethyl ethanoate the CH₂ quartet is near 4.1 ppm (CH₂ bonded to O), whereas in methyl propanoate the CH₂ quartet is near 2.3 ppm (CH₂ next to C=O). Both show a triplet/quartet/singlet pattern with areas 3 : 2 : 3, so chemical shift is the key difference.
chem34a3-nmr-8

An alcohol with molecular formula C₃H₈O gives a ¹³C NMR spectrum with only two peaks. Its ¹H NMR spectrum contains a doublet with relative area 6. Identify the alcohol and explain the evidence. (3 marks)

Propan-2-ol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₃; two ¹³C peaks show two carbon environments (the two equivalent CH₃ carbons and the CH carbon), whereas propan-1-ol would give three; the doublet with area 6 arises from 6 equivalent CH₃ hydrogens split by the single H on the adjacent CH carbon (n + 1 = 2).
chem-6-3-c1
The ¹H NMR spectrum of propan-2-ol, (CH₃)₂CHOH, shows peak areas in the ratio:
The two CH₃ groups are equivalent (6H), plus the CH (1H) and the OH (1H): three environments.
chem-6-4: chem-6-4-1
In HPLC, the components of a mixture are separated because they:
have different molar masses only
react with the mobile phase to form new compounds
differ in how strongly they adsorb to the stationary phase relative to how well they dissolve in the mobile phase
absorb different wavelengths of light in the column
Components that are more strongly attracted to the stationary phase move more slowly and elute later.
chem-6-4-2
Retention time in HPLC is defined as the time taken for a component to:
dissolve in the mobile phase
be adsorbed onto the stationary phase
evaporate from the column
travel from the point of injection to the detector
Retention time runs from injection until the component's peak reaches the detector. It is characteristic of a substance under fixed conditions.
chem-6-4-3
In reversed-phase HPLC the stationary phase is non-polar and the mobile phase is polar. Which component of a mixture would generally have the shortest retention time?
the most polar component
the least polar component
the component with the largest molar mass
the component present in the highest concentration
Polar molecules are attracted more to the polar mobile phase than to the non-polar stationary phase, so they pass through the column fastest.
chem-6-4-4
In quantitative HPLC analysis, the concentration of a component is determined from:
the retention time compared with standards
the peak area compared with a calibration curve made from standards
the width of the solvent front
the number of peaks in the chromatogram
Peak area is proportional to the amount of a component; standards of known concentration are used to build a calibration curve.
chem-6-4-5
If the flow rate of the mobile phase in an HPLC column is increased with all other conditions unchanged, the retention times of the components will:
increase
stay exactly the same
decrease
become identical for all components
A faster mobile phase carries all the components through the column more quickly.
chem-6-4-6
An analyst suspects a sports drink contains caffeine. The best way to confirm this using HPLC is to:
measure the height of the largest peak
increase the column temperature until one peak remains
compare the sample's peak area with the solvent peak
run a caffeine standard under identical conditions and compare retention times
A component is identified when its retention time matches that of a known standard run under the same conditions.
chem-6-4-7
A 25.00 mL aliquot of hydrochloric acid is titrated with 0.100 M sodium hydroxide. The average titre is 20.00 mL. What is the concentration of the hydrochloric acid?
chem-6-4-8
When ethanoic acid is titrated with sodium hydroxide, the pH at the equivalence point is:
exactly 7, so any indicator is suitable
greater than 7, so phenolphthalein is a suitable indicator
less than 7, so methyl orange is a suitable indicator
less than 7, so phenolphthalein is a suitable indicator
The ethanoate ion formed is a weak base, so the solution at equivalence is slightly basic. Phenolphthalein changes colour in a basic range.
chem-6-4-9
Which substance is suitable for use as a primary standard?
sodium hydroxide pellets
concentrated hydrochloric acid
anhydrous sodium carbonate
potassium permanganate solution left in the light
Anhydrous Na₂CO₃ is pure, stable and not hygroscopic once dried. NaOH absorbs water and CO₂, and HCl is volatile, so neither has a precisely known concentration.
Before a titration, the burette should be rinsed with:
deionised water only
the solution to be placed in the conical flask
ethanol, then allowed to dry
the solution it will contain
Rinsing with the titrant stops any water or residue diluting it, so its concentration stays as stated.
A 20.00 mL aliquot of 0.0500 M Na₂CO₃ reacts completely with 18.50 mL of HCl: Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂. What is the concentration of the HCl?
A 25.00 mL aliquot of an Fe²⁺ solution needs 15.00 mL of 0.0200 M KMnO₄ to reach the end point: MnO₄⁻ + 5Fe²⁺ + 8H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H₂O. What is the concentration of Fe²⁺?
A student leaves a few drops of deionised water in the conical flask before adding the aliquot. The effect on the calculated concentration is:
it is too high, because the solution is diluted
it is too low, because the solution is diluted
no effect, because the number of moles in the aliquot is unchanged
it is too high, because the titre is smaller
The amount (in mol) of analyte transferred by the pipette is unchanged, so the same volume of titrant is needed.
A burette is rinsed with deionised water but not with the NaOH solution before an acid is titrated. The calculated concentration of the acid will be:
too low, because the diluted NaOH gives a smaller titre
unaffected, because water is neutral
too low, because the indicator changes colour early
too high, because the diluted NaOH gives a larger titre
Diluted NaOH contains fewer moles per mL, so more is needed. Using the stated concentration with this larger titre overestimates the moles of acid.
In VCE titrations, titres are usually regarded as concordant if they agree within:
1.0 mL
5% of the mean
Concordant titres lie within about 0.10 mL of each other; only these are averaged.

A 20.00 mL sample of vinegar is diluted to 250.0 mL in a volumetric flask. Titration shows the diluted solution is 0.0880 M ethanoic acid. What is the concentration of ethanoic acid in the original vinegar?
Dilution factor = 250.0 ÷ 20.00 = 12.5, so the original concentration is 0.0880 × 12.5 = 1.10 M.
The end point of a titration is best described as the point at which:
the reactants have reacted in exact stoichiometric proportions
the pH is exactly 7
the indicator changes colour
the burette is empty
The equivalence point is where reactants are in stoichiometric amounts; the end point is the observed colour change, ideally very close to it.
Aqueous ammonia is titrated with hydrochloric acid. The most suitable indicator is:
phenolphthalein, because the equivalence point is basic
phenolphthalein, because the equivalence point is exactly 7
no indicator, because the reaction is self-indicating
methyl orange, because the equivalence point is acidic
The ammonium ion formed is a weak acid, so the equivalence point pH is below 7. Methyl orange changes colour in an acidic range.

Standard solutions of caffeine give HPLC peak areas directly proportional to concentration, with a 20.0 mg/L standard giving a peak area of 3000 units. A diluted energy-drink sample gives a caffeine peak area of 4200 units. Calculate the caffeine concentration in the diluted sample.
Because the calibration is linear through the origin, concentration scales directly with peak area.

A 10.00 mL sample of vinegar was diluted to 100.0 mL. A 25.00 mL aliquot of the diluted solution needed 21.50 mL of 0.1000 M NaOH. Calculate the concentration of ethanoic acid in the original vinegar in % (w/v). M(CH₃COOH) = 60.05 g/mol.
Check the 1:1 ratio, the dilution factor of 10, and conversion to grams per 100 mL.
Explain why sodium hydroxide is not suitable as a primary standard.

Solid NaOH is hygroscopic (it absorbs water from the air) and reacts with atmospheric CO₂. Its mass therefore does not reflect the true amount of NaOH, so a solution of accurately known concentration cannot be made by weighing it.
Mention absorption of water and/or CO₂.
Explain why two different compounds in a mixture have different retention times in HPLC.

Each compound has a different balance of attraction to the stationary phase and solubility in the mobile phase (for example, due to differences in polarity). The compound more strongly adsorbed to the stationary phase moves more slowly and has a longer retention time.
Answers must refer to both stationary and mobile phase interactions.
A student rinses the pipette with deionised water instead of the solution being analysed. Explain the effect on the titre and on the calculated concentration of the analysed solution.
The water left in the pipette dilutes the aliquot, so it contains fewer moles of analyte. The titre is smaller, and the calculated concentration is lower than the true value.
Link fewer moles to a smaller titre and an underestimated result.

An iron tablet is dissolved in acid and all its iron is converted to Fe²⁺. The solution needs 12.40 mL of 0.0150 M KMnO₄ to reach the end point (MnO₄⁻ + 5Fe²⁺ + 8H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H₂O). Calculate the mass of iron in the tablet in mg. M(Fe) = 55.85 g/mol.
The 1 : 5 mole ratio is the key step; KMnO₄ acts as its own indicator (the first permanent pink colour).
Explain why HPLC columns are packed with very small particles and why this requires high pressure.

Small particles give the stationary phase a very large surface area, which improves separation and resolution. They also pack tightly and resist flow, so high pressure is needed to push the mobile phase through the column at a useful rate.
Credit both the surface area/resolution idea and the pressure requirement.
chem34a3-chr-1
In a thin-layer chromatogram, a dye spot travels 3.6 cm while the solvent front travels 8.0 cm from the origin. The Rf value of the dye is
Rf = distance travelled by component ÷ distance travelled by solvent front = 3.6 ÷ 8.0 = 0.45. Rf values must lie between 0 and 1, which rules out 2.2.
chem34a3-chr-2
In reversed-phase HPLC, the stationary phase is non-polar and the mobile phase is a polar solvent mixture. Which compound would be expected to have the shortest retention time?
hexane
octan-1-ol
ethanoic acid
1-chlorohexane

Ethanoic acid is the most polar (small, with a highly polar COOH group), so it is least attracted to the non-polar stationary phase and most soluble in the polar mobile phase. It therefore elutes first. The longer, less polar molecules adsorb more strongly and are retained longer.
chem34a3-chr-3
Which statement about the separation of components in chromatography is correct?
Components separate because they have different molar masses only
A component that adsorbs strongly to the stationary phase moves further in a given time
Components separate because of differences in their relative attraction to the stationary and mobile phases
The mobile phase must always be more polar than the stationary phase

Separation depends on the balance between adsorption to the stationary phase and solubility in (desorption into) the mobile phase. Strongly adsorbed components move more slowly. The relative polarity of the phases can be chosen either way.
chem34a3-chr-4

Caffeine standards of 20, 40, 60 and 80 mg L⁻¹ give HPLC peak areas of 1500, 3000, 4500 and 6000 units. A cola sample, diluted by a factor of 10 before injection, gives a caffeine peak area of 3750. The caffeine concentration in the original cola is
50 mg L⁻¹
5.0 mg L⁻¹
500 mg L⁻¹
375 mg L⁻¹

The calibration is linear at 75 area units per mg L⁻¹, so an area of 3750 corresponds to 50 mg L⁻¹ in the diluted sample. Multiplying by the dilution factor of 10 gives 500 mg L⁻¹ in the original cola. 50 mg L⁻¹ forgets the dilution.
chem34a3-chr-5

An analyst changes the mobile phase in a reversed-phase HPLC run from 80% water to 50% water (with the rest methanol, which is less polar). The most likely effect on the retention time of a moderately non-polar compound is that it
decreases, because the compound is now more soluble in the mobile phase
increases, because the compound is now less soluble in the mobile phase
stays the same, because retention time depends only on the column
increases, because the stationary phase becomes more polar

A less polar mobile phase dissolves a non-polar compound better, so it spends more time in the mobile phase and less adsorbed on the non-polar stationary phase, eluting sooner. The stationary phase itself is unchanged.
chem34a3-chr-6
State the information that can be obtained from (a) the retention time and (b) the peak area in an HPLC chromatogram, and explain how each is used. (3 marks)

(a) Retention time is used for qualitative identification: a component is identified by comparing its retention time with that of a known standard run under identical conditions (same column, mobile phase, flow rate, temperature); (b) peak area is proportional to the amount/concentration of the component; it is used quantitatively by comparing with a calibration curve made from standards of known concentration.
chem34a3-chr-7

A student identifies a pesticide in a water sample because a peak has the same retention time as a pesticide standard. Explain why this alone is not conclusive and suggest how the identification could be confirmed. (2 marks)

Different compounds can have the same (or very similar) retention time under a given set of conditions, so a match is not proof of identity; confirmation could be obtained by spiking the sample with the standard and checking that only the single peak increases (no new peak), by repeating with a different column or mobile phase, or by coupling HPLC to a mass spectrometer.
chem34a3-chr-8

A sports drink is analysed for its vitamin B₃ content using HPLC. 10.0 mL of drink is diluted to 50.0 mL. From the calibration curve, the diluted solution contains 12.4 mg L⁻¹ of vitamin B₃. Calculate the mass of vitamin B₃ in a 600 mL bottle of the drink, in mg. (2 marks)
Concentration in original drink = 12.4 × (50.0 ÷ 10.0) = 62.0 mg L⁻¹; mass in 0.600 L = 62.0 × 0.600 = 37.2 mg.

25.00 mL of vinegar is diluted to 250.0 mL. A 20.00 mL aliquot of the diluted solution requires 17.50 mL of 0.100 mol L⁻¹ NaOH(aq) to reach the endpoint. The concentration of ethanoic acid in the original vinegar is
0.0875 mol L⁻¹
0.700 mol L⁻¹

Which indicator is most suitable for titrating ethanoic acid (a weak acid) with sodium hydroxide (a strong base)?
methyl orange (colour change pH 3.1–4.4)
bromothymol blue (colour change pH 6.0–7.6)
phenolphthalein (colour change pH 8.3–10.0)
methyl red (colour change pH 4.4–6.2)

At equivalence the solution contains ethanoate ions, which are weakly basic, so the equivalence point pH is above 7 (about 8–9). Phenolphthalein changes colour in this range. The other indicators would change colour before equivalence is reached.

Ethanol is oxidised by acidified dichromate according to: 3CH₃CH₂OH(aq) + 2Cr₂O₇²⁻(aq) + 16H⁺(aq) → 3CH₃COOH(aq) + 4Cr³⁺(aq) + 11H₂O(l). A 10.00 mL sample of wine is diluted to 100.0 mL, and a 10.00 mL aliquot reacts with 15.20 mL of 0.0500 mol L⁻¹ K₂Cr₂O₇. The ethanol concentration in the wine is
0.507 mol L⁻¹
0.760 mol L⁻¹
0.114 mol L⁻¹
1.14 mol L⁻¹

n(Cr₂O₇²⁻) = 0.0500 × 0.01520 = 7.60 × 10⁻⁴ mol; n(ethanol) = 3/2 × 7.60 × 10⁻⁴ = 1.14 × 10⁻³ mol in the aliquot, so 1.14 × 10⁻² mol in 100.0 mL, which came from 10.00 mL of wine: 1.14 × 10⁻² ÷ 0.01000 = 1.14 mol L⁻¹. 0.507 uses the inverted ratio 2/3.

In a titration, the burette is rinsed with deionised water but not with the titrant solution before being filled. The effect on the calculated concentration of the analyte is that it will be
too high, because the titrant is diluted and a larger titre is needed
too low, because the titrant is diluted and a smaller titre is needed
unaffected, because water does not react

Residual water dilutes the titrant, so more volume is needed to deliver the required number of moles. Calculations use the labelled (higher) concentration, so the moles of titrant and hence analyte are overestimated.
