Vitamin C (ascorbic acid, C₆H₈O₆) reacts with iodine in a 1 : 1 mole ratio. Which indicator is commonly used to detect the endpoint, and what is observed?
phenolphthalein; colourless to pink
starch; the first permanent blue-black colour
methyl orange; red to yellow
starch; the blue-black colour disappears as iodine is added

Explain the meaning of 'concordant titres' and why the average of concordant titres, rather than all titres, is used in the calculation. (2 marks)

Concordant titres are titres that agree closely with each other, typically within 0.10 mL; averaging only concordant titres excludes the rough/trial titre and any outliers, which reduces the effect of random errors and improves the precision (and reliability) of the result.

A 0.250 g sample of an unknown monoprotic carboxylic acid is dissolved in water and titrated with 0.115 mol L⁻¹ NaOH(aq). The titre is 24.65 mL. Calculate the molar mass of the acid and suggest its identity from the following: propanoic acid (74.0 g mol⁻¹), butanoic acid (88.0 g mol⁻¹), benzoic acid (122.0 g mol⁻¹). (3 marks)

Which two functional groups are present in every 2-amino acid found in proteins?

Hydroxyl and carboxyl

Each 2-amino acid has an amino (–NH₂) group and a carboxyl (–COOH) group bonded to the same carbon atom.

peptide (amide) bond
glycosidic bond

The –COOH of one amino acid reacts with the –NH₂ of another, releasing water and forming a –CONH– amide (peptide) link.

How many water molecules are released when a single polypeptide chain of 150 amino acid residues is formed?
Each peptide bond releases one water molecule and a chain of n residues has n − 1 peptide bonds, so 149.

Glycine (C₂H₅NO₂, M = 75.0 g mol⁻¹) forms the dipeptide Gly-Gly. What is the molar mass of Gly-Gly?

168.0 g mol⁻¹
114.0 g mol⁻¹

Which level of protein structure is defined by the sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide chain?
Primary
Secondary
Tertiary
Quaternary
Primary structure is the order of amino acid residues, held together by covalent peptide bonds.

α-helices and β-pleated sheets in proteins are stabilised mainly by:
disulfide bridges between cysteine side chains
hydrogen bonds between C=O and N–H groups of the polypeptide backbone
ionic interactions between charged side chains
peptide bonds between side chains
Secondary structure results from regular hydrogen bonding between backbone carbonyl oxygen and amide hydrogen atoms.

A disulfide bridge in a protein forms between the side chains of which amino acid?
Serine
Glycine
Cysteine
Lysine
Cysteine has a –CH₂SH side chain; two –SH groups can be oxidised to form a covalent –S–S– bridge.

Which statement best describes the quaternary structure of a protein?
The folding of a single polypeptide chain into its overall 3D shape
The local coiling of the backbone into α-helices
The sequence of amino acids in the chain

Quaternary structure exists only in proteins made of more than one polypeptide subunit, such as haemoglobin with four chains.

When egg white is fried, the protein albumin is denatured. Which bonds remain intact?
Peptide bonds
Hydrogen bonds between side chains
Ionic interactions between side chains
Dispersion forces between non-polar side chains
Denaturation disrupts secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure, but the covalent peptide bonds of the primary structure are not broken.
Which of the following amino acids is not chiral?
Alanine
Glycine
Serine
Cysteine
Glycine's side chain is H, so its central carbon has two identical H atoms and is not a stereocentre.
An essential amino acid is one that:
is found in every protein in the body
is needed only to make enzymes
cannot be made by the body in sufficient amounts and must be obtained from the diet
is made in the liver from glucose
Humans cannot synthesise nine amino acids (or enough of them), so these must come from dietary protein.
Lysine has the side chain –(CH₂)₄NH₂ and aspartic acid has –CH₂COOH. At physiological pH (about 7.4) these side chains are most likely to interact through:
a disulfide bridge
a peptide bond
dispersion forces only
an ionic interaction between –NH₃⁺ and –COO⁻
At pH 7.4 lysine's amino group is protonated and aspartic acid's carboxyl is deprotonated, so the oppositely charged groups attract (a salt bridge).
In a strongly acidic solution such as pH 1, the amino group of an amino acid is present mainly as:
–NH₃⁺
–NH⁻
–NO₂
–NH₂
The amino group is basic, so at low pH it accepts H⁺ to become –NH₃⁺.
How many different dipeptides can be formed from one glycine molecule and one alanine molecule, each used once?
Gly-Ala and Ala-Gly are different because the free amino (N-terminal) and carboxyl (C-terminal) ends differ.
How many different tripeptides can be formed using one molecule each of three different amino acids?
The three amino acids can be arranged in 3 × 2 × 1 = 6 different sequences.
Complete acid hydrolysis of a protein produces:
glucose and fructose
glycerol and fatty acids
peptides only, because peptide bonds cannot be hydrolysed
amino acids
Hydrolysis breaks every peptide bond, releasing the individual amino acid monomers.
Valine has the non-polar side chain –CH(CH₃)₂. In a water-soluble globular protein, valine residues are most likely to be found:
in the interior of the protein, interacting with other non-polar side chains via dispersion forces
on the surface, forming hydrogen bonds with water
forming disulfide bridges with cysteine
forming ionic bonds with water molecules
Hydrophobic side chains are buried away from water in the core of globular proteins, held by dispersion forces.
Which statement about a linear polypeptide chain is correct?
It has free carboxyl groups at both ends
It has a free amino group at one end and a free carboxyl group at the other end
It has no free functional groups at either end
It has free amino groups at both ends
The chain begins with an N-terminal –NH₂ and ends with a C-terminal –COOH because each internal pair has been used in a peptide bond.
Write the semi-structural formula of the dipeptide formed when the carboxyl group of glycine (H₂NCH₂COOH) reacts with the amino group of alanine (H₂NCH(CH₃)COOH).
H₂NCH₂CONHCH(CH₃)COOH (water is also produced).
Glycine's –COOH and alanine's –NH₂ combine to form the –CONH– peptide link, leaving glycine's amino group and alanine's carboxyl group free.
Explain why heating an enzyme-containing protein solution to 80 °C causes the protein to lose its biological function.

The extra kinetic energy disrupts the hydrogen bonds, ionic interactions and dispersion forces that maintain the secondary and tertiary structure, so the protein unfolds (denatures). Its specific 3D shape (e.g. active site) is lost, so it can no longer function, even though the peptide bonds remain.
Mark for: weak bonds/interactions broken, change in 3D shape, primary structure unchanged.
Distinguish between the secondary and tertiary structure of a protein, referring to the bonding involved in each.

Secondary structure is the local folding of the backbone into α-helices or β-pleated sheets, held by hydrogen bonds between backbone C=O and N–H groups. Tertiary structure is the overall 3D folding of the whole chain, held by interactions between side chains (hydrogen bonds, ionic interactions, dispersion forces and covalent disulfide bridges).
Key distinction: backbone interactions (secondary) versus side-chain (R group) interactions (tertiary).
A dipeptide with molecular formula C₅H₁₀N₂O₃ is hydrolysed. One product is glycine (C₂H₅NO₂). Determine the molecular formula of the other amino acid.
C₃H₇NO₂ (alanine).
Dipeptide + H₂O = C₅H₁₂N₂O₄; subtracting glycine C₂H₅NO₂ leaves C₃H₇NO₂.
Explain why people following a vegan diet are advised to eat a variety of plant protein sources, such as legumes together with grains.

Many individual plant proteins are low in one or more essential amino acids (e.g. grains are low in lysine, legumes in methionine). Combining complementary proteins ensures all essential amino acids, which the body cannot synthesise, are obtained in sufficient amounts.
Must link variety to obtaining all essential amino acids.
Explain how adding lemon juice (lowering the pH) to milk can cause milk proteins to denature and curdle.

Lowering the pH protonates –COO⁻ side chains to –COOH, changing the charges on R groups. This disrupts the ionic interactions and hydrogen bonds that hold the tertiary structure, so the proteins unfold and clump together (coagulate).
Award marks for change in charge on side chains and disruption of tertiary structure.
Calculate the mass of water needed to completely hydrolyse 1.00 mol of a single-chain polypeptide containing 51 amino acid residues.
51 residues have 50 peptide bonds, so 50 mol H₂O × 18.0 g mol⁻¹ = 900 g.
chem34a3-prot-1
In a solution of very low pH, the amino acid glycine (H₂NCH₂COOH) exists mainly as
H₂NCH₂COO⁻
H₃N⁺CH₂COO⁻
H₃N⁺CH₂COOH
H₂NCH₂COOH

At low pH there is a high concentration of H⁺, so both the amine group (protonated to –NH₃⁺) and the carboxyl group (remaining –COOH) are protonated. The zwitterion H₃N⁺CH₂COO⁻ predominates near the isoelectric point, and H₂NCH₂COO⁻ at high pH.
chem34a3-prot-2
The secondary structure of a protein, such as an α-helix or β-pleated sheet, is held together mainly by
peptide bonds between adjacent amino acids
hydrogen bonds between C=O and N–H groups of the polypeptide backbone
disulfide bridges between cysteine side chains
ionic interactions between charged R groups

Secondary structure results from hydrogen bonding between backbone carbonyl oxygens and amide hydrogens. Peptide bonds define the primary structure; disulfide bridges and ionic interactions between R groups contribute to tertiary structure.
chem34a3-prot-3
A protein is heated to 80 °C and loses its biological activity. Which level of protein structure is NOT disrupted by this denaturation?
primary
secondary
tertiary
quaternary

Denaturation disrupts the weaker interactions (hydrogen bonds, ionic interactions, dispersion forces) that maintain secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure. The covalent peptide bonds of the primary structure remain intact.
chem34a3-prot-4
An enzyme increases the rate of a reaction in the body by
increasing the temperature of the reactants
providing an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy
making the reaction more exothermic
shifting the equilibrium position towards products

Enzymes are biological catalysts: they provide an alternative pathway with lower activation energy, so a greater proportion of collisions are successful. They do not change ΔH or the position of equilibrium.
chem34a3-prot-5
Three different amino acids, X, Y and Z, are each used once to form a tripeptide. How many different tripeptides are possible?

Each sequence is a different primary structure, and a tripeptide has distinct N-terminal and C-terminal ends. The number of arrangements of three different units is 3 × 2 × 1 = 6. 27 would apply if each amino acid could be used more than once.
chem34a3-prot-6
Explain, with reference to the active site, why a change in pH can reduce the activity of an enzyme. (3 marks)

Changing the pH alters the concentration of H⁺, which changes the charges on acidic and basic R groups (e.g. –COOH/–COO⁻ and –NH₂/–NH₃⁺) in the enzyme; this disrupts ionic interactions and hydrogen bonds that maintain the tertiary structure, changing the shape of the active site; the substrate can no longer bind as effectively (and charged groups involved in catalysis may be altered), so activity decreases; large changes cause denaturation.
chem34a3-prot-7
Many water-soluble vitamins act as coenzymes. Explain what a coenzyme is and why a deficiency of such a vitamin could slow certain metabolic reactions. (2 marks)

A coenzyme is a non-protein organic molecule that binds to an enzyme (often at or near the active site) and is required for the enzyme to catalyse its reaction, frequently by carrying electrons, atoms or groups; without enough of the vitamin, the coenzyme cannot be made, so the enzymes that depend on it are less active and those reactions proceed more slowly.
chem34a3-prot-8

Draw or describe the structure of the dipeptide formed when the amino group of alanine (H₂NCH(CH₃)COOH) reacts with the carboxyl group of glycine (H₂NCH₂COOH). Name the type of reaction and the bond formed. (3 marks)

H₂NCH₂CONHCH(CH₃)COOH, i.e. glycine is at the N-terminal end: the –COOH of glycine and the –NH₂ of alanine join to form –CO–NH–; it is a condensation reaction releasing one H₂O molecule; the bond formed is a peptide (amide) bond.
chem-7-1-c1
Which interaction is NOT part of a protein's tertiary structure?
Disulfide bridges between cysteine side chains
Ionic interactions between charged side chains
Hydrogen bonds between backbone C=O and N–H groups in an α-helix
Dispersion forces between non-polar side chains
Backbone hydrogen bonding forms secondary structure. Tertiary structure comes from interactions between side chains (R groups).
chem-7-2: chem-7-2-1
Glucose and fructose both have the molecular formula C₆H₁₂O₆. They are best described as:
the same compound
polysaccharides
structural isomers
disaccharides
They have the same molecular formula but different arrangements of atoms (glucose is an aldose, fructose a ketose).
chem-7-2-2
Complete hydrolysis of sucrose produces:
two glucose molecules
glucose and galactose
fructose and galactose
glucose and fructose
Sucrose is a disaccharide of one glucose and one fructose unit.
chem-7-2-3
Lactose, the sugar found in milk, is a disaccharide made from:
glucose and galactose
two glucose units
glucose and fructose
two galactose units
Lactose hydrolyses into glucose and galactose.
chem-7-2-4
Two monosaccharide molecules of formula C₆H₁₂O₆ (M = 180.0 g mol⁻¹) join to form a disaccharide. What is the molar mass of the disaccharide?
360.0 g mol⁻¹
342.0 g mol⁻¹
378.0 g mol⁻¹
324.0 g mol⁻¹
2 × 180.0 − 18.0 (one water released) = 342.0 g mol⁻¹.
chem-7-2-5
The linkage between monosaccharide units in a disaccharide is a:
peptide linkage
ester linkage
glycosidic (ether) linkage
hydrogen bond
Condensation between two –OH groups forms a C–O–C glycosidic link.
chem-7-2-6
Which polysaccharide is used by animals to store glucose, mainly in the liver and muscles?
Amylose
Cellulose
Amylopectin
Glycogen
Glycogen is a highly branched polymer of glucose stored in animal liver and muscle tissue.
chem-7-2-7
Humans cannot use cellulose as an energy source because:
they lack an enzyme that can hydrolyse the β-glycosidic links between its glucose units
cellulose is made of fructose rather than glucose
no organism can break down cellulose
cellulose contains peptide bonds
Human amylases only hydrolyse α-glycosidic links; we have no cellulase for the β links in cellulose.
chem-7-2-8
Compared with amylose, amylopectin:
is unbranched and digested more slowly
is branched, so it is hydrolysed more quickly and tends to give a higher glycaemic index
contains β-glycosidic links
is a polymer of galactose
Branching gives many chain ends for amylase to attack, so glucose is released faster.
chem-7-2-9
A food with a high glycaemic index (GI):
releases glucose slowly over several hours
contains no carbohydrate
causes a rapid rise in blood glucose level after it is eaten
is always high in dietary fibre
GI measures how quickly a carbohydrate food raises blood glucose; high-GI foods are digested and absorbed rapidly.
A triglyceride is formed by the condensation of:
glycerol and three amino acids
glucose and three fatty acids
three glycerol molecules
glycerol and three fatty acids
Each of glycerol's three –OH groups reacts with the –COOH of a fatty acid.
Which functional group links each fatty acid to glycerol in a triglyceride?
Ester
Ether
Amide
Hydroxyl
A carboxylic acid reacting with an alcohol forms an ester (–COO–) group.
A fatty acid has the molecular formula C₁₈H₃₂O₂. How many C=C double bonds does it contain?
A saturated C₁₈ fatty acid is C₁₈H₃₆O₂; it has 4 fewer H atoms, so 2 C=C double bonds.
Tristearin (made from saturated stearic acid) is solid at room temperature, but olive oil (rich in oleic acid) is liquid. The best explanation is that:
saturated fats form hydrogen bonds between their hydrocarbon chains
oleic acid has more carbon atoms than stearic acid
straight saturated chains pack closely together, giving stronger dispersion forces between molecules
oils contain ionic bonds that break easily
Cis double bonds in oleic acid put kinks in the chains, preventing close packing and weakening dispersion forces.
An omega-3 fatty acid is one in which:
there are exactly three C=C double bonds
the chain contains three carbon atoms
the carboxyl group is on carbon 3
the first C=C double bond is on the third carbon from the methyl (–CH₃) end of the chain
The omega numbering counts from the methyl end, so omega-3 means the first double bond starts at carbon 3 from that end.
Oxidative rancidity of an oil occurs mainly because of:
reaction of oxygen at C=C double bonds in unsaturated fatty acid chains
hydrolysis of glycosidic linkages
reaction of nitrogen with ester groups
dehydration of glycerol
Oxygen attacks the C=C double bonds, producing smaller volatile compounds such as aldehydes that smell and taste rancid.
What is the molecular formula of the triglyceride formed from glycerol (C₃H₈O₃) and three molecules of stearic acid (C₁₈H₃₆O₂)?
C₅₇H₁₁₆O₉
C₅₇H₁₁₀O₆
C₅₇H₁₀₄O₆
C₅₄H₁₁₀O₆
C₃H₈O₃ + 3 C₁₈H₃₆O₂ − 3 H₂O = C₅₇H₁₁₀O₆.
How many moles of I₂ react by addition with one mole of a triglyceride made from glycerol and three linoleic acid (C₁₈H₃₂O₂) chains?
Each linoleic acid chain has 2 C=C bonds, so the triglyceride has 6, and one I₂ adds across each.
How many moles of water are needed to completely hydrolyse one mole of a triglyceride?
There are three ester links and each hydrolysis uses one water molecule.
Explain why glucose is highly soluble in water, whereas a triglyceride is insoluble.

Glucose is a small molecule with five –OH groups that form many hydrogen bonds with water. A triglyceride is a large molecule dominated by long non-polar hydrocarbon chains that can only form dispersion forces, so it cannot form enough attractions with water to dissolve.
Refer to hydrogen bonding (glucose) versus mainly non-polar chains (triglyceride).
Name the products of complete hydrolysis of (a) starch and (b) a triglyceride.
(a) Glucose. (b) Glycerol and three fatty acids.
Starch is a polymer of α-glucose; triglycerides are esters of glycerol and fatty acids.
Explain why unsaturated vegetable oils generally have lower melting points than saturated animal fats of similar molar mass.

The cis C=C double bonds in unsaturated chains create kinks, so the molecules cannot pack closely. This weakens the dispersion forces between molecules, so less energy is needed to separate them and the melting point is lower.
Link structure (kinks) → packing → strength of dispersion forces → melting point.
Maltose (C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁) is a disaccharide of two glucose units. Calculate the mass of glucose (M = 180.0 g mol⁻¹) produced when 34.2 g of maltose is completely hydrolysed.
M(maltose) = 342.0 g mol⁻¹, so n = 0.100 mol; this gives 0.200 mol glucose × 180.0 = 36.0 g.
Explain how adding an antioxidant such as vitamin E to packaged nuts slows the development of oxidative rancidity.

Antioxidants are preferentially oxidised (they react with oxygen or free radicals more readily than the C=C bonds in the unsaturated fats), so the oils in the nuts are protected from oxidation and rancid-smelling breakdown products form more slowly.
The antioxidant is oxidised instead of the unsaturated fatty acid chains.
Distinguish between amylose and amylopectin, and state which is likely to give a food a lower glycaemic index.

Both are polymers of α-glucose. Amylose is unbranched (α-1,4 links only), while amylopectin is branched (α-1,4 and α-1,6 links). Foods high in amylose have a lower GI because the unbranched chains coil tightly and are hydrolysed more slowly.
Must state branching difference and that high amylose gives lower GI.
Linolenic acid has the formula C₁₈H₃₀O₂. Determine the number of C=C double bonds and classify it as saturated, monounsaturated or polyunsaturated.
3 C=C double bonds; polyunsaturated.
A saturated C₁₈ acid is C₁₈H₃₆O₂; it has 6 fewer H atoms, i.e. 3 C=C, and more than one double bond means polyunsaturated.
chem34a3-carb-1
Sucrose is a disaccharide formed from which two monosaccharides?
glucose and glucose
glucose and galactose
glucose and fructose
fructose and galactose
Sucrose is formed by a condensation reaction between glucose and fructose. Maltose is glucose + glucose and lactose is glucose + galactose.
chem34a3-carb-2
Which equation correctly represents the formation of maltose from glucose?
2C₆H₁₂O₆ → C₁₂H₂₄O₁₂
2C₆H₁₂O₆ → C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ + H₂O
C₆H₁₂O₆ + H₂O → C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁
2C₆H₁₂O₆ + H₂O → C₁₂H₂₄O₁₃
Two glucose molecules join by a condensation reaction forming a glycosidic link and releasing one water molecule, so maltose is C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁.
chem34a3-carb-3
Humans can digest starch but not cellulose, even though both are polymers of glucose. The main reason is that
cellulose contains fructose units that cannot be absorbed
cellulose is made from β-glucose, and humans lack an enzyme that hydrolyses its glycosidic links
starch is a monosaccharide and needs no digestion
cellulose is too soluble to be acted on by enzymes

Cellulose is a polymer of β-glucose, while starch is made of α-glucose. Human digestive enzymes (amylases) are specific to the α-glycosidic links in starch, and humans do not produce cellulase. Cellulose is insoluble, not too soluble.
chem34a3-carb-4
Amylose and amylopectin are both components of starch. Compared with amylose, amylopectin
is a polymer of fructose
is unbranched and coils into a helix
is branched, with α(1→6) links at branch points as well as α(1→4) links
contains β-glycosidic links

Amylopectin is branched: chains of α(1→4)-linked glucose with α(1→6) links at branch points. Amylose is the unbranched, helical component. The many chain ends make amylopectin hydrolyse faster, giving a higher glycaemic index.
chem34a3-carb-5
A polysaccharide molecule is made from 500 glucose units joined in a single unbranched chain. How many water molecules are needed to completely hydrolyse it to glucose?
An unbranched chain of 500 units contains 499 glycosidic links. Hydrolysis of each link uses one water molecule, so 499 water molecules are needed.
chem34a3-carb-6
Glycogen and starch are both energy-storage polysaccharides. Describe one structural difference between them and explain why glycogen is well suited to rapid release of glucose in animals. (2 marks)

Glycogen is more highly branched than starch (amylopectin), with α(1→6) branch points occurring more frequently; the many branch ends provide many sites where enzymes can hydrolyse glucose units at the same time, allowing rapid release of glucose when needed.
chem34a3-carb-7

Aspartame is an artificial sweetener about 200 times sweeter than sucrose. Explain why a soft drink sweetened with aspartame has a much lower energy content than one sweetened with sucrose to the same sweetness, even though aspartame is metabolised and releases energy. (2 marks)

Because aspartame is about 200 times sweeter, only a tiny mass is needed to achieve the same sweetness; although it releases a similar amount of energy per gram to sucrose (it is a dipeptide derivative, around 17 kJ g⁻¹), the very small mass contributes negligible energy to the drink.
chem34a3-carb-8
Foods rich in amylose tend to have a lower glycaemic index (GI) than foods rich in amylopectin. Explain this observation and give one health benefit of low-GI foods. (3 marks)

Amylose is unbranched and coils tightly into a helix, so it has fewer exposed chain ends for amylase enzymes to act on and is hydrolysed more slowly; glucose is therefore released into the bloodstream more slowly, giving a smaller, slower rise in blood glucose (lower GI); a benefit is better blood-glucose control (e.g. for people with diabetes) or feeling full for longer / more sustained energy release.
chem34a3-fat-1
A triglyceride is formed when glycerol reacts with three fatty acid molecules. The products of this reaction are the triglyceride and
one water molecule
three water molecules
three hydrogen molecules
one ethanol molecule

Each of the three –OH groups of glycerol reacts with the –COOH of a fatty acid in a condensation reaction forming an ester link and releasing one water molecule, giving three water molecules in total.
chem34a3-fat-2
Linoleic acid has the formula C₁₇H₃₁COOH. How many carbon–carbon double bonds does one molecule contain?
A saturated C₁₈ fatty acid is C₁₇H₃₅COOH (stearic acid). Linoleic acid has 4 fewer hydrogens, and each C=C removes 2 hydrogens, so it has 2 double bonds.
chem34a3-fat-3
Olive oil is a liquid at room temperature, while butter is a soft solid. The best explanation is that olive oil contains a higher proportion of
saturated fatty acid chains, which have stronger dispersion forces
cis-unsaturated fatty acid chains, whose kinks prevent close packing and weaken dispersion forces
glycerol, which forms hydrogen bonds with water
fatty acids with longer carbon chains

Cis double bonds introduce kinks in the hydrocarbon chains, so molecules cannot pack closely. The dispersion forces between them are weaker, giving lower melting points. Longer and saturated chains would raise the melting point.
chem34a3-fat-4
Which vitamin is fat-soluble and therefore can be stored in body fat?
vitamin C
vitamin B₁₂
vitamin D
vitamin B₃

Vitamin D is a largely non-polar molecule with only one –OH group, so it dissolves in fats and is stored in fatty tissue. Vitamin C and the B vitamins have many polar groups capable of hydrogen bonding with water, so they are water-soluble and must be consumed regularly.
chem34a3-fat-5
How many moles of hydrogen gas are needed to completely hydrogenate 1 mol of a triglyceride made from glycerol and three linolenic acid (C₁₇H₂₉COOH) chains?
3 mol
6 mol
9 mol
12 mol
Linolenic acid has 3 C=C double bonds (C₁₇H₂₉COOH is 6 H short of C₁₇H₃₅COOH). The triglyceride has 3 chains × 3 C=C = 9 double bonds, each requiring 1 mol of H₂.
chem34a3-fat-6
Explain what is meant by an omega-3 fatty acid and give one reason why omega-3 fatty acids are described as 'essential' in the diet. (2 marks)

An omega-3 fatty acid is an unsaturated fatty acid whose first carbon–carbon double bond is located at the third carbon counting from the methyl (omega) end of the chain; it is essential because the human body cannot synthesise it (cannot insert a double bond at that position), so it must be obtained from food (e.g. fish, flaxseed).
chem34a3-fat-7
Polyunsaturated oils become rancid more quickly than saturated fats when exposed to air. Explain why, and describe one way food manufacturers slow this process. (3 marks)

Oxidative rancidity occurs when oxygen reacts at carbon–carbon double bonds, breaking the chains into smaller, unpleasant-smelling aldehydes, ketones and acids; polyunsaturated oils have more C=C bonds, so they oxidise more readily than saturated fats; manufacturers add antioxidants (e.g. vitamin E/tocopherols), store in airtight, opaque or nitrogen-flushed containers, or refrigerate to slow oxidation.
chem34a3-fat-8

Vitamin C contains several –OH groups, whereas vitamin A consists mainly of a long hydrocarbon chain with a single –OH group. Use these structural features to explain the different solubilities of the two vitamins and one dietary consequence. (3 marks)

Vitamin C's many –OH groups form hydrogen bonds with water, making it water-soluble; vitamin A is largely non-polar, so it interacts by dispersion forces with fats and is fat-soluble rather than water-soluble; consequence: vitamin C is not stored and excess is excreted, so it must be consumed regularly, whereas vitamin A is stored in body fat/liver and excessive intake can accumulate to toxic levels.
chem-7-2-c1
Linoleic acid has 18 carbons and two C=C bonds. How many moles of H₂ are needed to fully saturate 1 mol of a triglyceride made from three linoleic acid units?
Each chain has 2 C=C bonds, and there are 3 chains: 6 C=C, each needing one H₂.
chem-7-3: chem-7-3-1
Enzymes increase the rate of reactions in the body by:
providing an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy
increasing the activation energy of the reaction
making the reaction more exothermic
being used up as a reactant
Like all catalysts, enzymes lower activation energy without changing ΔH and are not consumed.
chem-7-3-2
The active site of an enzyme is:
the place in the cell where the enzyme is made
the region where the substrate binds and the reaction is catalysed
the C-terminal end of the polypeptide
a region that forms only at high temperatures
The active site is a specifically shaped pocket formed by the tertiary structure, into which the substrate fits.
chem-7-3-3
The induced-fit model of enzyme action proposes that:
the active site is rigid and an exact match to the substrate
an enzyme can bind any substrate
the active site changes shape slightly when the substrate binds, improving the fit
the substrate changes the enzyme's primary structure
In induced fit, binding causes a small conformational change that strains the substrate's bonds and assists the reaction.
chem-7-3-4
A typical human enzyme is heated from 37 °C to 70 °C. The rate of the reaction it catalyses will most likely:
keep increasing, because particles move faster
stay the same, because catalysts are unaffected by temperature
increase, because the enzyme is converted into more substrate
decrease, because the enzyme denatures and its active site loses its shape
Above the optimum temperature the weak interactions holding the tertiary structure break and the enzyme denatures.
chem-7-3-5
Pepsin works best at about pH 2. If pepsin is placed in a solution at pH 8, its activity will:
decrease, because the change in pH alters the charges on side chains and the shape of the active site
increase, because more OH⁻ ions are present
remain unchanged, because pH does not affect proteins
increase, because peptide bonds in pepsin break more easily
Changing pH changes the ionisation of R groups, disrupting ionic interactions and hydrogen bonds that shape the active site.
chem-7-3-6
The specificity of an enzyme for its substrate mainly arises from:
the very large molar mass of the enzyme
the complementary shape and chemical properties of the active site and the substrate
carbohydrate groups attached to the enzyme
the number of peptide bonds in the enzyme
Only a substrate whose shape and functional groups match the active site can bind and react.
chem-7-3-7
A coenzyme is best described as:
an inorganic metal ion bound to an enzyme
a second enzyme that works alongside the first
a non-protein organic molecule, often derived from a vitamin, that an enzyme needs to function
the substrate of the enzyme
Coenzymes are small organic cofactors, e.g. many B vitamins act as coenzyme precursors.
chem-7-3-8
The Zn²⁺ ion required by the enzyme carbonic anhydrase is an example of:
a coenzyme
a substrate
a product
an inorganic cofactor
Metal ions that enzymes require for activity are inorganic cofactors; coenzymes are organic.
chem-7-3-9
A competitive inhibitor reduces the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction because it:
binds to the active site and prevents the substrate from binding
binds to the enzyme and hydrolyses its peptide bonds
raises the activation energy of every reaction in the cell
is converted into extra substrate
A competitive inhibitor resembles the substrate and competes for the same active site.
Food is stored in a refrigerator at 4 °C. The effect of this on the enzymes in the food is that they:
are permanently denatured
work more slowly because there are fewer successful collisions, but are not permanently denatured
work faster because cold stabilises their shape
have their peptide bonds hydrolysed
Low temperature reduces kinetic energy and collision frequency; activity largely returns when warmed.
Which group of vitamins is fat-soluble?
B group and C
C and D
A, D, E and K
B, C and K
Vitamins A, D, E and K are largely non-polar and dissolve in fats; B and C are water-soluble.
Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is water-soluble mainly because:
it is a large non-polar ring system
it is an ionic compound
it has a long hydrocarbon chain
it has several hydroxyl groups that form hydrogen bonds with water
Its small molecule carries multiple –OH groups (and C=O groups), allowing extensive hydrogen bonding with water.
Vitamin D is fat-soluble because:
its molecule is mostly non-polar hydrocarbon with only one hydroxyl group
it has many hydroxyl groups
it is an ionic compound
it is a protein
The single –OH group is insufficient to overcome the large non-polar ring and chain structure, so it dissolves in fats, not water.
Why is it more important to consume vitamin C regularly than vitamin A?
Vitamin C is fat-soluble and is stored in the liver
Vitamin C is water-soluble, is not stored in large amounts and the excess is excreted in urine, whereas vitamin A is stored in fatty tissue
Vitamin A is water-soluble and is rapidly excreted
Vitamin C is made in the body from vitamin A
Water-soluble vitamins are not stored significantly, so a regular dietary supply is needed.
Vitamins are described as essential in the human diet because:
they provide a large proportion of the body's energy
they are the main structural material of cells
the body cannot synthesise them, or cannot synthesise enough, yet they are needed for normal function
they are themselves enzymes
Vitamins are needed in small amounts, often as coenzymes, but most cannot be made by the body.
Humans can synthesise vitamin D when:
vitamin C is eaten in large amounts
the body is fasting
the body is exposed to cold temperatures
the skin is exposed to ultraviolet light from the sun
UV-B radiation converts a cholesterol derivative in the skin into vitamin D, so sun exposure is a major source.
Boiling broccoli in a large volume of water reduces its vitamin C content mainly because vitamin C:
is water-soluble, so it leaches into the cooking water, and it is also broken down by heat
is fat-soluble and is lost in the steam
is converted into vitamin D on heating
evaporates as a gas at 100 °C
Water-soluble, heat-sensitive vitamin C is lost both by dissolving and by decomposition; steaming retains more.
Lactose intolerance is caused by:
an excess of salivary amylase
insufficient lactase enzyme to hydrolyse lactose in the small intestine
an inability to absorb glucose
an allergy to milk fats
Without enough lactase, undigested lactose passes to the large intestine, where bacteria ferment it, causing symptoms.
Use the idea of enzyme specificity to explain why amylase can hydrolyse starch but not cellulose, even though both are polymers of glucose.

Amylase's active site has a shape and chemical environment complementary to the α-glycosidic links in starch. Cellulose has β-glycosidic links, giving a different 3D shape that does not fit the active site, so amylase cannot bind and hydrolyse it.
Must refer to the active site being complementary only to α-linkages.
Explain why the activity of a human enzyme increases from 20 °C to 37 °C but drops sharply above about 45 °C.

From 20 °C to 37 °C, particles have more kinetic energy, so enzyme–substrate collisions are more frequent and energetic, increasing rate. Above about 45 °C the hydrogen bonds and other interactions holding the tertiary structure break, so the enzyme denatures, the active site changes shape and activity falls.
Two parts: collision theory below optimum; denaturation above.
Distinguish between a cofactor and a coenzyme, giving an example of each.

A cofactor is a non-protein component needed for enzyme activity; inorganic cofactors are metal ions such as Mg²⁺ or Zn²⁺. A coenzyme is an organic cofactor, often derived from a vitamin, such as NAD⁺ (from niacin, vitamin B3).
Coenzymes are a type of cofactor; the key difference is organic versus inorganic.
Explain why vitamin C toxicity is rare, whereas excessive intake of vitamin A or D can be harmful.

Vitamin C is water-soluble, so excess dissolves in blood and is excreted in urine. Vitamins A and D are fat-soluble, so excess is stored in the liver and fatty tissue and can accumulate to toxic levels.
Link solubility to excretion versus storage.
A student states: 'An enzyme denatured by high temperature has been broken down into amino acids.' Evaluate this statement.

The statement is incorrect. Denaturation disrupts the secondary and tertiary (and quaternary) structure by breaking weak interactions, but the covalent peptide bonds of the primary structure are not broken. Breaking the protein into amino acids would require hydrolysis.
Distinguish denaturation from hydrolysis.
Explain, in terms of intermolecular forces, why vitamin D is stored in the body's adipose (fat) tissue.

Vitamin D is mostly non-polar, so it forms dispersion forces with the non-polar hydrocarbon chains of triglycerides in fat tissue. It cannot form enough hydrogen bonds with water to dissolve in blood plasma, so it dissolves in and is stored in fat.
'Like dissolves like': non-polar vitamin with non-polar fat.
Fresh pineapple contains bromelain, a protease. Explain why fresh pineapple stops gelatine (a protein) from setting, but canned pineapple, which has been heated, does not.

Bromelain in fresh pineapple catalyses hydrolysis of peptide bonds in gelatine, breaking it into smaller peptides that cannot form a gel. Heating during canning denatures bromelain, so its active site is lost and it can no longer hydrolyse the gelatine.
Mark for: protease hydrolyses gelatine; heat denatures the enzyme.
chem-7-3-c1
Vitamin C is water-soluble but vitamin D is fat-soluble because:
Vitamin D is an ionic compound that dissolves in fats; vitamin C is a covalent molecule that dissolves in water
Vitamin C has a much higher molar mass than vitamin D, so it dissolves more easily in water
Vitamin D forms hydrogen bonds with fats, while vitamin C forms only dispersion forces with water
Vitamin D is mostly non-polar hydrocarbon with one OH group; vitamin C has several OH groups that bond with water
Solubility depends on polarity: like dissolves like.
chem-7-4: Using standard food energy values, approximately how much energy is released per gram of fat in the body?
Fats and oils release about 37 kJ g⁻¹, compared with about 16 kJ g⁻¹ for carbohydrate and 17 kJ g⁻¹ for protein.
A muesli bar contains 20.0 g carbohydrate, 5.0 g fat and 3.0 g protein. Using 16 kJ g⁻¹, 37 kJ g⁻¹ and 17 kJ g⁻¹ respectively, what is its total energy content?
A 150 g sample of water is heated by burning a food and its temperature rises by 12.0 °C. How much energy did the water absorb? (c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹)
A calorimeter is calibrated by passing a current of 2.50 A at 6.00 V for 90.0 s, which raises the temperature by 1.35 °C. What is the calibration factor?
A bomb calorimeter has a calibration factor of 850 J °C⁻¹. Burning 0.400 g of peanut raises its temperature by 4.80 °C. What is the energy content of the peanut?
Fats release more energy per gram than carbohydrates when metabolised because fat molecules:
are less oxidised, containing proportionally more C–H bonds and fewer oxygen atoms
Carbohydrates already contain a lot of oxygen (partly oxidised), so less energy is released when they are oxidised to CO₂ and H₂O.
The heat of combustion of glucose (M = 180.0 g mol⁻¹) is 2805 kJ mol⁻¹. How much energy is released per gram of glucose?
In a simple 'can' calorimeter experiment, the measured energy content of a food is usually lower than the accepted value. The main reason is:
the water absorbs more energy than the food releases
heat is lost to the surrounding air and the food may not combust completely
the food is weighed before burning
Not all the heat released reaches the water, and incomplete combustion releases less energy than expected.
The purpose of electrically calibrating a calorimeter before a food is burned in it is to:
measure the mass of the food sample
determine the energy needed to raise the temperature of the whole calorimeter by 1 °C
cool the water to a known starting temperature
The calibration factor accounts for all parts of the calorimeter, not just the water, giving a more accurate energy value.
Chemical digestion of starch begins in the:
Salivary amylase starts hydrolysing starch into maltose and shorter chains while food is chewed.
Chemical digestion of protein begins in the:
Pepsin, active in the acidic stomach, begins hydrolysing peptide bonds.
The role of bile in the digestion of fats is to:
hydrolyse the ester bonds in triglycerides
emulsify fats into small droplets, increasing the surface area for lipase to act on
act as an enzyme that breaks peptide bonds
Bile is not an enzyme; it physically disperses fat so lipase can hydrolyse it faster.
The products of fat digestion that are absorbed from the small intestine are mainly:
Lipase hydrolyses triglycerides into fatty acids, glycerol and monoglycerides, which are absorbed.
Chemical digestion of carbohydrates, proteins and fats in the body involves which type of reaction?
Digestive enzymes break glycosidic, peptide and ester bonds by adding water.
In aerobic cellular respiration, glucose reacts with oxygen. The products are:
C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O, releasing energy for the body.
A serve of a breakfast cereal provides 1500 kJ. An adult's average daily energy requirement is 8700 kJ. What percentage of daily energy needs does one serve provide?
A serve of peanut butter provides 370 kJ of energy from fat. What mass of fat is in the serve? (fat: 37 kJ g⁻¹)

A spirit burner burns 0.50 g of ethanol (M = 46.0 g mol⁻¹, heat of combustion 1360 kJ mol⁻¹), heating 100 g of water by 25.0 °C. What is the approximate efficiency of the energy transfer to the water? (c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹)

A 2.00 g cracker is burned under a can containing 250 g of water, and the water temperature rises by 18.0 °C. Assuming all the heat is absorbed by the water, calculate the energy content of the cracker in kJ g⁻¹. (c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹)

A calorimeter is calibrated using 5.00 V and 3.00 A for 180 s, giving a temperature rise of 2.25 °C. A 1.20 g food sample is then burned and the temperature rises by 3.60 °C. Calculate the energy content of the food in kJ g⁻¹.
Explain why the energy content of a food measured using a simple can-and-burner apparatus is usually lower than the value on the food label, and suggest one improvement.

Heat is lost to the surroundings (air, the can and the clamp), and the food may burn incompletely, leaving soot or unburnt residue, so the water absorbs less energy than the food contains. Improvements include using a bomb calorimeter or insulating/shielding the apparatus and calibrating it electrically.
Any valid source of heat loss plus a matching improvement.
Describe the chemical digestion of a triglyceride, naming the main enzyme, where it occurs and the products formed.

In the small intestine, bile emulsifies the fat and the enzyme lipase (from the pancreas) catalyses hydrolysis of the three ester bonds. The products are glycerol and fatty acids (often absorbed as monoglycerides and fatty acids).
Must identify lipase, small intestine, hydrolysis of ester links and the products.
Explain why the body stores excess energy mainly as fat rather than as glycogen.

Fat releases about 37 kJ g⁻¹ compared with about 16 kJ g⁻¹ for carbohydrate, because it is less oxidised. Fat is also stored without water (it is non-polar), whereas glycogen is stored hydrated, so fat stores far more energy per unit mass.
Mention higher energy per gram and/or lack of associated water.
A 30 g slice of toast contains 14.4 g carbohydrate, 1.2 g fat and 3.0 g protein. Using 16, 37 and 17 kJ g⁻¹ respectively, calculate the energy content of the slice.
Explain why dietary fibre such as cellulose provides humans with very little energy even though it is a polymer of glucose.

Humans lack the enzyme cellulase needed to hydrolyse the β-glycosidic links in cellulose, so it cannot be broken down into glucose and absorbed. It passes through the digestive tract largely unchanged, though it aids digestive health.
Key point: no enzyme for β-linkages, so no glucose is released.

A serving of breakfast cereal contains 6.0 g of protein, 15.0 g of carbohydrate and 5.0 g of fat. Using energy values of 17 kJ g⁻¹ (protein), 16 kJ g⁻¹ (carbohydrate) and 37 kJ g⁻¹ (fat), the energy content of the serving is approximately
Energy = 6.0 × 17 + 15.0 × 16 + 5.0 × 37 = 102 + 240 + 185 = 527 kJ. Fat provides more than twice as much energy per gram as carbohydrate or protein.
A bomb calorimeter is calibrated by passing a current of 2.00 A at 5.00 V for 120 s, causing a temperature rise of 0.480 °C. The calibration factor is
In a spirit burner experiment, 200 g of water is heated from 20.0 °C to 35.0 °C by burning ethanol. Assuming all the heat is absorbed by the water (c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹), the energy absorbed is
q = mcΔT = 200 × 4.18 × 15.0 = 12 540 J = 12.5 kJ (3 significant figures). Using the final temperature (35.0 °C) instead of ΔT would give 29.3 kJ.
The experimentally determined enthalpy of combustion of ethanol from a spirit burner is usually much less negative than the data book value. Which of the following is the most significant reason?
Heat is lost to the surroundings and combustion may be incomplete
The water absorbs more heat than calculated
Ethanol has a higher molar mass than assumed

In an open spirit burner much of the heat escapes to the air and the container rather than entering the water, and incomplete combustion (soot, CO) releases less energy. Both make the measured energy per mole smaller than the true value.
Glucose has a molar enthalpy of combustion of −2803 kJ mol⁻¹ (M = 180.0 g mol⁻¹). The energy released per gram of glucose is closest to
Energy per gram = 2803 ÷ 180.0 = 15.6 kJ g⁻¹, consistent with the value of about 16 kJ g⁻¹ used for carbohydrates.

A bomb calorimeter has a calibration factor of 2.50 kJ °C⁻¹. When 1.20 g of a dried food sample is combusted completely, the temperature rises by 6.40 °C. Calculate the energy content of the food in kJ g⁻¹. (2 marks)
Energy released = 2.50 × 6.40 = 16.0 kJ; energy content = 16.0 ÷ 1.20 = 13.3 kJ g⁻¹.

0.850 g of ethanol (M = 46.0 g mol⁻¹) is burnt in a spirit burner, raising the temperature of 200 g of water by 15.0 °C (c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹). Calculate the experimental molar enthalpy of combustion of ethanol and state why it differs from the accepted value of −1364 kJ mol⁻¹. (3 marks)

q = 200 × 4.18 × 15.0 = 12 540 J = 12.54 kJ; n(ethanol) = 0.850 ÷ 46.0 = 1.848 × 10⁻² mol; ΔH = −12.54 ÷ 1.848 × 10⁻² = −679 kJ mol⁻¹; much less negative than −1364 kJ mol⁻¹ because heat is lost to the surroundings/container (and combustion may be incomplete), so not all the energy released is absorbed by the water.
Explain, in terms of the composition of the molecules, why fats release more than twice as much energy per gram as carbohydrates when fully oxidised. (2 marks)

Fats consist mostly of long hydrocarbon chains with many C–H bonds and very little oxygen, so they are in a much less oxidised (more reduced) state than carbohydrates, which already contain many C–O/O–H groups; oxidising fats to CO₂ and H₂O therefore forms many more strong C=O and O–H bonds per gram, releasing more energy (about 37 kJ g⁻¹ versus 16 kJ g⁻¹).
A snack contains 10.0 g of carbohydrate, 5.0 g of fat and 3.0 g of protein. Using 16, 37 and 17 kJ/g respectively, find its energy content.
chem-8-1: chem-8-1-1
Which statement best describes the green chemistry principle of 'prevention'?
It is better to prevent waste from forming than to treat or clean it up after it has formed.
Hazardous waste should be stored securely on site until it can be incinerated.
All waste products should be diluted before release to the environment.
Pollution controls should be added at the end of a production line.
Prevention is the first green chemistry principle: avoiding waste is preferable to treating it afterwards.
chem-8-1-2
A manufacturer replaces dichloromethane with supercritical carbon dioxide as the extraction solvent for decaffeinating coffee. Which green chemistry principle is mainly being applied?
Design for degradation
Use of safer solvents and auxiliaries
Use of renewable feedstocks
Real-time analysis for pollution prevention
Supercritical CO₂ is non-toxic and easily removed, replacing a hazardous chlorinated solvent.
chem-8-1-3
Why are catalysts considered consistent with green chemistry?
They shift the equilibrium position towards products, increasing the equilibrium yield.
They are consumed in the reaction, so no excess reagent is needed.
They lower activation energy, allowing reactions at lower temperatures and are not consumed, reducing energy use and waste.
They increase the enthalpy change of the reaction, releasing more useful heat.
Catalysts provide an alternative pathway of lower activation energy and are regenerated, so they save energy and are not waste; they do not change equilibrium position.
chem-8-1-4
Explain why green chemistry focuses on preventing waste rather than treating waste.

Preventing waste avoids the need for extra treatment processes, which themselves use energy, materials and money and can still produce hazardous residues. It also removes the risk of waste escaping into the environment.
Mention cost/energy of treatment and environmental risk.
chem-8-1-5
Producing ethanol by fermenting sugar cane rather than by hydrating ethene from crude oil best illustrates which principle?
Design for energy efficiency
Catalysis
Safer chemical design
Use of renewable feedstocks
Sugar cane is a renewable biological feedstock, whereas ethene from crude oil is non-renewable.
chem-8-1-6
Which practice best illustrates the principle of 'design for energy efficiency'?
Choosing a catalyst that allows a process to run at ambient temperature and pressure
Increasing reactor pressure to increase reaction rate
Distilling products several times to improve purity
Using a fossil-fuel feedstock that is cheaper to purchase
Energy requirements should be minimised; running at ambient conditions avoids heating and compression.
chem-8-1-7
A detergent company redesigns a surfactant so that it is broken down by microorganisms in waterways within days. Which principle does this demonstrate?
Prevention of waste
Design for degradation
Atom economy
Less hazardous chemical syntheses
Products should be designed to break down into harmless substances after use rather than persisting in the environment.
chem-8-1-8
State two green chemistry principles that are applied when an enzyme is used as a catalyst in a fermentation process at 35 °C, and explain each briefly.

Catalysis: the enzyme speeds up the reaction without being consumed, reducing waste. Design for energy efficiency: the reaction proceeds at low temperature and atmospheric pressure, so less energy is needed. (Use of renewable feedstocks also accepted if a plant sugar is the substrate.)
Two correctly named principles, each linked to the enzyme process.
chem-8-1-9
Real-time analysis for pollution prevention refers to:
testing waste water once a year to meet EPA Victoria requirements.
analysing finished products in a laboratory before sale.
monitoring a process continuously during production so that formation of hazardous substances can be detected and controlled immediately.
calculating atom economy before a process is built.
In-process monitoring allows conditions to be adjusted before hazardous by-products build up.
Which of the following is the best example of 'inherently safer chemistry for accident prevention'?
Storing large stockpiles of chlorine gas to avoid supply interruptions
Running exothermic reactions at higher temperatures to finish faster
Using a volatile, flammable solvent because it evaporates easily
Generating a toxic reactant in small amounts as needed rather than storing large quantities of it
Minimising the amount and hazard of substances on site reduces the risk of explosions, fires and releases.
Reducing derivatives in a synthesis means:
avoiding unnecessary protecting groups or temporary modifications, as these steps require extra reagents and generate waste.
using derivatives of petroleum as feedstocks.
making as many different products as possible from one reactant.
converting all products into salts for easier storage.
Each blocking/protecting step uses extra reagents and creates waste, so they should be avoided where possible.
Supercritical CO₂ is used as a solvent in some industrial processes. Give one advantage and one disadvantage of its use in terms of green chemistry.

Advantage: it is non-toxic and non-flammable and can be removed simply by releasing pressure, leaving no solvent residue. Disadvantage: high pressures are needed, requiring energy and specialised equipment (and CO₂ is a greenhouse gas if released).
One valid advantage and one valid disadvantage.
Which change to an industrial process is LEAST consistent with green chemistry principles?
Switching from a stoichiometric oxidising agent to a catalytic process
Replacing a catalysed route at 40 °C with an uncatalysed route at 400 °C
Recycling unreacted gases back into the reactor
Replacing an organic solvent with water
Raising the temperature without a catalyst greatly increases energy use, contrary to design for energy efficiency.
A Victorian company converts waste cooking oil from restaurants into biodiesel. Which green chemistry principle is most directly applied?
Real-time analysis for pollution prevention
Design for degradation
Use of renewable feedstocks
Reduce derivatives
Waste cooking oil is a renewable, plant-derived feedstock, replacing petroleum-derived diesel.
Why is water often considered a 'green' solvent?
It dissolves all organic compounds well.
It has a low specific heat capacity, so it is cheap to heat.
It evaporates readily, so it needs no energy to remove.
It is non-toxic, non-flammable, cheap and abundant.
Water is safe and abundant; its main drawbacks are poor solubility of some organics and high energy to evaporate.
Explain the difference between a renewable and a non-renewable feedstock, giving a chemical example of each.

A renewable feedstock can be replaced by natural processes within a human timescale, e.g. sugar cane or vegetable oils. A non-renewable feedstock is used faster than it forms, e.g. crude oil or natural gas.
Definition plus an example of each.
Which statement about green chemistry principles is correct?
Green chemistry aims to reduce or eliminate the use and generation of hazardous substances across the whole life cycle of a product.
Green chemistry only applies to the disposal stage of a product.
Green chemistry requires that all reactions have 100% percentage yield.
Green chemistry means only using naturally occurring chemicals.
Green chemistry considers design, manufacture, use and disposal, aiming to minimise hazards throughout.
The principle 'designing safer chemicals' is best demonstrated by:
increasing the concentration of a pesticide so less volume is transported.
developing a pesticide that is effective against the target insect but has low toxicity to bees and mammals.
storing pesticides in sealed containers.
manufacturing a pesticide at a lower temperature.
Safer chemicals keep their function while minimising toxicity to people and non-target organisms.
Hydrogen produced by electrolysis of water using electricity from a Victorian wind farm is described as 'green hydrogen' mainly because:
it has a higher energy content per gram than hydrogen from natural gas.
the electrolysis reaction has 100% atom economy for hydrogen.
the energy input comes from a renewable source and no carbon dioxide is produced in the process.
the hydrogen produced is purer than any other source.
Green hydrogen uses renewable electricity, avoiding the CO₂ produced in steam reforming of methane; electrolysis of water has only 11.1% atom economy for H₂.
Explain how real-time analysis can reduce pollution in a chemical plant.

Continuous monitoring during a reaction detects changes such as rising temperature or formation of unwanted by-products as they occur, so operators can adjust conditions immediately. This prevents large amounts of hazardous waste forming or being released.
Must link monitoring during the process to preventing hazardous products.
Catalytic reagents are preferred over stoichiometric reagents because:
stoichiometric reagents always give lower equilibrium yields.
catalysts increase the atom economy shown by the balanced equation to 100%.
catalysts are always cheaper than stoichiometric reagents.
catalysts are used in small amounts and regenerated, whereas stoichiometric reagents are consumed and become waste.
A catalyst is not consumed, so it does not add to waste; a stoichiometric reagent ends up as by-product.
Which feature of the Haber process is most consistent with green chemistry principles?
The reaction N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃ has 100% atom economy and unreacted gases are recycled.
The process uses hydrogen obtained from natural gas.
The process operates at high pressure, around 200 atm.
The iron catalyst is replaced after each batch.
All reactant atoms end up in ammonia, and recycling unreacted gases reduces waste; using natural gas and high pressure are less green.
Which of the following best describes 'design for degradation' as applied to plastics?
Producing polymers with very strong cross-links so they last longer
Producing polymers such as PLA that can be broken down by microorganisms under composting conditions
Adding stabilisers to stop plastics breaking down in sunlight
Burning plastic waste to generate electricity
Biodegradable polymers break down into harmless products after use rather than persisting for centuries.
A chemical plant stores large quantities of a toxic, flammable solvent. Suggest two changes, based on green chemistry principles, that would reduce the risk of a serious accident.

Replace the solvent with a safer one such as water or supercritical CO₂ (safer solvents), and minimise the quantity stored by generating or ordering it as needed (inherently safer chemistry for accident prevention).
Any two valid changes linked to principles.

Explain why producing hydrogen from natural gas by steam reforming (CH₄ + H₂O → CO + 3H₂) is less consistent with green chemistry than producing hydrogen by electrolysis of water powered by solar energy.

Steam reforming uses a non-renewable fossil fuel feedstock, needs high temperatures (often from burning fossil fuels) and produces carbon monoxide/carbon dioxide. Solar-powered electrolysis uses a renewable energy source and water, and produces only oxygen as a by-product.
Compare feedstock, energy source and by-products.
chem-8-1-c1
Which change to an industrial process best follows the green chemistry principle of designing for energy efficiency?
Increasing the temperature to speed up the reaction
Adding an excess of one reactant
Using a catalyst that lets the reaction run at room temperature and pressure
Using a solvent that must be distilled off afterwards
Lower temperatures and pressures cut energy use. A catalyst is also preferred to stoichiometric reagents.
chem-8-2: chem-8-2-1
Atom economy is calculated as:
(actual mass of product ÷ theoretical mass of product) × 100
(mass of waste ÷ mass of desired product) × 100
(molar mass of desired product ÷ total molar mass of all reactants) × 100, using coefficients from the balanced equation
(moles of product ÷ moles of limiting reactant) × 100
Atom economy uses the balanced equation and measures the fraction of reactant mass ending up in the desired product.
chem-8-2-2
Ethanol can be made by fermentation: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂. Given M(C₆H₁₂O₆) = 180.0 g/mol and M(C₂H₅OH) = 46.0 g/mol, the atom economy for ethanol is:
AE = (2 × 46.0) ÷ 180.0 × 100 = 51.1%. 25.6% forgets the coefficient of 2; 48.9% is the CO₂ fraction.
chem-8-2-3
The atom economy for ethanol made by hydration of ethene, C₂H₄ + H₂O → C₂H₅OH, is:
Addition reactions have only one product, so all reactant atoms end up in ethanol: (46.0 ÷ (28.0 + 18.0)) × 100 = 100%.
chem-8-2-4
Chloromethane is made by CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl. Calculate the atom economy for chloromethane. M(CH₄) = 16.0, M(Cl₂) = 71.0, M(CH₃Cl) = 50.5 g/mol.
Use the balanced equation; total reactant mass in the denominator.
chem-8-2-5
Which type of reaction always has an atom economy of 100% for the single product formed?
Substitution reaction
Addition reaction
Condensation reaction
Elimination reaction
In an addition reaction all reactant atoms combine into one product; substitution, condensation and elimination all form by-products.
chem-8-2-6
Hydrogen can be produced by steam reforming: CH₄ + H₂O → CO + 3H₂. Using M(CH₄) = 16.0, M(H₂O) = 18.0 and M(H₂) = 2.0 g/mol, the atom economy for hydrogen is:
chem-8-2-7
Lime is made by heating limestone: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. Given M(CaCO₃) = 100.1 g/mol and M(CaO) = 56.1 g/mol, the atom economy for CaO is:
AE = 56.1 ÷ 100.1 × 100 = 56.0%; the remaining 44.0% of the mass is lost as CO₂.
chem-8-2-8

Aspirin can be made from salicylic acid (M = 138.0 g/mol) using either ethanoic anhydride (M = 102.0 g/mol, by-product ethanoic acid) or ethanoic acid (M = 60.0 g/mol, by-product water). M(aspirin) = 180.0 g/mol. Calculate the atom economy for each route and state which is greener on this basis.
With anhydride: 180.0 ÷ 240.0 × 100 = 75.0%. With ethanoic acid: 180.0 ÷ 198.0 × 100 = 90.9%. The ethanoic acid route has the higher atom economy.
Both calculations plus a conclusion. (In practice the acid route is slow and has low yield.)
chem-8-2-9
Iron is extracted in a blast furnace: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂. Given M(Fe₂O₃) = 159.6, M(CO) = 28.0 and M(Fe) = 55.8 g/mol, the atom economy for iron is:
Ethyl ethanoate is made by esterification: CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH → CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O. Given M(CH₃COOH) = 60.0, M(C₂H₅OH) = 46.0 and M(CH₃COOC₂H₅) = 88.0 g/mol, the atom economy for the ester is:

Chloroethane can be made by two routes. Route 1: C₂H₄ + HCl → C₂H₅Cl. Route 2: C₂H₆ + Cl₂ → C₂H₅Cl + HCl. Given M(C₂H₅Cl) = 64.5, M(C₂H₆) = 30.0 and M(Cl₂) = 71.0 g/mol, the atom economies of Routes 1 and 2 respectively are:
Explain why atom economy is described as a 'theoretical' measure while percentage yield is an 'experimental' measure.

Atom economy is calculated only from the balanced equation and molar masses, assuming complete reaction, so it shows the maximum fraction of reactant atoms that can end up in the product. Percentage yield compares the mass of product actually obtained with the theoretical maximum, so it requires experimental data.
Contrast equation-based vs measured.

Electrolysis of brine: 2NaCl + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂ + Cl₂. Given M(NaCl) = 58.5, M(H₂O) = 18.0, M(NaOH) = 40.0 and M(Cl₂) = 71.0 g/mol, the atom economy if both NaOH and Cl₂ are considered useful products is:
The atom economy for hydrogen produced by electrolysis of water, 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂, is:
AE = (2 × 2.0) ÷ (2 × 18.0) × 100 = 4.0 ÷ 36.0 × 100 = 11.1%; most of the mass ends up as oxygen.
Which change would increase the effective atom economy of a process?
Increasing the reaction temperature
Finding a use for, and selling, the by-product
Adding a catalyst
Increasing the pressure of gaseous reactants
If a by-product becomes a useful co-product, it is counted in the numerator, increasing effective atom economy; temperature, pressure and catalysts do not change the balanced equation.
Explain how selling the CO₂ produced in the fermentation of glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂) to the beverage industry affects the atom economy of the process.

If CO₂ is also a useful product, its mass is included in the numerator, so the effective atom economy rises from 51.1% (ethanol only) to 100%, because all the mass of the reactant ends up in useful products.
Show change from 51.1% to 100%.
Aspirin (M = 180.0 g/mol) is made from salicylic acid (M = 138.0 g/mol) and ethanoic anhydride (M = 102.0 g/mol), with ethanoic acid (M = 60.0 g/mol) as by-product. The atom economy for aspirin is:
Copper can be obtained by reducing copper(II) oxide with hydrogen: CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O. Given M(CuO) = 79.5, M(H₂) = 2.0 and M(Cu) = 63.5 g/mol, the atom economy for copper is:
Ethene can be made by dehydrating ethanol: C₂H₅OH → C₂H₄ + H₂O. Given M(C₂H₅OH) = 46.0 g/mol and M(C₂H₄) = 28.0 g/mol, the atom economy for ethene is:
AE = 28.0 ÷ 46.0 × 100 = 60.9%; water is the by-product of this elimination reaction.
Ethene can be made by dehydrating ethanol or by cracking ethane (C₂H₆ → C₂H₄ + H₂). Calculate the atom economy for ethene in the cracking reaction. M(C₂H₆) = 30.0, M(C₂H₄) = 28.0 g/mol.
Only one reactant, so the denominator is 30.0 g/mol.
Which statement about atom economy is correct?
Atom economy can be measured experimentally by weighing the product.
A reaction can have a high percentage yield but a low atom economy.
Atom economy depends on how much reactant is used.
Atom economy is always equal to percentage yield for a single-step reaction.
Atom economy is theoretical, from the balanced equation; yield is experimental. They are independent, so a high-yield reaction may still waste many atoms as by-products.
Methanol is produced industrially by CO + 2H₂ → CH₃OH. A student claims this reaction is 'perfectly green'. Which is the best response?
The student is correct because 100% atom economy means no environmental impact.
The student is wrong because the atom economy is only 50%.
Its atom economy is 100%, but its greenness also depends on the source of feedstocks and energy, e.g. syngas from natural gas.
The student is correct because methanol is a renewable fuel no matter how it is made.
Atom economy is only one measure; feedstock source, energy use, catalysts and conditions also matter.
Thermite reaction: Fe₂O₃ + 2Al → 2Fe + Al₂O₃. Given M(Fe₂O₃) = 159.6, M(Al) = 27.0 and M(Fe) = 55.8 g/mol, the atom economy for iron is:
Explain why addition polymerisation (e.g. making polyethene from ethene) has a higher atom economy than condensation polymerisation (e.g. making a polyester).

In addition polymerisation all monomer atoms are incorporated into the polymer, giving 100% atom economy. In condensation polymerisation a small molecule such as water is eliminated each time a link forms, so some reactant mass is lost as by-product and atom economy is less than 100%.
Identify the by-product in condensation.
Calculate the atom economy for sodium hydroxide alone in the electrolysis of brine: 2NaCl + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂ + Cl₂. M(NaCl) = 58.5, M(H₂O) = 18.0, M(NaOH) = 40.0 g/mol.
Coefficients must be included in both numerator and denominator.
chem-8-2-c1
Calculate the atom economy for making ethanol by fermentation, C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂, and compare it with making ethanol by hydration of ethene.
51.1% for fermentation; 100% for hydration
Atom economy = 2 × 46.0 ÷ 180.0 × 100 = 51.1%; the CO₂ is waste. Ethene + water → ethanol has a single product, so 100%.
chem-8-3: chem-8-3-1
Percentage yield is calculated as:
(actual mass of product ÷ theoretical mass of product) × 100
(molar mass of product ÷ molar mass of reactants) × 100
(theoretical mass of product ÷ actual mass of product) × 100
(mass of product ÷ total mass of reactants added) × 100
Percentage yield compares the mass actually obtained to the maximum possible from the limiting reactant.
chem-8-3-2
10.0 g of glucose is fermented: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂, producing 4.20 g of ethanol. M(glucose) = 180.0, M(ethanol) = 46.0 g/mol. The percentage yield is:
Theoretical: 10.0 ÷ 180.0 = 0.0556 mol glucose → 0.111 mol ethanol × 46.0 = 5.11 g. Yield = 4.20 ÷ 5.11 × 100 = 82.2%. 164% forgets the 2:1 ratio.
chem-8-3-3
In the Haber process, 28.0 kg of N₂ reacts with excess H₂ (N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃) and 5.10 kg of NH₃ is collected. M(N₂) = 28.0, M(NH₃) = 17.0 g/mol. The percentage yield is:
n(N₂) = 1000 mol → 2000 mol NH₃ theoretical = 34.0 kg. Yield = 5.10 ÷ 34.0 × 100 = 15.0%. 30.0% ignores the 1:2 ratio.
chem-8-3-4
A two-step synthesis has step yields of 85% and 60%. Calculate the overall yield and explain why reducing the number of steps in a synthesis is consistent with green chemistry.
Overall yield = 0.85 × 0.60 × 100 = 51%. Fewer steps means less product lost overall, fewer reagents and solvents used and less waste and energy consumed.
Correct multiplication plus a green chemistry link.
chem-8-3-5
6.00 g of ethanoic acid (M = 60.0 g/mol) reacts with excess ethanol, giving 5.72 g of ethyl ethanoate (M = 88.0 g/mol). The percentage yield is:
n(acid) = 0.100 mol → 0.100 mol ester = 8.80 g theoretical. Yield = 5.72 ÷ 8.80 × 100 = 65.0%. 83.0% is the atom economy.
chem-8-3-6
12.0 g of ethanoic acid (M = 60.0 g/mol) is mixed with 6.90 g of ethanol (M = 46.0 g/mol), and 9.90 g of ethyl ethanoate (M = 88.0 g/mol) is obtained. The percentage yield is:
n(acid) = 0.200 mol, n(ethanol) = 0.150 mol, so ethanol is limiting: theoretical = 0.150 × 88.0 = 13.2 g. Yield = 9.90 ÷ 13.2 × 100 = 75.0%. 56.3% wrongly uses the acid.
chem-8-3-7
A synthesis has three steps with yields of 90%, 80% and 70%. The overall percentage yield is:
Overall yield = 0.90 × 0.80 × 0.70 × 100 = 50.4%; step yields multiply rather than average.
chem-8-3-8
Give two reasons why the actual yield of an industrial reaction is usually less than the theoretical yield.

Any two of: the reaction reaches equilibrium and does not go to completion; side reactions form unwanted products; product is lost during separation and purification (e.g. filtration, distillation); reactants are impure.
Two distinct valid reasons.
chem-8-3-9
A student calculates a percentage yield of 108% for a crystallised product. The most likely reason is:
some product was lost during filtration.
the reaction did not go to completion.
the product was not fully dried and still contained solvent.
a side reaction produced a by-product.
A yield above 100% means the measured mass includes something other than pure product, such as water or impurities; the other options lower the yield.
Which factor would NOT cause a percentage yield below 100%?
Loss of product during transfer between containers
The reaction reaching equilibrium before completion
Competing side reactions forming other products
Recording the mass of a product that is still damp
Damp product adds mass and raises the apparent yield; the others reduce the amount of pure product collected.
50.0 g of CaCO₃ (M = 100.1 g/mol) is heated and 25.2 g of CaO (M = 56.1 g/mol) is collected. The percentage yield is:
Theoretical CaO = (50.0 ÷ 100.1) × 56.1 = 28.0 g. Yield = 25.2 ÷ 28.0 × 100 = 89.9%. 50.4% divides by the reactant mass.
Explain why a chemical engineer would aim to improve both the atom economy and the percentage yield of a process.

High atom economy means the reaction itself produces little by-product, while high yield means most of the possible product is actually obtained. Improving both minimises wasted raw materials and waste disposal, lowering cost and environmental impact.
Must distinguish the two and link to waste/cost.
2.76 g of salicylic acid (M = 138.0 g/mol) gives 2.70 g of aspirin (M = 180.0 g/mol). The 1:1 reaction ratio applies. The percentage yield is:
Methanol is produced by CO + 2H₂ → CH₃OH. 56.0 kg of CO (M = 28.0 g/mol) reacts with excess H₂, and 48.0 kg of CH₃OH (M = 32.0 g/mol) is produced. The percentage yield is:
n(CO) = 2000 mol → 2000 mol CH₃OH = 64.0 kg. Yield = 48.0 ÷ 64.0 × 100 = 75.0%. 85.7% is product mass divided by reactant mass.
A company needs 23.0 g of ethanol (M = 46.0 g/mol) from C₂H₄ + H₂O → C₂H₅OH, which has an 80.0% yield. The minimum mass of ethene (M = 28.0 g/mol) required is:
Theoretical ethanol needed = 23.0 ÷ 0.800 = 28.75 g = 0.625 mol, so ethene = 0.625 × 28.0 = 17.5 g. 14.0 g ignores the yield; 11.2 g multiplies by 0.8.

In an esterification, 0.250 mol of propanoic acid (M = 74.0 g/mol) reacts with excess methanol to form methyl propanoate (M = 88.0 g/mol). If 15.4 g of ester is collected, calculate the percentage yield.
1:1 mole ratio; use moles of the limiting reactant.
In the Contact process, 2SO₂ + O₂ → 2SO₃. 128.2 g of SO₂ (M = 64.1 g/mol) gives 155.4 g of SO₃ (M = 80.1 g/mol). The percentage yield is:
200 g of CaCO₃ (M = 100.1 g/mol) is decomposed with a 95.0% yield. The mass of CaO (M = 56.1 g/mol) obtained is closest to:
Theoretical CaO = (200 ÷ 100.1) × 56.1 = 112.1 g; × 0.950 = 106.5 g. 112 g ignores the yield; 118 g divides by 0.95.
How does a catalyst affect the percentage yield of an equilibrium reaction once equilibrium is reached?
It increases the equilibrium yield by shifting the equilibrium to the right.
It decreases the yield because it is consumed.
It does not change the equilibrium yield, but the maximum yield is reached in less time.
It increases the yield only for exothermic reactions.
Catalysts speed up forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium position, and therefore equilibrium yield, is unchanged.
Explain why unreacted N₂ and H₂ are recycled in the Haber process, referring to percentage yield.

Only about 15% conversion occurs in a single pass because the reaction reaches equilibrium. Recycling the unreacted gases back to the reactor means they eventually react, giving an overall yield of about 98% and reducing waste of feedstock.
Link single-pass equilibrium yield to overall yield.
For the exothermic reaction N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, which change increases the equilibrium yield of ammonia?
Adding an iron catalyst
Decreasing the pressure
Adding argon at constant volume
Lowering the temperature

Lowering temperature favours the exothermic forward reaction; a catalyst and an inert gas at constant volume do not shift the equilibrium; decreasing pressure favours the side with more gas particles (the reactants).
16.0 g of Fe₂O₃ (M = 159.6 g/mol) reacts with excess aluminium (Fe₂O₃ + 2Al → 2Fe + Al₂O₃), forming 9.50 g of iron (M = 55.8 g/mol). The percentage yield is closest to:
n(Fe₂O₃) = 0.100 mol → 0.200 mol Fe = 11.19 g. Yield = 9.50 ÷ 11.19 × 100 = 84.9%. 42.4% forgets the 1:2 ratio.
A reaction has a 100% atom economy but only a 40% percentage yield. Which statement is correct?
60% of the reactant atoms formed by-products according to the balanced equation.
In theory every reactant atom could end up in the product, but in practice only 40% of the maximum product mass was obtained.
The reaction must be an elimination reaction.
The reaction is fully green because atom economy is 100%.
100% atom economy means no by-products in the equation; a 40% yield reflects incomplete reaction, losses or side reactions in practice.
A student needs 5.00 g of aspirin (M = 180.0 g/mol). The reaction of salicylic acid (M = 138.0 g/mol) to aspirin is 1:1 and has a 70.0% yield. Calculate the mass of salicylic acid needed.
Theoretical aspirin needed = 5.00 ÷ 0.700 = 7.14 g = 0.0397 mol. Mass of salicylic acid = 0.0397 × 138.0 = 5.48 g.
Divide by the yield fraction before converting to moles.
Explain why a percentage yield greater than 100% indicates an experimental error, and give one possible cause.

Mass cannot be created, so the mass of pure product cannot exceed the theoretical maximum from the limiting reactant. A yield over 100% means the product contains extra mass, e.g. residual water/solvent from incomplete drying or impurities.
Conservation of mass plus a valid cause.
chem-8-3-c1
5.00 g of magnesium is added to 0.150 mol of HCl: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂. 0.0600 mol of H₂ is collected. Find the percentage yield.
n(Mg) = 0.206 mol, which needs 0.412 mol HCl, so HCl is limiting. Theoretical n(H₂) = 0.150 ÷ 2 = 0.0750 mol. Yield = 0.0600 ÷ 0.0750 = 80.0%.
chem-8-4: chem-8-4-1
Which statement best describes a circular economy?
An economy in which raw materials are extracted, made into products and disposed of after use
An economy that only uses products made from recycled materials
An economy in which materials are kept in use for as long as possible through reuse, repair, remanufacture and recycling, with waste designed out
An economy in which all waste is burned to generate electricity
A circular economy designs out waste and keeps resources circulating, in contrast to the linear 'take–make–dispose' model.
chem-8-4-2
A linear economy is best described as:
reduce, reuse, recycle
make, use, recycle, remake
design, use, repair, reuse
take, make, use, dispose
In a linear economy resources are extracted, made into products, used and then discarded as waste.
chem-8-4-3
Which of the following is the best example of a circular economy approach to PET drink bottles?
Collecting bottles through the Victorian container deposit scheme and reprocessing them into new food-grade bottles
Sending used bottles to landfill lined with clay
Making bottles thinner so they weigh less
Exporting used bottles to other countries
Collecting and reprocessing bottles into new bottles keeps the material in use and avoids waste.
chem-8-4-4
Explain the difference between a linear economy and a circular economy.

A linear economy follows a take–make–use–dispose model in which resources are extracted, made into products and discarded as waste. A circular economy designs out waste and keeps materials in use for as long as possible through reuse, repair and recycling, with materials recovered at the end of a product's life.
Must describe both models.
chem-8-4-5
Why is burning a plastic waste to generate electricity considered less circular than recycling it?
Burning produces no useful energy.
The material is permanently lost and the carbon is released as CO₂, so new raw materials are needed for future plastics.
Recycling releases more CO₂ than burning.
Burning plastic is not allowed anywhere in Australia.
Energy recovery captures some value, but the material leaves the economy, unlike recycling which retains it.
chem-8-4-6
Which property makes thermoplastics such as PET easier to recycle than thermosetting polymers?
They have strong covalent cross-links between chains.
They are biodegradable.
They soften on heating and can be remoulded, because there are only weak forces between chains and no cross-links.
They do not melt at any temperature.
Thermoplastics lack cross-links so they can be melted and reshaped; thermosets have covalent cross-links and char instead of melting.
chem-8-4-7
In chemical (feedstock) recycling of plastics, polymers are:
melted and remoulded into a new shape.
shredded and buried in landfill.
burned to generate electricity.
broken down into monomers or small molecules that can be used to make new polymers or chemicals.
Chemical recycling depolymerises or cracks polymers into feedstock molecules, allowing high-quality new materials.
chem-8-4-8
Give one advantage and one disadvantage of using bioethanol produced from sugar cane as a fuel in terms of sustainability.

Advantage: it is made from a renewable feedstock and is close to carbon neutral, since the CO₂ released on combustion was absorbed during plant growth. Disadvantage: growing sugar cane uses land, water and fertiliser that may compete with food crops, and processing (e.g. distillation) requires energy.
One valid advantage and one valid disadvantage.
chem-8-4-9
Which of the following is a sustainability benefit of producing biodiesel from canola oil compared with diesel from crude oil?
The carbon released on combustion was recently absorbed from the atmosphere by the canola plants, so net CO₂ emissions are lower.
Biodiesel releases no CO₂ when it burns.
Biodiesel has a higher energy content per kilogram than petrodiesel.
Growing canola requires no land or water.
Biofuels are close to carbon neutral over their life cycle, although farming, processing and transport still produce some emissions.
A concern about producing biofuels from food crops such as wheat or sugar cane is that:
